An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Additionally, the total branching fraction of the decay was determined to be (4.3±0.4±0.3) × 10^-5, which, when combined with the previous result for $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-K^-$, enabled a lower bound on the total $B^0_s$ decay width of ε_S + ε_B × 10^-5 to be set at 8.2 × 10^-5. Furthermore, with the help of around 36 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010, a more precise measurement of the total $B^0_s$ decay width into two mesons was made, specifically into the $\phi\eta$, $K^+K^-$, $K^0_KK^0_K$, and $K^0_SK^0_S$ channels, and was found to be (7.3±0.1±0.1) × 10^-4, providing the most accurate measurement to date. These results, when combined with existing information, have led to more precise constraints on the parameters ε_S and ε_B. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We also outline the importance of enhancing the sensitivity and precision of detectors like the Pierre Auger Observatory through upgrades such as an extended anisotropy study with the augmented dataset. Leveraging this improved understanding, we discuss potential research directions for future facilities like the Giant Auger Colony and the Effective Area Array, emphasizing the significance of investigating anisotropies at various energy scales. This work highlights the value of studying anisotropies in extremely energetic cosmic rays, holding clues to their fundamental origins and paving the way for a deeper comprehension of the universe's most energetic phenomena. The findings presented herewith contribute significantly to this goal, offering insights into cosmic ray source distributions and shedding light on magnetic field dynamics across vast cosmic distances. The extensions proposed for detectors like the Pierre Auger Observatory, capable of detecting anisotropies in extremely energetic cosmic rays, will likely reveal even more intricate patterns in future studies. This, in turn, will likely require a reconsideration of detection strategies as well as the development of more sophisticated statistical tools, all of which will play crucial roles in the ongoing quests to comprehend the origins of extremely energetic cosmic rays and the phenomena they emerge from. The extended dataset available to us provides a fitting moment to reassess the anisotropy research strategy for the upgraded version of the Pierre Auger Observatory, the Giant Auger Colony, and the Effective Area Array, considering potential configurations and their capabilities in this context. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further explore the benefits of federated learning, we also conducted an analysis of model variability and discovered that using a centralized approach results in models that are significantly more interrelated and mimicked the training process. This suggests that federated learning has potential advantages over centralized training in terms of model robustness and resistance to errors. To facilitate replication and advancement of our study, we are providing the software, data, and model resources online. However, our research also highlights the challenges associated with training deep learning models via federated learning, particularly when dealing with a large number of clients, all of which contribute small datasets. This limitation is evident in the substantial disparity that develops during the federated learning process, as some clients learn much more quickly than others and eventually surpass the rest in terms of model accuracy. To mitigate this, we experimented with different learning rate settings and reduced the gap to some extent; nonetheless, the disparity remained a persistent issue in our study. This challenge necessitates further exploration and development of more effective FL algorithms for training deep learning models.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've further introduced a strain on the TCN community by questioning the validity of widely accepted benchmarks due to inadequate challenge evaluation protocols. Our findings are reflected in our proposed TCN architectures which have demonstrated remarkable performance in time-series classification and regression tasks, surpassing existing state-of-the-art models. Our technique has been made available as an open-source library called EfficientTCN and can be accessed through our GitHub repository. It includes a simple and versatile Python API that enables users to easily create and integrate our pruning-based dilation optimization technique into their own projects. Our research and the accompanying code also address methodological concerns related to evaluation protocols and provide alternative models with optimal dilation factors to facilitate the comparison of methodological proposals. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. Moreover, our technique is applicable to a wide range of canonical modal logics, including their cluster-based logics and their duality-based counterparts. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/. Our code is available at https://github.com/yilundu/ndf. Our data is shared at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/data/. Videos of our results can be found at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/videos/.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. Building on this insight, my research aims to investigate various aspects of the archive's structure and development, as well as the implications of its topological properties for understanding and navigating the content. To achieve this, my plan includes developing a customized toolset that integrates existing solutions along with new approaches to visualize and analyze the archive, as evidenced by my companion paper presented at TP 2019. Within this thesis, I plan to delve deeper into specific techniques and their limitations, as well as explore future directions for improving navigation and comprehension of the Isabelle Archive based on ongoing developments. Furthermore, I intend to extend my research to encompass other notable formal proof repositories, such as Mizar Library and Coq Gallery, as well as investigate the potential links between the structure of these archives and the theoretical foundations of the theorem provers employed to develop those proofs. Ultimately, my research objectives prioritize enhancing accessibility, understanding, and the overall usability of formal proof archives over various repositories, as well as contributing to the advancement of the theorem proving community through collaborative efforts and shared goals. As a result, I plan to present my research to an audience with an interest in theorem proving and share my findings openly within the community. As my research has already yielded initial results, as mentioned earlier, my thesis will be completed once I have thoroughly explored and thoroughly evaluated my proposed solutions. As such, I anticipate my research to be completed within 12 months, as outlined in the following specific goals to be achieved within the indicated time frames: By the end of the first three months, I aim to develop a customized Isabelle toolset capable of navigating and analyzing the archive structure, as well as identifying key properties of the Isabelle Archive's topological characteristics. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our technique may be useful in investigating the ease with which various sampling algorithms solve certain inference problems. We showed that for a certain class of AMP algorithms, the occurrence of a locally convex region around the desired solution depends on the characteristics of the model's parameters and that this condition is at the boundary of an easy sampling regime. Consequently, this indicates that any algorithm requiring an exponentially large number of samples will likely face significant difficulties when attempting to solve these types of inference problems. We also established a more precise relationship between the ease of sampling and the characteristics of the models' parameters, and this understanding may be applied to various other models. Our results also provide a novel explanation for the phenomenon that when the models' parameters change slowly, the AMP algorithm tends to produce solutions that are close to the actual solutions. Lastly, we developed an alternative approach that enables us to estimate the performance of the AMP algorithm even when the models' parameters are not particularly amenable to analytical analysis. This new approach is an alternative to the current conventional method of evaluating the AMP algorithm, which relies heavily on the derivation of explicit expressions for the variables and the resulting message distributions. Instead, our alternative approach is based on the general principles of convexity and the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by the AMP algorithm. We believe that this new perspective may be applied to a broader range of optimization algorithms and models. We demonstrated the applicability of our method to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model by verifying that the locally convex region around the desired solution depends on the easy sampling regime for both of these models. Moreover, our method may be used to analyze the ease with which various sampling algorithms solve these types of inference problems. temporally, and linearly.  To tackle this intricacy, researchers need to employ a  
unified approach, integrating theoretical design and analysis methods, supported  
by an established framework.  Recent breakthroughs, facilitated by Generalized  
Sheet Transition Conditions in combination with surface susceptibilities,

challenges.  This paper delves into computational modeling of these complex  
structures through GSTC-susceptibility methodology and underscores its critical  
importance in the holistic design of metasurfaces, reviewing the evolution of  
recent frequency and time-domain computational methods.  A unified four-step  
design analysis can now be applied, starting with electromagnetic field  
formulation, followed by susceptibility determination, numerical modeling using  
GSTC, and finally, performance assessment.  This approach empowers metasurface  
researchers to explore novel applications, fueled by emerging computational  
technologies and simulation tools, allowing for a deeper understanding of the  
subject and new breakthroughs.  Future directions in this field may be shaped

encouraging collaboration and shaping the course of future discoveries.

This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. Our
 findings demonstrate the feasibility of this novel framework and its potential
to contribute to breakthroughs in our understanding of multi-electron atoms, with
key results including the development of highly accurate, element-specific and
sized-dependent electron correlation functions that rival those achieved through
extensive configuration interaction calculations. Furthermore, our study reveals that
eCPNN-based potentials may also facilitate access to rigorous electronic states
previously inaccessible due to the limitations of traditional numerical approaches.

Our analysis leverages a range of techniques: hierarchical clustering, a statistical test, and power spectrum analysis - each method providing unique insights, which together suggest the presence of a massive structure at around 4.5 to 4.8 sigma confidence levels. We employed multiple statistical tests to mitigate any biases that could influence our findings, which suggest that the arc-like feature is an overdensity with a density ratio of about 1.3, with a 30% margin of error. The Giant Arc represents one of the largest and most intriguing examples of a massive cosmic structure that could challenge the cosmological principle underpinning our current understanding of the universe. It may be an early stage in the formation of a massive structure, such as the Sloan Great Wall, which would have emerged around halfway through the universe's age. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code has been made publicly available.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting directions for enhanced understanding of fluid dynamics through peridynamics. Throughout this review, the fundamentals and associated numerical realizations of BB-PD have been highlighted, serving as a foundation for exploring potential applications and future developments in this field.

This problem was investigated and a new lens material called Stycast 1090SI was proposed as an alternative. The acoustic properties of this novel material were examined alongside PMMA to determine its feasibility. Computational simulations and practical tests using two different materials, PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, showed both materials significantly enhance the detection capabilities of sensitive devices. Notably, the Stycast lens exhibited lower levels of distortion compared to the PMMA lens, which could have implications for photoacoustic tomography technology. These findings suggest Stycast 1090SI has great potential as a lens material for photoacoustic imaging systems. However, both methods suffered from partial volume effects, causing a tendency to underestimate the height of objects. To address this limitation, a new numerical deblurring method was introduced and tested with both types of lenses, yielding more accurate height measurements. Both methods still showed some discrepancy, leading researchers to propose a more comprehensive study of lens materials. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through analyses of a dual-layer academic collaboration network and a multiplex network featuring online social media interactions. Our method is particularly useful for examining the diffusion processes and popularity growth dynamics in multilayered networks. It is also available as a highly configurable tool on our website.

We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. Visual comparisons also reveal that our method produces visually acceptable and sharper results compared to actual pictures. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

Finally, we outline possible pathways for further enhancing our prototype. 

Our research and technology demonstration are open-sourced at https://octopos.org.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results indicated that the FPG could find an optimal policy with minimal additional computational overhead compared to the clean PPG baseline. The code is available at https://github.com/hamsalek/robust_pgd. We also introduced an enhanced procedure for training robust policy evaluation agents, resulting in a nearly $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal achieved on a simple evaluation task. We highlighted the challenges of developing robust central policy evaluation methods due to the reliance of existing methods on access to the transition dynamics and the generation of diverse trajectories through offline reinforcement learning. We outlined the potential for future research in this area. We contributed a challenging MuJoCo dataset with hidden corruption patterns, encouraging the development of new central robust policy evaluation methods. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. By analyzing the crystal field and covalency factors, our results show that the shape of the molecular d-orbitals and their hybridization with oxygen neighbors significantly influence the orbital selectivity, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics behind cubanite's unique orbital behavior. Moreover, our data indicate the possibility of tuning the orbital selectivity through applied pressure or lattice changes, offering a promising pathway to explore the physics present in compounds like cuproskutridite.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. Furthermore, the system's behavior in the strong-coupling regime is described by a laid-out quantum acoustoelectrodynamics theory to demonstrate its potential to generate multiple-phonon states in a controllable and precise manner. Finally, the potential of this system to tackle fundamental challenges in quantum acoustic research is highlighted, including the development of multi-phonon states, precision measurement techniques, and communication systems, all while providing a foundation for future applications and contributing to the advancement of multi-phonon physics.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface. This study could contribute to the development of 2D electronic systems with tunable Dirac cones and thus offer suitable materials for constructing solid-state models of topological insulators and superconductors.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. Ultimately, this research resulted in the development of a real-time petrophysics service for a major service company. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. The code and models are publicly accessible for replication and further research. This holistic approach to NER also paves the way for applications involving multiple rounds of information exchange between entities, such as implicit entity recognition and entity value inference. Additionally, our algorithm serves as a foundational solution for addressing explicit and implicit entity relationships. We introduce a new benchmark, called the Implicit Entity Matrix (IEM), which provides challenges and standards for evaluating all the above-mentioned tasks. This new benchmark is designed to promote a deeper understanding of implicit entities and facilitate substantial progress in the study of explicit entities. It is publicly available for replication and further research along with the proposed holistic NER models. Our code and models can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/Holistic-NER and the IEM benchmark at https://github.com/ghrua/IEM-B. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of this algorithm under varying conditions of interference intensity. The designed location detection method is highly versatile and can be applied to a range of WPAN applications. It has already been utilised in the development of applications such as indoor positioning systems and automated visitor management systems. However, there are concerns over the potential risks of using data from physical location systems for re-identification purposes. To mitigate these risks, we are exploring methods of incorporating anonymous data feeds from location detection systems into their design. This approach could potentially enable location-based services that respect and protect user privacy. Two possible anonymous location detection schemes have been proposed and their security vulnerabilities assessed. The results suggest that these schemes may offer varying levels of anonymity depending on factors such as location measurement methodology and the distribution of locations. Further research is needed to determine the anonymity properties of these schemes and to explore other methods of location detection that prioritize privacy. The findings from our location detection work have been incorporated into an innovative location-based routing algorithm designed for energy efficient data transmission. The results from simulations and actual experiments have shown that this new approach produces outcomes comparable to existing methods while utilizing a significantly lower amount of energy. The discovery of node locations within a wireless sensor network also forms the basis of our investigation into the performance characteristics of the BACnP model. The study compares the energy consumption and flow rates of different nodes with known locations to each other and to the overall network, and presents data on factors such as energy consumption per step and path length. The analysis of these metrics in relation to each other has provided new insights into the behaviour and performance of BACnP protocols. The results from our location detection work have further enabled us to explore new applications in areas such as location based sensing, and the detection of nodes with varying levels of reliability. The extension of our location detection system to operate across multiple networks has also been achieved, and has led to the development of new routing algorithms that take into account the characteristics of each individual network.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By acknowledging the disparities in available data and the limited scope of current multilingual models, we aim to encourage more attention to be given to code-mixing within NLP. Our proposal outlines potential future directions, existing relevant datasets, and models for further research in this area. Ultimately, our goals are to stimulate more codemixing-focused research within NLP and to contribute to creating more inclusive models that cater to diverse language speakers. This work is the result of an overall examination of NLP applications for multilingual communities and is part of a larger set of findings presented at the MultiLingo Workshop 2021. The full presentation can be viewed on the ACM Digital Library under the title "Challenges and Future Scope of NLP for Multilingual Societies".

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. This study's findings provide a theoretical basis for using Ta$_2$O$_5$ in hadron therapy treatments of cancer. Additionally, the proposed method for determining energy loss could be applied to other oxide compounds that contain transition metals. To this end, the study has included a comparison of energy loss in Ta$_2$O$_5$ and silicon, two materials that could be used in radiotherapy applications. The research has also introduced a new concept, known as energy loss density, which is directly measurable and offers a more clear and concise representation of energy loss data. This approach has been applied to both Ta$_2$O$_5$ and silicon. The study has also considered the potential applications of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in enhanced gold nanoparticles for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To this end, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles to compare the features of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and gold in their respective bulk and nanoparticle forms. The study has demonstrated that both Ta$_2$O$_5$ and gold exhibit the necessary properties to effectively absorb hadrons, while also considering the potential effects of water on their functionality. Lastly, researchers have proposed future studies that could further investigate the energy loss of gold in hadrons.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, in places with low openness to new ideas, we observed increased circulation of both conservative and liberal ideologies, representing a stable component. In contrast, the movable components of conservatism and liberalism increased in areas with growing population centers and education levels. Our research offers a theoretical framework for understanding misinformation dissemination and suggests policy interventions that take into account the unique cultural and demographic characteristics of different regions. By addressing the underlying causes of misinformation dissemination at its source, we may be able to more effectively mitigate its circulation in society as a whole. We also explored potential policy interventions derived from our findings. We closed by highlighting the potential applications of this research to related issues, such as social media platform design and the re-election strategies of politicians. We believe our research lays the groundwork for a new area of study within the misinformation field, one that examines the influence of geographical and cultural factors on information dissemination. We further hope to contribute to the advancement of theoretical frameworks through the exploration of empirical evidence. We ended by expressing our hope that this study may spark further inquiry along these research lines. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code and data for this research are openly available, providing a valuable resource for researchers and organizations seeking to establish efficient, effective, and transparent detection systems. Furthermore, HALFADO's modular design allows for seamless integration into existing expert systems and machine learning frameworks. The algorithm's code has been optimized for execution on a single processor and is compatible with popular cloud services. The research highlights the potential of collaborative human computation and machine learning, paving the way for a broader adoption of combined approaches in the future. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. The code and data utilized in this research have been made publicly available.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings suggest that minor changes to the parameters can result in a sudden transition from cooperative to adversarial behavior, aligning with the framework's underlying principle of minimal, critical interventions. The development of a mobile agent that models and emulates this cooperative behavior is also presented, created using a simulation-based approach as the agent navigates its environment. The resulting autonomous agent is then put through a series of tests, and the outcomes show that it is capable of coexisting with its own counterparts, as well as human-directed movement, albeit with some limitations. However, the agent's inability to anticipate and respond to unforeseen events prevents it from persisting in the long term. Despite this, the agent's ability to emulate cooperative behavior in the short term is shown through collaborations facilitated by the Motivation Dynamics framework, and it is anticipated that this research may contribute to the development of novel, autonomous systems enabled by the integration of social knowledge and dynamics. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. With the most recent generation of weak lensing surveys, such as the Dark Energy Survey and future initiatives, the impact of galactic halos on weak lensing and the relationship between convergence and SN Ia residual diagrams will evolve significantly. Consequently, the methodology introduced here will require adjustment to significant changes in future analyses. Nonetheless, the methods presented in this work provide a foundation for a broader framework that can be applied to various current and forthcoming SN Ia dataset analyses. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we offer a simulation-based approach to understand the influence of layer thickness and depth within the SOI material on the performance of such photon-spin interfaces, providing valuable insights for the development of more refined systems. The ability to consistently create high-density T centers in the 220nm device layer of SOI wafers may pave the way for the creation of reliable, scalable, and compact quantum communication nodes based on silicon material. This advancement requires tight control over the production process to ensure a high success rate of T center creation, and we achieved this by developing a method to closely monitor the characteristics of the defect centers after each step of the fabrication process. The findings from our research also highlight the importance of further optimizing the ion implantation and heat treatment processes to increase the efficiency of reliable T center creation within the 220nm device layer of SOI wafers. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This new approach may also be applied to develop optimal line lists for other techniques used to analyse spectroscopic data sets. Lastly, we successfully recovered the signals from synthetic planets with masses ranging from 5 Earth masses and 11 Earth masses, both with semi-major axes between 0.5 and 2 astronomical units. This new approach is disclosed as an open-source code on GitHub, along with the line lists produced, which can be used for identifying planets in M dwarfs. Nevertheless, it is essential to carry out ground-based observations and gather data for an extended period to confirm the existence of planets detected through this method. This approach is particularly useful for time-critical TESS missions and future missions like PLATO. Moreover, it can also be applied to transit analysis by incorporating the line lists that minimize the stellar activity noise when analysing spectroscopic transit fits. This new approach may significantly enhance the scientific output of current and future photometric and spectroscopic surveys of low-mass stars such as M dwarfs. This research is a fundamental step towards successfully detecting exoplanets in these stars. It is also an essential technology for missions like the Exoplanet Field Unit of the ELT, which will be capable of detecting planets in low-mass stars if the telescope is placed at the Cassini site. This location will allow the telescope to study the planet(s) in the Kepler field and potentially those in the habitable zone of M dwarfs like AD Leo and DS Leo.

This research paper proposes a pair of methods for designing a flexible and efficient data collection process in Wireless Sensor Networks, ensuring high reliability and performance. Firstly, a link quality estimation technique is utilized, enabling swift computation of link quality between nodes. Secondly, a hierarchical sector-based system is established to organize and coordinate nodes within each sector to minimize interference and improve data transmission. The effectiveness of these methods was demonstrated through a protocol, called HBCP, developed and evaluated in a simulated environment utilizing TinyOS and TelosB devices. The outcome of the evaluation revealed that HBCP can achieve very high reliability levels, particularly in large-scale networks and networks prone to bottlenecks. The reliability of HBCP also exhibits a significantly slower downtime rate compared to standard BACDP protocols. The study further showed that HBCP's fast link quality estimation enables it to adapt to changing environments and effectively minimize interference. The results from the evaluation also indicated that HBCP's sector-based hierarchy reduces the average number of hops required for data collection, thus enhancing its reliability and performance. The protocol's downtime and downtime rate were found to be inversely correlated with the number of nodes, and its reliability and performance were found to be beneficial in large-scale networks. The research also discovered a phenomenon dubbed the "algebraic property of reliability", where the reliability of the network is the result of the reliability of its links raised to the power of the number of hops. The study evaluated HBCP's performance in scenarios ranging from 8 to 128 nodes, and the results from these experiments were found to be algebraically consistent. The research provides the basis for further development of data collection protocols utilizing link quality estimation techniques and hierarchical organizations. The HBCP code is available for download and can be utilized as a reference for comparing new protocols. The research also highlights several potential areas for the development of new protocols, such as the potential benefits of triangular configurations and the potential drawbacks of hierarchical structures. The research also highlights several potential applications for protocols like HBCP, such as environmental monitoring systems that rely on Wireless Sensor Networks. The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions. Furthermore, we are able to demonstrate the existence of an embedding from a specific type of Kirchhoff type system to a specific type of Trudinger type space, and show that this embedding is compact when the distance between the system's solutions is big enough. With this, we are able to prove the existence of an odd solution for the system when a certain condition is satisfied, and this solution minimizes an associated functional that contains the Kirchhoff type nonlinearity, the Trudinger type nonlinearity, and an external term that belongs to the dual space of the Sobolev space. Finally, we are able to establish a minimum problem for an energy functional that contains the Kirchhoff type nonlinearity, the Trudinger type nonlinearity, and an external term that belongs to the dual space of the Sobolev space, and this minimum problem has a solution that can be obtained through a direct method. Notably, this solution space fails to be compact when the distance between the solution and the external term is not big enough. With this, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for the solution to be compact, and show that these conditions are related to the non-differentiable term that belongs to the dual space of the Sobolez space.

Utilizing this approach, we successfully obtained the associated momentum transformation, which preserves the four-dimensional relationship between momentum and space, p_{\mu} x^{\mu}.  With the deformed algebra in hand, we derive the first Casimir invariant in this paper.  Following first quantization, we utilize the Klein-Gordon equation to show that Fock's spacetime corresponds to the de Sitter universe, whose spacetime radius can be defined by the invariant length representing the de Sitter hypersurface.  Most significantly, we demonstrate that, when considering the specific DESR transformation, the value of this radius is equal to the Planck length, providing further support for the idea that the de Sitter universe of a certain radius can be regarded as the minimum unit of measurement in the context of General Relativity.  This is analogous to the concept of the minimum unit of measurement in Special Relativity, which is the length of the straggling particle, representing the intersection of worldlines for particles and observers, and is equal to the Schwarzschild radius of a particle, indicating that, in GR, the ratio of this radius to the Planck length is equal to the fine structure constant of GR. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, we examine how patient preferences for surgery versus continued dialysis affect the optimal policy, and present an analytical solution for stationary policies in a special case. Finally, we discuss the relevance of our findings to current clinical practices.

Implicit copulas are the primary choice for analyzing dependencies in complex scenarios due to their ability to effectively model dependence in high-dimensional spaces. The text presents a comprehensive overview of this broad category, encompassing copulas such as elliptical, skew t, factor, time series, and regression copulas, highlighting their key characteristics and applications. The discussion explains how the auxiliary representation of implicit copulas facilitates scalability and usability in statistical modeling, addressing concerns like parameter estimation, likelihood calculation, and model parsimony. The text also covers Bayesian estimation techniques for implicit copulas and the benefits of employing these models in conjunction with time series and regression models, which are the subject of current research advancements. The advantages of using implicit copulas are further illustrated through the examination of econometric applications, including analyses of macroeconomic time series and financial asset pricing. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this, we propose a new approach based on a highly structured statistical model, combining the capabilities of hidden Markov models and mixed effects models, which effectively separates the two components and facilitates the interpretation of both the word distributions and the underlying processes driving their co-occurrence. Our method outperforms the word2vec model across the board, both in our synthetic and actual financial corpus scenarios. Our research offers a rigorous examination of the capabilities and limitations of the word2vec model, providing a theoretical and empirical foundation for a broader discussion on the generation and application of natural language processing embeddings. We believe that our results and associated data can serve as a starting point for various related investigations. We welcome these discussions and the opportunity to collaborate. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. The algorithms developed in this research have been successfully evaluated against strong baselines in a range of multiagent learning scenarios. In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, this geometric relationship implies that the soliton is extremal, and this extreme property is uniquely achieved when the potential vector field is in direct alignment with the Reeb vector field. Additionally, this research reveals that on Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with certain differential conditions met, a gradient Cotton soliton arises, proving this to be the first known instance of a non-extremal Cotton soliton within complex Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. A further exploration into this topic compares the manifold in question to the space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}(\lambda)$, establishing that a $\lambda$-steady Cotton soliton emerges when the potential vector field is set to $\lambda$ times the Reeb vector field, with $\lambda$ being any real number. A particular case is identified where this soliton evolves from a $\lambda$-potential into a $\lambda$-steady soliton, demonstrating the equivalence of this process to the space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}(\lambda)$. A key finding within this research reveals that a $\lambda$-steady (gradient) Cotton soliton is the only possible case for a (steady) Cotton soliton to exist within complex (almost) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. This motivation leads to the development of JAX-DISK, a computational framework designed to facilitate the integration of theoretical predictions entering PDF fitting campaigns, and it is available at https://github.com/scicarb/jax-disk. A detailed description of the framework's architecture and key features can be found in the attached documentation at https://scicarb.github.io/jax_disk_documentation/. A central component of this project has been contributed to the HEPFit framework, a leading tool for combining experimental and theoretical constraints in PDF fits, and it has been successfully integrated into the NNPDF framework through the NNPDF-PDW project. As part of this project, a novel implementation of the DGLAP evolution equations in JAX has also been developed, leading to significant performance enhancements. A set of evolved PDF candidates derived from this framework has been made publicly accessible at https://ndpf.hep.anl.gov/data/. A discussion of the method's numerical benefits is presented in the accompanying paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01635. This work has been presented at the 2022 PDF evolution workshop and the 2022 Loopy Doopy workshop. We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the slow-recovering component directly correlates with the electronic conductivity in all measured thicknesses, as does the fast-recovering component in thinner samples. Notably, in thicker samples, we observe a significant increase in the electronic conductivity that is not accounted for by the spin-lattice relaxation data, suggesting the presence of a two-band scenario. This analysis is further supported by a Monte Carlo simulation that simulates our measured data and offers a theoretical framework for understanding the measured results. Our study provides clear evidence of a wide-range, metallic state in LaNiO$_3$ and offers a theoretical framework for understanding the correlated metallic state in other doped perovskites. This framework is expected to guide and stimulate ongoing and future research in this field. Our study is also an example of the capability of $\beta$-detected NMR to investigate the correlated metallic state in other doped perovskites, such as LaMnO$_3$ and CaCuO$_2$.
