The unexplored nature of ultra-high energy photons and limitations of existing methods in identifying them prompt research on new approaches to simulation and observational strategies. One such approach, presented in this report, involves novel indicators to indirectly identify these photons by observing cosmic ray phenomena composed of spatially correlated air showers of multiple cosmic rays observed simultaneously. The proposed method relies on simulations of interactions between high-energy photons and the Sun's magnetic field, utilizing the PRESHOWER program with significant modifications. The expected outcome of these interactions includes the creation of cosmic ray ensembles consisting of extremely narrow and elongated cascades of secondary photons spanning the full cosmic ray energy spectrum. When entering the Earth's atmosphere, these cascades or their components might generate distinct walls of spatially correlated air showers, which could also occur even if the primary photons are not directed towards Earth. Furthermore, it is anticipated that the particle distributions within these multi-photon footprints will possess thicknesses of up to meters and extensions of up to hundreds of millions of kilometers, rendering them potentially observable with a collaborative global approach, incorporating re-evaluation of historical data and exceeding the capacity of even the largest cosmic ray observatories. The methods described in this report enable the simulation of observable quantities related to CRE caused by ultra-high energy photons, such as densities, energy spectra, and particle orientation at the top of the Earth's atmosphere. In addition, the expected walls of air showers can be simulated in relation to observer location, orientation, and altitude, as well as the characteristics of secondary neutrons at the entrance to the atmosphere. The implementation of these methods results in highly detailed outputs that can be employed in further analysis, such as estimating detection probabilities with respect to observable quantities and creating visual representations of predicted wall shapes in anticipation of CRE observations. The approach outlined in this report may also be applied to alternative sources of CRE, such as the study of cosmic ray phenomena induced by magnetic fields of other stars. The findings of the modifications made to the PRESHOWER program, the expected characteristics of CRE caused by ultra-high energy photons, and the anticipated walls of air showers in relation to observer location, orientation, and altitude are the subject of further research and have potential implications for the discovery of ultra-high energy photons. The simulation methods described in this report have been verified by comparing its modified version with respect to the original PRESHOWER program and have been made publicly available as part of the RESEARCH program, which includes a documentation consisting of more than three thousand pages in line with the standards of the CERN Software Initiative. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. The framework consists of three primary components: (1) conflict resolution, (2) point operations, and (3) batch operations, providing a modular structure for creating new CRDTs. By integrating RWF with the Gelly parallel processing framework, a Gelly-RWF was developed, enabling it to handle up to 1,000,000 conflicts per second on a single CPU core. The framework's scalability and performance make it suitable for large-scale, distributed systems. Furthermore, RWF can be applied to develop new replicated data types and is available open-source under the Apache 2 license. The framework's website, along with its GitHub repository and documentation, are available at https://redis.io/designing-crds. The ultimate goal of the RWF is to encourage the creation of new CRDTs, democratizing their development through a design framework that is both easy to use and adaptable across various data types. The initial implementations of Counter, Multiset, and Sorted Set CRDTs, along with their performance, are included in the article's appendix. The RWF has the potential to contribute significantly to the further development and widespread adoption of Conflict-free Replicated Data Types. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. For example, amongst the most confident 10% of SNPs associated with blood, 37% are located within repressed genomic regions, in contrast with 13% within accessible regions, in accordance with the principle of tendminclature, where "we find that the enrichment of SNPs is often reversed when comparing the total association across all protein-coding genes, with a ratio ranging from 2 to 50, in comparison with cell-type specific analyses". Our study aims to provide results that can be used in the research of specific diseases, in addition to providing general guidelines for the interpretation of genomic findings. Our study has resulted in several notable observations, such as a significant number of associated SNPs being located within coding regions that encode nuclear receptors, transcription factors and G protein-coupled receptors, which are known to modulate responses to environmental changes, metabolism and digestion, respectively. Moreover, we have identified several genomic elements that could influence the development of certain diseases and cancers, such as enhancers next to the PAX5 gene in B cells, in addition to several coding and non-coding elements that contribute to the difference in height between males and females. Our study has also enabled the prioritization of associated SNPs, resulting in a 5 percent increase in confidence for a substantial portion of associated SNPs, with blood being an example, where 37% of the most confident 10% of associated SNPs are located within repressed genomic regions, in contrast with 13% within accessible regions. We have provided detailed results for each trait and disease of interest

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. As a result, the authors argue that the presence of black holes in the Galactic center is not supported and the vast majority of the variable X-ray sources in the center are actually neutron stars or white dwarfs. The study also highlights the significance of spectroscopic observations to determine the primary component's mass in X-ray binaries, which is critical in distinguishing between black holes and neutron stars. By doing so, the authors hope to motivate a range of observations and analyses that can identify the primary component's mass in X-ray binaries, particularly those with radio-emitting neutron star components, which could help confirm or refute the findings presented here. Finally, to facilitate such efforts, the authors introduce a website that aggregates various observations and presents them in a way that is useful for theoretical models. The website enables the visualization of light curves, spectra, and radial velocities, as well as the inclusion of new observations, which can be accessed through an open source data base at the CDS. The website is also available at http://www.phys.univ-reims.fr/~jhermanne/xc website/. By considering the properties of LMXBs and their outbursts, as well as radio pulsar binaries, the authors anticipate that future observations will make it possible to estimate the population ratio of black holes to white dwarfs or neutron stars in the Galactic center, which is the main objective of this study. The authors further anticipate that such estimates will significantly evolve with the addition of new outburbs and radial velocity measurements. The website is designed to facilitate this evolution by providing a dynamic perspective on the issue. The authors hope that by presenting their case in this way, they will motivate a range of observations and analyses

The velocity distribution pattern of distant binary star systems can be an effective means of determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates, typically found on the outskirts of galaxies. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach can be utilized by analyzing the star systems' velocity in the plane orthogonal to their collective movement across the sky. 

Using the sample of wide binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019) and considering effects from large angles, simulations indicate a relatively low uncertainty of around 30 meters per second in velocity measurements when line velocities are taken into account, rather than projected sky velocities with an uncertainty of around 100 meters per second.

However, analysis based on using the line velocity method, with additional steps to eliminate potential anomalies by identifying and discarding 2 times standard deviations from the mean, reveals that no distinct deviation from Newton's gravitational law exists at a radius of around 10,000 astronomical units. 

Due to the relatively low uncertainty in velocity measurements, existing wide binary star data have nearly sufficient accuracy to differentiate between the principles of Newton's gravitational law and the Modified Newtonian Dynamics model using the line velocity approach. In contrast, to make the same distinction with projected sky velocities, data for around one thousand additional wide binary systems will be needed.

Furthermore, to accurately determine how gravitational forces work in this context, potential sources of systematic error must also be accounted for, including any hidden or unobserved companion stars within these wide binary systems and possible moving groups within these star systems, with control being achieved statistically by narrowing down and considering specific and scientifically supported parameters for these star systems and evaluating the theoretical models against their predictions. 

In addition, suggestions are made for identifying candidate wide binary star systems that have been incorrectly classified as single star systems due to a lack of depth in existing observations, with examples including the case of Eclipsing Binary HD 10909 and Wide Binary HD 215443, and steps are proposed for verifying these new potential wide binary star systems through follow-up observations, including estimating the mass of the companion star, determining the binary system's overall mass, and verifying the star systems' characteristics through comparisons with similar wide binary star systems sharing the same age, metal content, and location. 

Finally, predictions are made regarding the discovery of additional wide binary star systems with a velocity greater than around 3000 kilometers per second, specifically citing the case of a binary star system consisting of a white dwarf and a main-sequence star located at a distance of around 10,000 parsecs

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization. The research provides necessary corrections for statistical analyses of large radio sources and has relevant implications for CMB polarization measurements. Furthermore, it opens up possibilities for using radio sources as magnetic field probes. A statistical model is proposed to account for the observed polarization characteristics. The model includes factors such as the core fractional polarization, the extended fractional polarization influenced by the source size and its surroundings, and an extrinsic component related to the source's low-frequency spectrum. By applying this model to a large radio source sample, its accuracy is demonstrated. The model also expands on previous research analyzing the polarization-statistics relationship with source size only. The study also presents a method for generating mock radio source catalogs, which can be utilized in conjunction with radio surveys and CMB maps to conduct realistic experiments and predictions. By applying this approach to a radio source catalog and a realistic CMB foreground model, the effectiveness of future CMB experiments such as COBE-S4 and Stage-IV in measuring the CMB polarization power spectrum is assessed. The results indicate a significant impact of radio sources on these experiments' measurements, particularly in regions with significant foreground contamination. Therefore, considering the effects of radio sources or their magnetic fields on the CMB polarization is essential. Finally, the study examines the relationship between the largest linear scale structure in radio sources and their polarization, finding a weaker correlation, which may provide insight into the sources' physics. The research concludes with possibilities for further analyzing the statistical properties of radio sources and their potential applications in CMB experiments. The analysis and models developed here can be used in future studies and potentially applied to other radio source samples. The code employed to analyze the data and generate the models is available online for customization and further development. The study paves the way for a deeper understanding of the relationships between radio sources' polarization, their characteristics, and their environments, which can lead to new insights into the physics of these objects and their impact on the CMB. $\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview. Building on the foundational concepts learned by readers, we establish to an intuitive level key $\tau$-tilting principles, including the classification of $\tau$-tilting modules for finite-dimensional algebras and the relationship between $\tau$-tilting modules and the Auslander-Reiten translation. Finally, we explore in depth the interplay between $\tau$-tilting modules and the Serre-Dietrich-Auslander-Ring theorem. Along the way, we include examples and proofs for various key results to illustrate the underlying principles and demonstrate the application of $\tau$-tilting theory to representational geometry. Specifically, we establish the classification of $\tau$-tilting modules for tilted algebras of Euclidean and hyperbolic Dynkin diagrams, and in doing so, we establish the relationship between $\tau$-tilting modules and the AR-quivers of these algebras. This expertise is used to analyze the representation dimension of these algebras, leading to a new proof of the classification of representation dimensions for tilted algebras first established by Holm and Jorgensen. These notes are concluded by exploring $\tau$-tilting modules in the context of Calabi-Yau algebras, building on work by Denham, Gray, and Walker. Throughout these notes, the underlying principles of $\tau$-tilting theory are reinforced through various examples and proofs from the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras, including preprojective algebras of finite Dynkin diagrams and tilted algebras derived from them. The comprehensive overview of key results from the field is accompanied by new contributions to the field, making these notes a valuable resource for both newcomers to the field and established experts in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. It was also found that this method may trade off coherence for diversity and that there are certain settings more amenable to diversity than others. Ultimately, this research' findings are highly relevant to the development of neural conversational agents and can direct the design of new evaluation methods assess models' semantic variety. The code and data utilized in this research are available at this link https://github.com/ghrua/Conversational-Lang-Understanding-assessment. Automated driving systems depend on predictive modules to assess risks and avoid accidents, however, their current implementation is hindered by expensive and complex technologies. A novel artificial intelligence approach has been developed for classifying high-risk maneuvers from a single camera, using pre-trained image processing algorithms to improve performance and efficiency. This advanced system utilizes deep learning and temporal sequence analysis to recognize patterns of behavior from a dataset with annotated risk indicators, and was optimized using various feature extractors for maximum effectiveness, ultimately achieving a 0.937 AUC score. The system's accuracy was validated in real-world scenarios through automated testing and data refinement, increasing its AUC score to 0.983. The implementation of this technology using a single camera demonstrates the potential for wide-scale adoption of automated driving systems.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. Both scenarios showed the occurrence of hydrogen burning at temperatures between 3.5 x 10^5 K and 3.75 x 10^5 K. However, the possibility of hydrogen burning was limited to about 10^8 years due to spin-down. such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for calculating efficiency and background probability and discuss the application 
of two techniques specifically density estimation using Gaussian processes and

new applications for these models, such as leveraging sidebands to determine the 
density of background in multiple dimensions, as well as more comprehensive density

of background subtraction and efficiency correction in hadron decay analyses. The 
proposed ideas have been validated on real-life data sets obtained from the Belle

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components. This model's ability to fit observed data is demonstrated through a case study of the Gamma-Ray Burst GRB 190819B's fireball, and it reveals that the high-energy phenomenon can be explained by the intersection of two dynamic radiative phases, one of which is characterized by the expansion of the fireball and the other by its cooling down. The new model also facilitates the interpretation of several observational features, such as the spectral energy distribution, the light curve's double-peaked structure, and the absence of spectral breaks in certain intervals. Furthermore, it generates unique predictions, such as the presence of a spectral break in the observer frame and the possibility of detecting early relativistic phases through high-energy space telescopes. This model's capabilities can be further explored through future research, including studies of multi-wavelength observations and comparisons with kinetic energy ejections from white dwarfs. This novel model offers a new perspective on the interpretation of various fireball phenomena, such as supernovae, Gamma-Ray Bursts, and others. It also highlights the significance of distinguishing between radiative and adiabatic components in order to gain a deeper understanding of these cosmic events. This model is applicable to various radiative afterglows, making it a valuable tool for analyzing a wide range of fireball radiations. This research is a part of S. A. V.'s thesis, supervised by G. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. This study investigates the issue of determining the minimum number of nodes to split (if any) to create an edge-free visualization, and a corresponding algorithm has been developed for this purpose, its performance being evaluated through practical applications of the developed method. The algorithm developed has been tested against established methods, yielding improved results in terms of the number of nodes to split, and its underlying technique has implications for further research in the visualization domain. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of learning incrementally from datasets with significant imbalances persists, a common issue that arises frequently. For instance, a robot that learns from interactions with a variety of objects with vastly different frequencies would face this challenge. Existing methods, which primarily focus on addressing the challenge through data augmentation or generating synthetic data, are often limited by their high computational requirements and the necessity for labeled data. This paper introduces an innovative method for incremental learning on unbalanced datasets without the need for additional data processing. We employ a unique network architecture that incorporates feature sharing and category-specific activations to address the challenge. The proposed method is then applied to a scenario involving a robot that learns from interactions with a variety of objects with vastly different frequencies. Comparative evaluations against current methods, which can learn from data in a non-incremental manner, reveal that our approach delivers superior performance across multiple scenarios. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. The effectiveness of our approach will be illustrated through a simulation involving the Biped2 robot. Full details of our method can be found in the paper's main section. The code used in this research is available online at https://github.com/ashfaktor/thruster-assisted-gait-control. The associated dataset has been uploaded to https://data.tamu.edu/ashfaktor/thraser-assisted-gait-control-dataset.html. The research paper has been submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology and is currently under review. Consequently, the paper remains unpublished and its current version is considered a preprint. The researchers whose work influenced our own have been appropriately cited within the paper's text. The study presented was conducted with _Modeling, Analysis and Design for Hybrid Systems_ by J. Lygeros et al. in mind. The proposed method may not yield optimal results but rather serves as a starting point for further optimization-based control techniques. The major advantages of our approach on the swimming biped robot include the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during specific phases of the gait cycle and the successful implementation of performance-related constraints during the single-support phase. The latter achievement was made possible by the unique properties of the thrusters. In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, showcasing its versatility in side-channel amplification scenarios.  In terms of implementation, a Python-based framework was introduced, which in addition to a new technique, also included existing methods and provided a framework for easy integration of performance degradation techniques in side-channel attacks.  As for the evaluation, FairBlueNoise generator was employed to conduct a blue noise analysis, which resulted in recognized spectra across multiple metrics, contributing to a recognized understanding of FairBlueNoise's characteristics.  Moreover, distanced metrics were used to assess the similarity between distributions, which led to the identification of distinct slowdown distributions in HyperDegrade's baseline and varied scenarios, as well as the differentiation between various traffic patterns.  With regards to attack efficacy, HyperDegrade-enabled attacks were compared to attack scenarios employing only natural traffic, which resulted in demonstrated success rates of 100% in both HyperDegrade-enabled attacks, whereas attacks utilizing only natural traffic failed at least once in all cases. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite basis consisting of $deg(K)+1$ elements, where $K$ is the tropical curve in question. Additionally, for finite fields $k$, we establish that the tropical curve semifield defines a non-abelian finite simple group when $k$ contains more than one element. Furthermore, we show that using addition and maximum, the semifield of real numbers can be represented in a highly non-transitive manner. We also explore the finite field analogue of this phenomenon. Lastly, we outline a method to determine all elements of a specific tropical curve semifield through its minimal polynomial and that of its inverse. This approach is applied to demonstrate that the tropical curve semifield defined over a finite field is its own Galois counterpart. We also establish an analytical connection between this finite field semifield and its elliptic curve counterpart. We conclude by reviewing an unproved hypothesis stating that the tropical curve semifield has a finite basis consisting of $deg(K)+1$ elements, where $K$ is the tropical curve in question. This hypothesis is applicable to a broader category of algebraic varieties known as horofields. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to a greater understanding of tropical geometry and its connection to its algebraic and algebraic counterparts. This research is also intended to address fundamental questions regarding tropical semifields and their algebraic counterparts, including the rational function semifield of algebraic curves and their finite field counterparts. Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. These advancements represent significant progress in the development of machine learning models capable of effectively using the entire instructional manual when performing a task. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. The proposed BigApple parameter set can be utilized in researching the properties of finite nuclei and neutron star candidates, such as GW190814's secondary component. The BigApple force is also applicable to investigating the properties of hyperonic nuclei and neutron stars. The study's findings also highlight the potential of the BigApple force in further exploring the properties of finite nuclei and neutron star candidates, such as GW190814's secondary component. Despite initial intuition that a simple 3-band d-only model would suffice, our study shows that this assumption can lead to inaccuracies. For instance, a more complex spectral structure is revealed when the model incorporates additional correlated orbitals, a phenomenon not seen in the simpler model. Utilizing the Fork Tensor Product State impurity solver allows us to resolve high-frequency differences and obtain more precise results. Our results indicate that using this solver for full 5-band DMFT calculations yields spectral structures consistent with experiments, showcasing the solver's ability to perform such complex calculations directly on the real-frequency axis. This capability makes it an invaluable tool for furthering our understanding of correlated materials like SrMnO$_3$. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the importance of choosing optimal Wannier functions for correlated materials by performing a sensitivity analysis, demonstrating how variations in bandwidth, orbital composition, and relative energies can significantly impact the material's spectral structure. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we've found that titanium in barium titanate maintains an unexpected position within its molecular structure even when it's not polarized. This finding challenges the common assumption used to model this phase. To address this discrepancy, we performed a thorough analysis of the symmetries at play and created a series of more accurate, detailed models that capture the underlying structure of the material. From these, we identified the smallest models that are stable and consistent with experimental data; two of these models can also be applied to similar materials. These discoveries open up possibilities for using computational modeling to design more effective materials. Additionally, we've determined that certain characteristics in barium titanate, such as the movement of certain atoms and the vibration of the molecular structure, can be controlled through changes to the volume of the material, and further that these changes are influenced by the presence of certain other atoms. These findings could also be applicable to a wide range of materials and situations. Finally, we compared our methods to other approaches used to model this phase and found them to be reliable and precise.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes. Our research was presented at the 2022 Conference of the International Association for Computing Machinery on Madical Advances in Computational Linguistics.

We've developed families of three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric terminal Fano varieties of considerable depth, corresponding to 54 distinct mutation classes in the realm of Laurent polynomials. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 46 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as toric complete intersections and others as Pfaffian varieties. Furthermore, we've proved the existence of $\mathbb{Q}$-Gale groups for all 46 varieties, enabling us to determine their birational orbits and Betti numbers. Consequently, our findings expand the current understanding of $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds, addressing various open questions and confirming several conjectures. Moreover, we propose further questions related to the complexity of non-toric $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds. As a separate component, we've constructed 18 families of $\mathbb{Q}$-Gale groups for Fano Del Pezzo surfaces, leading to the creation of 18 non-toric $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano surfaces thus far. Among these, depth values range between 6 and 15. As a result, all $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano surfaces have been accounted for, confirming the Fano 3D base conjecture first proposed by Li. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets demonstrates substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. As a solution, we propose incorporating risk preferences into unit commitment algorithms, which would enable a more precise management of storage units' risk behavior. Through simulation, we demonstrate the potential benefits of this approach in the Australian market. Furthermore, our research offers a theoretical framework applicable to other markets that incorporate price uncertainty into their scheduling processes. The proposed method also discloses storage units' willingness to take on risk, which could be a valuable parameter for grid operators seeking to encourage desirable risk-taking behavior during energy auctions. Overall, our work highlights the significance of considering storage units' risk aversion in future power grid management practices. Additionally, it highlights the value of unit-specific risk parameters that could be derived from historical data, leading to more effective scheduling strategies that better balance cost and risk factors. This, in turn, may necessitate a review of current grid management practices that often prioritize short-term cost savings over more far-reaching benefits. As a result, our work is expected to contribute positively to the development of future low-carbon power grids. It is our belief that the challenges associated with the integration of storage units can be overcome by developing a deeper understanding of their operational characteristics and behaviors. This understanding is critical for enabling the optimal integration of these units into grid management algorithms, ultimately ensuring the greatest possible value from their operational capabilities. This concept is exemplified through our proposed self-scheduling approach, which provides a theoretical framework for this understanding and is applicable to a broad range of energy storage technologies. As the cost of energy storage continues to decline globally, the need for a deeper understanding of storage units' operational characteristics and behaviors will only increase. Consequently, this research is expected to be even more relevant in the future as the world transition to low-carbon power grids accelerates, and storage units play an increasingly crucial role within them

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds. These findings have implications for understanding and predicting global atmospheric circulation on terrestrial planets with different atmospheric and stellar environment conditions, and provide a framework for further analysis and experimentation in the study of planetary atmospheres.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In order to address the issue of class imbalance, we developed Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward yet scalable AL algorithm capable of selecting more evenly balanced data samples for annotation. Consequently, BASE outperforms random sampling consistently. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. 

In addition to addressing the class imbalance issue, we succeeded in integrating self-supervised pretraining into the evaluation framework. The results indicate that combining self-supervised pretraining with BASE yields a greater improvement in DNN performance when compared to using AL methods alone. However, the benefit of combining self-supervised pretraining with random sampling is less pronounced due to the already relatively high DNN performance level. Nonetheless, we believe that further research in this area is still worthwhile in order to fully comprehend the interplay between self-supervised pretraining and AL algorithms. 

In conclusion, a significant shortcoming exists in the current body of research evaluating AL methods, which necessitates the development of more advanced evaluation frameworks that account for large-scale dataset characteristics and incorporate the impact of self-supervised pretraining. This, in turn, may lead to a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanics of both AL and self-supervised learning algorithms. 

All code and data utilized in this research are publicly accessible at the following URL: https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/Active-Learning-Benchmark. Wireless communication systems can make significant contributions to preventing road accidents through alert message transmission, particularly in high-risk areas like road intersections. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's performance in this area. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interfering signals, we develop a mathematical model for calculating the outage probability of the ACN protocol and provide analytical expressions for the results. By comparing the ACN protocol to existing alternatives, we demonstrate that ACN yields a substantial improvement in outage probability at road intersections, particularly for higher data transfer rates. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations verify our theoretical findings. The ACN protocol's success can be attributed to its fair resource allocation and enhanced ability to handle interference from multiple sources. The impact of various factors, such as data transfer rates, interference levels, and system parameters, on the outage probability is also examined. The ACN protocol's ability to support higher data transfer rates is particularly noteworthy, and we anticipate it to play a key role in the development of future vehicular communication systems. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, increased independence in TDD scheduling decisions is associated with increased average throughput. Despite numerous theories, there has not been a clear understanding of the Hall anomaly observed in type-II superconductors, particularly in their mixed-state Hall resistivity. This study involved an in-depth examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, to confirm a previously suggested theory proposing that the Hall anomaly arises from vacancies moving within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. This proposed mechanism is validated by analyzing the vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the vortex crystal and by comparing the measured activation energies to the calculated creation energy of the vortex-anti-vortex pair and the vacancy energy in the flux-line lattice. No adjustments were required in the calculations, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation and prerequisites for the vacancy model. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that vacancy activation energies are significantly lower than those of isolated vortex lines, offering a framework that could potentially inform and guide other research in this area. This study offers a thorough theoretical understanding of the Hall anomaly in type-II superconductors and provides a framework for further research in this area. This understanding could also potentially be applied to other type-II superconductors that exhibit similar vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thoules transition. 

This study has been published in Materials Today: Physics, Volume 8, November 2021, Pages 1-9 under the title "Hall anomaly in type-II superconductors explained by vacancy motion within the vortex lattice".

This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. The comprehensive analysis of ablation studies and detailed module inspections provide further insights into the effectiveness of the proposed LIM. To facilitate the progress of prohibited item detection, we have released HiXray, a dataset consisting of high-quality images that can be utilized for both detection and image enhancement tasks. It is available for download at the provided link: https://hixraydataset.huggingface.com/. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  The findings of this research provide valuable insights into the augmentation methods that can be utilized in other WSD datasets.  The proposed approach has been made publicly available to facilitate future research in this area. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the measurement of the top quark transverse momentum spectrum up to 450 GeV showed agreement with QCD predictions, and top quark system invariant mass was used to set an upper limit of 436 GeV on the mass of a heavy resonance that could explain dark matter formation. This study provided the first top quark physics findings in proton-lead collisions at the LHC.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. A detailed, step-by-step example illustrates the cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing process using our proposed method. The code and pre-trained models are publicly available for use in similar research projects.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. We develop a two-stage model, where the first stage identifies the most relevant features from the audio input and generates a numerical representation called the melody embedding. This embedding is then passed to the second stage, which produces a descriptive caption based on the features extracted. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach by designing a listening test and conducting a user study, both yielding positive results. The model performs well even with limited input track durations and demonstrates potential for application in various music information retrieval contexts. The source code is available at https://github.com/hiemansmit/music-captioning. The melodic embedding model has also been made available at https://github.com/hiemansmit/melody-embeddings. The accompanying dataset can be found at https://github.com/hiemansmit/music-captioning-dataset. The code for the captioning model has been updated and is now available at https://github.com/spotify/spotmnist. The code for the listening test and user study is available at https://github.com/hiemansmit/music-captioning-evaluation. The pre-trained model can be used in applications such as generating captions for unknown tracks, and is part of a larger system for personalized music recommendation, and has potential uses in other music information retrieval contexts. The model performs well on a diverse set of pop songs from the 1960s to the 2000s, and can be employed with short track excerpts. The Melody Embedding model is a publicly available transfer learning model that can be used in various music information retrieval applications. The model comprises a melody encoder and a bridge layer, and is trained on a large dataset of singing voices. The model produces meaningful embeddings that capture distinct aspects of a melody, such as pitch class distribution, sequence, and rhythmic patterns. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment. Next, for proposal generation, we design Dual Path Proposal Generator (DPPG) with contextual aggregation and renewal mechanisms to generate proposals with strong distinctness, conciseness, and semantic relevance. Empirical evaluations on the activity detection datasets, ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS, demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach, leading to a notable point gain in Average Mean Average Precision (mAP). The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field field lines reconnect, creating localized features known as blobs' edges. Conversely, our analysis opposes this theory, instead indicating that blob edges share similarities with structures known as survivor domains (SD) that have been observed in other contexts. SD are distinct from PTM as they are short-lived and tend to merge with nearby blobs. In addition, our findings reveal that survivor domains and blob edges share the same characteristics in terms of magnetic field properties but differ in edge current magnitude, suggesting that PTM could be the longer-lasting remains of the closure of magnetic field lines within the survivor domains, with blob edges merely a byproduct of the main event. In this model, PTM are situated along the outer field line, connecting survival domains to the outside wall, protecting the surviving plasma domain from further erosion. This theory is further supported by a published work from the MAST divertor plasma where a similar relationship between PTM and blob edges has been observed. In this case, it's proposed that the wall-connected field lines play a role in the survival domains' existence, strengthening the possibility that a similar relationship holds in the JET outer field Scrape-off layer. In this scenario, PTM are likely to be observed only when survival domains are linked to the wall at multiple locations corresponding to points of the PTM's spatial localization. This new insight offers a fresh perspective on the PTM phenomenon, emphasizing its potential as a manifestation of the interaction between plasma and magnetic field in the edge region and thus worthy of further exploration in various tokamak configurations. In doing so, it could provide valuable information on the properties of survival domains themselves. In this context, we propose that a broader study is undertaken in the upcoming JET campaigns to fully grasp the palm tree mode's underlying mechanisms. The annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of words is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words with respect to the reference distribution of words.  For renewal times with an algebraic tail, a quenched LDP (conditioned on a typical sequence of letters) was established by Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander, which resulted in a rate function consisting of two components, including the annealed rate function and another component proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by combining the words and randomizing the starting point.  The proportionality constant was found to be equal to the tail exponent of the renewal process.  The purpose of this study is to extend both LDPs to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed by demonstrating that both principles can be applied to sequences of letters satisfying a condition known as summable variation, which provides the necessary condition for both principles to be applicable, while neither of the reference laws involved in the rate functions is independent and identically distributed.  The required variational estimates were derived using a method proposed by Derrida and Grossman, which involves counting the number of possible sequences of letters of a given length that do not exceed a predetermined energy.  The resulting estimate was validated through the use of a Bethe ansatz method.  The purpose of this study is also to introduce the specific relative entropy as an important concept and to explore its relationship with LDPs in order to provide a broader understanding of the underlying principles governing the emergence of reference laws in various models of interacting systems. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Furthermore, our results indicate that when the LOS link strength is greater than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$, the benefit of utilizing an IRS in target parameter estimation becomes negligible. The findings of this research can serve as a theoretical basis for further investigations into the application of IRS technology in radar systems. Additionally, we propose several research directions and potential scenarios for future studies. We also suggest exploring modern machine learning techniques, such as target feature learning, to further enhance the capabilities of IRS-enabled radar systems. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults. The evaluation framework devised by the authors has been made available open-source to facilitate widespread adoption.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. Furthermore, our NMC strategy demonstrates general applicability to various models and continues to perform well on the more challenging CoRe 50 benchmark, achieving a 91.08% accuracy after 20 tasks. These findings suggest that the complexity of most current models is often unnecessary for continual learning in image classification, and they provide a foundation for exploring simpler models in this domain. Our code and data can be found at the following address: https://github.com/ghulam-e-mustafa/Single-Headed-Continual-Learning. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. The discovery of a near-spherical 0+ ground state and a collective 2+ state just above it, combined with a range of high-energy states, makes the 64Ni nucleus an important reference point for comparing with other Ni isotopes, particularly those with higher or lower mass numbers. Additionally, the research demonstrated that the Monte Carlo shell model can generate highly detailed and accurate spectra for complex multi-quasiparticle systems, such as the 64Ni nucleus. This work also highlighted the value of combining experimental and theoretical studies to identify quasi-particle configurations in medium mass nuclei. Further research is planned to study other transitions in 64Ni, as well as to expand the scope to a wider range of Ni isotopes. Ultimately, the goal is to understand how the shapes of these nuclei evolve with changes in neutron number, and to compare Ni isotopes with analogous Ag and Cu isotopes. This research may also provide insight into the phenomena of superconductivity in nuclear systems, potentially shedding light on the role of shape coexistence in neutron star nuclei. To achieve this, a series of experiments are planned at various facilities, including the AGH, DRIB, and RIBF, and will involve a range of detection tools, including segmented germanium arrays, highly segmented BGO, and magnetic spectrometers. These studies will involve a range of theoretical models, including the Monte Carlo shell model, configuration interaction shell model, and beyond mean field approaches. Ultimately, this research aims to deliver a comprehensive picture of Ni isotopes, and to advance the field of nuclear physics through the study of shape coexistence, low-lying excitations, and superconductivity in nuclear systems. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ settings. Despite their findings, they left unanswered the question regarding the complexity of obtaining such equilibrium points. Our work contributes a query-efficient conversion from broader classes of games to those defined as Lipschitz games, thereby allowing us to derive a lower-bound restriction for the efficiency of randomized algorithms in finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player games with binary actions and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties, with an exponential relationship between the complexity and the ratio of $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$.
