Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which prioritizes minimizing performance estimation variance over bias. Notably, this approach allows for effective parameter tuning, as demonstrated in our experiments using multiple datasets and models. Our results show a notable improvement in performance, as measured by the test error, when compared to traditional 5-fold and 10-fold CV methods. In particular, our study yields superior outcomes across a range of models, including discriminant analysis, logistic regression, and neural networks, as demonstrated in our accompanying appendix. Our source code is available for review at https://github.com/kuhnair/j-k-fold-cv, along with the results of our experiments. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. We also presented a general methodology for calculating optical recoil in atomic transitions anywhere across the spectrum. We further explored the impact of our findings on future experiments aimed at detecting dark matter and performed a preliminary analysis of an established protocol for solving the stochastic problem of nature. A notable feature of our study is the provision of a publicly accessible application specifically designed to generate graphs of absorption versus frequency for various atomic species and experimental configurations. This software can be accessed via a web-based interface located at https://fbasu.github.io/recoil-absorption/. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Additionally, this conceptual framework enables the identification of a new material constant, associated with the resilience of networks formed through weak interparticle forces, that exerts a significant influence on the shear thickening transition. Consequently, this work is expected to significantly contribute to a deeper understanding of the physics governing the shear thickening transition and its associated material constants, which are essential for developing predictive models that can be useful in a broad range of applications. Moreover, by linking the microscale to macroscopic viscosity, this research offers insights that can be applied to other state transitions in materials with strong interactions, also contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of such transitions in general. Lastly, the proposed framework has implications for the detection of shear jamming, which could be observed through a change in the volume change caused by shear, providing a new approach for identifying this state transition in the future. Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a suitable path to achieving magnetic analogs of twisted
superfluid and supersolid phases previously found in ultracold atomic condensates
trapped in optical lattices. Employing a cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory,
we prove that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions are responsible for stabilizing
these phases within a magnetic framework, whereas in ultracold atomic systems,
the required mechanism involves the pair hopping process. Moreover, we reveal
that the DMI strength at which these twisted phases are achieved is sensitive to
the strength of the interlayer interactions which can be adjusted through the
application of external pressure or interlayer shearing force. Additionally, we
show that DMI can be precisely manipulated by incorporating circularly
polarized light into the system. Our findings will provide valuable direction
for researchers in the experimental search for twisted superfluid and supersolid
phases in quantum magnets.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. Moreover, this research emphasizes the significance of considering the angle of the recoil itself when analyzing these events, rather than solely focusing on the associated energy levels, thereby underscoring the necessity of employing a more detailed and three-dimensional velocity distribution model in such analyses. Ultimately, our simulation yields practical guidelines for improving the interpretation of direct detection data, specifically when attempting to constrain the velocity distribution properties of low mass WIMPs. By doing so, we believe it could either drive the advancement or make use of existing particle accelerators, specifically taking advantage of established infrastructure if constructed at places like Brookhaven National Laboratory, Fermilab, or CERN. In this concept, we outline various design parameters for several collider configurations and evaluate potential for scientific discoveries with studies on deep inelastic scattering processes, Higgs boson and vector boson production, top quark creation, and leptoquark beyond Standard Model. Additionally, considerations for detector designs and potential paths to realization are also discussed. Given its research capabilities and relatively modest cost, we believe this concept has significant potential to drive the advancement of particle and nuclear physics through either expansion of current facilities or development of new projects.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This technique's accuracy and efficiency make it suitable for further development into real-time protocols.

The methods described in this section are applicable to a broader range of continuous-scan protocols and allow for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous. Additionally, it highlights the advantages of its method over alternative approaches in terms of performance and adaptability.

The focus here is on domain representations via approximation spaces with CF-structures, which involve introducing the concepts of CF-approximation spaces and CF-closed sets. It's demonstrated that the collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space, ordered by inclusion, forms a continuous domain and every continuous domain can be mapped isomorphically to the collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space. Building on this foundation, the notion of relations approximable by CF is developed using a categorical perspective, which subsequently enables the proof that the category of CF-approximation spaces with approximable relations is equivalent to that of continuous domains with Scott continuous functions. This interpretation is characterized by a strategy for playing a game associated with a continuous domain and demonstrates that it aligns with the established category theoretic constructions. Consequently, this provides a direct relationship between game-theoretic interpretations and the underlying continuous domains. Leveraging this connection, new names can be given to objects in the category of CF-approximation spaces with approximable relations by defining the winning strategies for a specified game. This enables the formulation of signatures within this category and, ultimately, allows for the definition of algebraic theories whose models are effectively domains represented via CF-approximation spaces. As a concrete example, a theory is developed that corresponds to the data type of lists based on the game-theoretic interpretation of morphisms and the associated continuous domains. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Since this test is widely used across numerous NLP applications, we believe our exact algorithm will prove useful to the community. It has already been incorporated into reputable NLP tools such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE libraries. We also examined the impact of exact paired-permutation testing on the evaluation of three popular NLP tasks - sentence classification, textual entailment and semantic similarity. Our results showed that Monte Carlo approximations can produce inconsistent and unreliable results, whereas exact calculations provide more stable and accurate outcomes. In conclusion, our exact algorithm offers a faster and more reliable alternative to Monte Carlo methods, one that is already being utilized in the NLP community. It's also possible that similar exact algorithms exist for other statistical tests used in NLP, and we encourage researchers to explore and integrate them into existing projects and libraries. We have made our code publicly available for the benefit of the community, along with comprehensive benchmarks and instructions on how to employ the exact algorithm instead of Monte Carlo approximations. We believe this advancement will contribute to the advancement of empirically defensible NLP research. We hope this initiative will spark discussion among NLP researchers, researchers, and practitioners, and that it will be widely adopted to achieve more reliable and accurate results. We invite you to use this exact algorithm and share your own experiences with us. We have made our code available under the MIT license on our GitHub repository, along with our benchmarks and instructions on how to use it, and we look forward to hearing from the community. We have also created an open discussion forum where we can exchange views and best practices. We plan to monitor this forum closely and consider suggestions from the community for future improvements. Finally, we have already integrated this exact algorithm into the popular NLP evaluation frameworks GLUE and SuperGLUE, and we have made the exact algorithm available through an easy-to-use Python class that can be accessed via the GitHub repository mentioned earlier

Furthermore, the evidence reveals that the combinatorial thickness of such a triangulation is equal to the topological entropy of the corresponding pseudo-Anosov flow. This discovery extends previous findings of Iminov and Schafer, while also providing a direct connection between the combinatorial thickness of link spaces and the topological entropy of associated pseudo-Anosov flows. Additional outcomes include the definition of a combinatorial complexity for loom spaces and a corresponding inequality relating their complexity and dimension. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Additionally, this study introduces a new feedback-receiving sketch called FResSk, which can handle both the traditional CountSketch setting and the feedback-receiving setting, and its performance shows that it achieves the same level of security as the quadratically improved estimator in the feedback-receiving setting but with significantly fewer queries (namely, k times the number of key components instead of k^2). FResSk's efficacy in the traditional CountSketch setting surpasses several current techniques, especially in cases where the input vectors have limited element sparsity. The novel approach to constructing FResSk sketches, utilizing matroid-based substructures, may also provide a useful framework for addressing other related problems. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the practical applicability of MEF-estimation techniques, including deep learning-based alternatives, resulting in low implementation costs for operators and aggregators alike. The associated code is available online.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, reflecting the emotional state of investors' willingness to invest, where various techniques such as Machine Learning and Neural Networks have been employed. From simple linear regression to advanced neural networks, researchers and investors have experimented with multiple methods to forecast the stock market. It is evident from recent market fluctuations how news headlines and cryptocurrency prices are affected. This research paper presents an ensemble of state-of-the-art techniques to forecast stock prices. It starts with applying a BERT-based sentiment analysis model to analyze the emotional state of Apple Inc investors listed on NASDAQ. A subsequent GAN-based model predicts the company's stock price based on technical indicators, global stock indexes, commodity prices, and historical prices along with the sentiment scores. This model's performance is compared to benchmark models including LSTM, GRU, vanilla GAN, and ARIMA. The study concludes by highlighting the advantages of combining technical analysis, sentiment analysis, and the fundamental aspects of the stock market, and suggests potential areas of improvement, including the integration of additional alternative assets and incorporating market trends. The code for this research has been made available online for the community's benefit.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This current work will establish the groundwork for advanced simulations and new perspectives on this physics, which will be informed by emerging observational data and the need for more sophisticated modeling as part of these simulations. This could, in turn, provide a more accurate basis for the prediction of future gravitational waves, mergers, and other significant cosmic events. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. We demonstrate that the ILC, with its higher luminosity and lower center of mass energy, offers better sensitivity to the mass scale of the new physics, whereas CLIC, with its higher center of mass energy, is more suited to differentiate between different dimensional operators. This research paves the way for a comprehensive study of the predicted rates in various final states and an in-depth sensitivity analysis at the two planned colliders CLIC and ILC. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. A clear distinction was also observed between the flow of highly frictional grains and that of low-friction grains, with the former exhibiting more complex patterns of flow and greater anisotropy. A theory was proposed to explain how the shape of an object moving through a granular material could be optimized to reduce its drag, and this was successfully applied to our own findings. A previous study was also cited which demonstrated that objects with the same dimensions but different densities could experience different levels of drag when moving through granular materials, a phenomenon we sought to explore in more depth in our own study. However, our research was focused primarily on objects of a singular density, and those specific to cylindrical intruders. A formula was derived to estimate the drag experienced by a cylindrical object moving through a granular material, and this was found to align with previous research. A dimensionless number was also identified which captured the behavior of granular materials under various conditions, and this was found to align with trends observed in other research. A notable finding of our study was that objects which moved quickly through granular materials exhibited different patterns of flow and levels of anisotropy, and that objects which moved slowly through such materials exhibited different patterns of flow and levels of anisotropy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. The code for BoAnon is openly available at https://github.com/whunada/BoAnon.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Yet, initial geometry's influence on $v_2$ and $v_3$ differed, revealed through elliptical flow's centrality dependence in minimum-bias conditions. Our findings demonstrate the importance of distinguishing between triangular and elliptical flow in understanding initial conditions and the properties of viscosity in quantum chromodynamics.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  In our findings, our proposed distribution strategy outperforms the in-memory approach by up to 25%, highlighting the benefits of Spark's cluster-enabled capabilities.  All code and data employed in this research are readily available for replication and further development on our GitHub repository.

When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. The benefits of minimum density power divergence estimators are illustrated through a simulation of AR(1) processes and a real-world examination of electron temperature data. The associated software is publicly available online.  This general approach can be applied to various statistical analyses, enabling the evaluation of model assumptions while preserving efficiency to a significant degree. The minimum density power divergence estimator is particularly relevant in the context of dependent data sets, a topic that has been given limited attention in the literature so far. The methods introduced here provide a robust framework that can be used for a broad range of applications, including the assessment of model assumptions in the presence of dependent data sets. This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. The ability to produce molecular gas outflows, seen in Mrk 79, seems to be a fundamental attribute of Seyfert galaxies with extremely high brightness levels. This paper also includes a detailed analysis of Mrk 348's ionization structure, presenting spatially resolved evidence supporting the coexistence of ionization cones and gas outflows, a crucial feature of high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. The framework's capabilities were demonstrated through a case study of an Energy Management System, and its performance benefits were verified through a comparative analysis with traditional testing methods. The source code for Frisbee has been openly contributed to the Eclipse IoT project.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our results indicate that SceneGen is a powerful tool for creating realistic traffic scenarios, one that can be used in conjunction with other methods, such as physics-based simulation, to generate even more nuanced and detailed scenes. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation. These measures are unique to Cayley trees, and we prove they are strictly periodic. We explore their properties and show they correspond to dicyclic groups, a type of double cover of the group itself. We also establish a direct relationship between the periodic measures and the group's abstract representation. This relationship enables us to identify periodic measures through the group's fundamental properties alone. Finally, we demonstrate that all periodic measures arise from this theoretical framework. This work develops an earlier study of the Ising model on a Cayley tree by Domanski and Scardo well. Our results offer a more intuitive understanding of the measures they identified and reveal the novel periodic measures we found to be a specific subset of those measures. Our analysis also establishes a direct link between the measures and the underlying group structure. This new perspective provides a simplified view of the measures and their relationships. Our results may prove useful in analyzing the Ising model on Cayley trees using the methods of group representation theory. Our study explores the interplay between the dynamics of the Ising model and its underlying group structure. This relationship may lead to further discoveries, potentially revealing new insights into the dynamics of the Ising model and its connections to the group itself. Our results demonstrate that the group structure plays a fundamental role in determining the measures, and our analysis raises the question of whether the group itself could be determined by the dynamics of the Ising model alone. This work also raises the inquiry of whether similar measures exist for other statistical mechanics models. Our results suggest that the interplay between the underlying group structure and the dynamics of the model could lead to the existence of novel measures that can be understood through the lens of group representation theory. This perspective could provide a unifying view of various measures and their relationships and might facilitate the analysis of other statistical mechanics models using the methods of group representation theory. This approach is particularly relevant to the Cayley tree, a graph known for its intriguing properties arising from the interplay between its local and global structure. This work explores a new layer of this interplay by examining how the underlying group structure affects the dynamics of the Ising model and raises the inquiry of whether similar measures could exist for other graphical structures or models. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, by incorporating a stability-preserving extrapolation technique, the method is shown to provide an efficient way to achieve both high accuracy and system preservation. This novel iteration strategy is examined across three exemplary applications: the one-dimensional Burgers' equation, the two-dimensional Allen-Cahn equation and the Rayleigh-Bénard problem. The findings highlight the method's ability to attain both high accuracy and preserve system properties. The proposed method also demonstrates a competitive performance in comparison to existing techniques. The proposed iteration strategy opens up fresh avenues for innovative numerical schemes, and the source code is shareable and accessible. The research described in the paper has been realized using the FEniCS Project, an open-source, unified finite element solver capable of solving various PDEs encountered in scientific computing, and the source code for the novel iteration strategy, along with references to the underlying solvers employed, is available on GitHub under the MIT License. We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. Notably, our reasoning employs a novel ergodic variant of a technique initially explored by Peluse and Prendiville in establishing quantitative versions of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem's application. We also establish the ergodic variant of a conjecture advanced by Iovitski and Lehnert. We also establish the ergodic variant of a higher-dimensional application of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles
to become irregularly shaped and driven mostly by expanding hot gas through low
density pathways. Our findings show that in large ($\sim 10^7M_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds hosting large ($\sim 5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot}$) superclusters, dust grain
growth contributes $4.8\times 10^{-5}M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ to dust accumulation
over 2.5 million years. However, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
increase dust supplies up to $\sim 1200M_{\odot} (M_{SC}/5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot})$, 
with $M_{SC}$ denoting the stellar mass of the supercluster. Consequently, dust
production by both grain growth and supernovae could lead to considerable dust
accumulation within low-metallicity molecular clouds, a process compatible with
galactic dust formation patterns during early cosmic reionization phases. However,
this could lead to an excessive dust content, given far more substantial dust
supplies from pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae. Consequently, we

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. The code for our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/Clarifai/3d-fusion-nms. The code for our evaluation protocol and the far-field validation dataset has also been made publicly available at https://github.com/Clarifai/3d-far-field-benchmark. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecular systems such as hydrogen chains, water, and hydrogen-rich molecules, only a relatively small number of nuclear coordinates were sufficient to generate ground states with an extremely low error margin of $10^{-5}$ or smaller in most cases. This finding implies the potential for a wide range of chemical applications using this quantum ground state preparation method. However, several challenges remain including how to choose the initial parameters for the classical neural network and how to increase the input coordinate dataset beyond the current limitation of 64, which is also the maximum number of nuclear coordinates that can be evaluated by quantum computers currently available. Nevertheless, this study provides a groundbreaking proof of concept for using quantum machine learning to efficiently prepare chemical reaction states. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. The use of this approach allows for faster and more accurate preoperative volume mapping, enabling real-time tracking during surgery and reducing the need for multiple adjustment steps. The implementation of this method also makes it possible to integrate real-time navigation with surgical planning, resulting in improved procedure outcomes. The open-source code is available online. The technique we developed is particularly useful for liver surgery, but it could also be applied to other soft tissues with featureless surfaces. The algorithm is highly efficient, requiring around 5ms for real-time processing, making it suitable for various medical navigation applications. For a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent forms found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Moreover, specific degenerate subcases may still harbor non-degenerate Ricci inheritance collineations. Conversely, non-degenerate energy-momentum tensors always support conformal matter collineations at a maximum of fifteen. The results are validated through analysis of the energy-momentum tensor for a static, spherically symmetric dust distribution. The associated conformal collineations are shown to boil down to geodesic collineations on the manifold defined by the gravitational potential. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. The comprehensive analysis of our framework and findings is accessible at https://flow-benchmark.com/. We have made our code and benchmark data available at https://github.com/linguo/Adversarial-Metric-Learning-Scene-Flow. Linguo Ding is corresponding to this work at linguo.ding@cs.umn.edu for further discussion and feedback.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. Our research contributes a novel, efficient classification framework that incorporates the capabilities of spiking neural networks and demonstrates its performance across multiple real-world classification datasets. Our proposed approach uses a random neural network as the model, combining the computational benefits of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, thereby creating a classification system with both low energy consumption and high classification accuracy. Our research evaluates the proposed approach on multiple real-world classification datasets, achieving a high classification accuracy of over 99% and low energy consumption equivalent to that of spiking neural networks. Our proposed approach provides a feasible pathway for developing a wide range of classifier models, such as support vector machines, logistic regression, and decision trees, among others. Our research code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/hwangbo/Spiking-Neural-Networks-for-Classification. Our study's findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how random neural networks operate and can serve as a foundation for exploring their applications in other data classification scenarios. Our research also highlights the potential for further improvement by integrating the low-cost predictions of multiple models. Our proposal also includes a prototype implementation using the Numpy library and the NeuronFlow framework, showcasing the efficient operation of spiking neural networks. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Additionally, we calculated the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter under these conditions, including entropy, free energy, and chemical potential, all as functions of volume. Our model also enabled us to simulate the behavior of the entropy per unit volume in spin-polarized strange quark stars. Last, we developed an equation relating the entropy per unit volume to the temperature in spin-polarized strange quark matter. This equation enables us to plot the entropy per unit volume as a function of temperature for various magnetic field strengths, revealing the expected increase in entropy with rising temperature across all considered conditions. This study offers a theoretical framework for understanding the thermal behavior of spin-polarized strange quark matter and, by extension, spin-polarized strange stars. This framework holds particular significance for the recently proposed model of spin-polarized quark stars exhibiting pulsar-like behavior. This includes the famous PSR J16145633+4857367, a pulsar situated in the cluster of blue giant stars called the Cassiopeia III, which has been hypothesized to be, in fact, a spin-polarized strange star rather than a white dwarf or neutron star. This research may be employed to further explore the properties of this star and provide insight into the fundamental nature of matter and its potential configurations. This study may also be expanded to incorporate additional models, such as the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, to gain a more comprehensive understanding of spin-polarized strange quark matter and its associated stars. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. This research also introduces the spider graph, a new infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs, as well as defining the relationship between papillon and spider graphs to establish the papillon graph as a sub-class of the spider graph class. Finally, our work concludes by identifying a necessary condition for a cubic spider graph to have the PMH-property by introducing the concept of 'normal' papillon graphs and demonstrating that no normal papillon graph can exhibit the PMH-property. This leads to a conclusion that a cubic spider graph can satisfy the PMH-property only if it is a normal papillon graph, thereby establishing the papillon graph as the general class of cubic E2F non-bipartite graphs. However, this conclusion raises further questions about the papillon graph's properties and conditions under which they would no longer be E2F. Our research finally proposes a possible approach to addressing these questions.

Recent research on block designs by Amarra, Devillers, and Praeger, involving specific quadratic polynomials, shows potential connections to two influential conjectures. The Bunyakovsky Conjecture would yield a crucial implication - infinitely many instances of the required designs. A vast number of prime values of the involved polynomials have been found and their quantities match closely the expectations based on a refined variant of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture. Although the infinite prime values of the polynomials have yet to be definitively confirmed, the results provide significant support for both the Bunyakovsky and Bateman-Horn Conjectures. The study also establishes that the densities of the resulting designs' properties align with the densities of the applied prime values, further contributing to the understanding of the underlying dynamics. The work builds upon and extends previous related research by Chen, Dietmann, and Pomerance and the legacy of the latter two specifically. The proposed extensions require the application of highly sophisticated tools, including the GPY formula for the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions and the GPZ formula for the distribution of primes generated by quadratic polynomials. The study demonstrates the practical utilization of these formulas in a context of certified instances and for a vast number of instances across a wide-range spectrum. The research provides comprehensive analyses and comparisons of various instances and their subsets, all of which have a direct connection to the involved prime values. The work is finalized by contributing it to the book series "Number Theory: Advanced Techniques," pointing out relevant open problems and highlighting the potential for further research and extensions. The book is intended for skilled graduate students and experienced researchers in number theory who are actively working in the field of prime values of polynomial equations and want to explore more about the applied problems of block designs. The book presents an overview of the recent achievements and the applied techniques by the leading researchers in the field, such as Richard K. Guy and R. A. Wilson, and also highlights the achievements of the notable researchers, like Chen, Dietmann, and Pomerance, who have made significant breakthroughs and discoveries in this area. The book is set to contribute to the progress of prime values of polynomial equations and will facilitate further research in the area of block designs due to its clear and comprehensive presentation of the underlying mathematics. The work is expected to become a reference point for the ongoing and future research projects, will likely inspire the development of new approaches and solutions and is poised to become a seminal work in the field of prime values of polynomial equations and block designs. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. In the future, we believe Timeloops has the potential to contribute to the development of secure, containerized applications. The source code for this project is currently available under the APSL open-source license. A demonstration of this research has been turned into a video that has been submitted to this conference as a demonstration. However, due to technical difficulties with the demonstration, we have opted not to include it in the conference proceedings. Nevertheless, the underlying source code has already been made available as mentioned earlier.

Investigating global $B-L$ symmetry within the Standard Model is necessary due to the anomaly cancellation requirements which necessitate three right-handed neutrinos that enable the natural generation of small Standard Model neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism. Within an extension of the Standard Model featuring a $B-L$ symmetry, we introduce a pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter framework where the imaginary component of a complex $B-L$ Higgs field constitutes the dark matter present in the universe. The universe's dark matter abundance is dictated by the Standard Model Higgs boson-mediated process, yet its interaction with nucleons via the exchange of Higgs bosons is heavily suppressed due to its pseudo-Goldstone nature. As a result, the proposed model avoids restrictions imposed by direct dark matter detection experiments. Furthermore, we pinpoint model parameter regions that replicate the observed dark matter density in accordance with the Large Hadron Collider constraints and the findings of Fermi-LAT and MAGIC in their dark matter search endeavors. The model additionally forecasts the occurrence of monochromatic gamma-ray lines at 7 TeV and 8 TeV, which can be analyzed through the study of future gamma-ray detectors such as the Great Wide Field Gamma-ray Field-Viewer like CERES. The model may be validated or disproven through the examination of neutrino mass patterns, the observation of neutrino less double decay at the Large Hadron Collider, or the investigation of neutrino trileptons at the Future e+ e- Colliders like the Chinese e+ e- Collider. The proposed framework also presents an opportunity to analyze the neutrino sector through the study of lepton colliders, particularly in instances where the Standard Model is not the complete theory. This research offers an analysis of a complex $B-L$ Higgs system that can function as a pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter model, a system worthy of further investigation in the context of the Standard Model and its neutrino sector. This study has been undertaken in the parameter space compatible with the observed neutrino mass pattern, essentially in the framework of the simplest $A$4-based model. Nevertheless, this research can be expanded to accommodate a broader range of neutrino mass patterns generated through effective four-lepton interactions at the one-loop level. This is achievable through the incorporation of a broader range of $B-L$ symmetry groups like $S$4, A$_{4}$$\otimes$Z$_{3}$, and Z$_{5}$, which enable a more intricate neutrino mass matrix configuration

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Our approach builds upon a previous framework introduced by Rousseau and Torres, and involves utilizing the internal degeneracy of the diffusion component to establish the required observability inequality directly from the adjoint system's Carleman estimate. A consequence of this approach is that it facilitates the application of this technique to a broader class of models. For completeness, we also discuss a specific numerical implementation and present corresponding results. The primary focus, however, lies in the theoretical aspects and the development of a general strategy for addressing control problems associated with nonautonomous partial differential equations. These equations often arise from modeling systems that experience periodic changes, such as daily rotations in circadian systems, and thus demonstrate significant practical value. The proposed method can also be applied to a variety of other mathematical models, such as the Allen-Cahn equation, for the purpose of analyzing and resolving convection problems. Ultimately, this research aims to establish the concept that highly sensitive estimates for the adjoint system in its entirety can lead to the creation of suitable observability inequalities, and that these inequalities can, in turn, drive the development of null controllability proofs. The success of this approach has the potential to address even more complex control problems associated with nonstandard partial differential equations. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. The model's performance, despite dealing with actions that have delayed and diverse impacts on the game, highlights the effectiveness of our method. To facilitate further research, we are making the dataset and associated code publicly available. By offering a novel strategic framework combined with actual soccer data, we aim to spur more advanced research into game theory and reinforcement learning through the lens of soccer. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, both single-frequency and multi-frequency extensions of WRI and ESI are evaluated through synthetic and real-world tests, and the results demonstrate that these methods yield improved impedance models when compared to the conventional FWI. Additionally, the implied increased computational expense for time-domain solvers may be justified by various means, including upgrading hardware or employing modern solver technologies that can expedite the wave equation solution, leading to decreased overall processing time. As an example, a 24 GHz Intel Xeon processor was found to have a roughly 10 times increase in acceptable mesh size for a specific case with the conjugate gradient solver, when comparing time and frequency domain iterations. Nevertheless, considerable improvements in modeling and inversion processes can be achieved with these new inversion methods, and the associated increased computational expenses will continue to be justified as modern hardware capacities evolve. 

This research is an initial exploration into WRI and ESI, and multiple possible future directions have been identified, including further optimization techniques, introducing time-domain data misfit functions, and investigating alternative formulations. Ultimately, both WRI and ESI have been demonstrated as effective alternatives to the conventional FWI, with considerable advantages in modeling and inversion processes, and will continue to be developed in an effort to expand the applicability of full waveform inversion.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our method allows for low-loss optical communication. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the ability to control the flow of light through our system using a relatively weak control light, effectively enabling the development of nonreciprocal optical transistors. This innovative approach could play a significant role in the creation of more complex photonic networks and other sophisticated optical systems. We hope this finding will contribute to the advancement of quantum communication and other applications requiring high levels of isolation and control over the flow of light. We anticipate that our discovery will also lead to a greater understanding of the phenomenon of quantum squeezing and its interaction with classical light in nonlinear resonators. This new perspective could, in turn, reveal additional features and capabilities of these systems. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Our findings are consistent with previous observations, showcasing the long-term stability of the pulsar's spin period and its spectral characteristics. However, the variation we detected in the pulsar's spectral shape, specifically the increase in hardness ratio towards the end of the outburst, suggests that IGR J19294+1816 exhibits dynamic behavior that may be influenced by the pulsar's rotational phase. This study leverages the unique capabilities of AstroSat's spectrum and timing data to provide new insights into the physics and behavior of this intermediate spin pulsar. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The effects of dispersal and noise on the system's phase portrait were also analyzed, and the model's predictions were verified through concurrent simulations with a species competition model featuring separate dispersal and replacement processes. The model provides a framework for exploring the complex interrelations of species competition, dispersal, and demographic noise through analytical and numerical methods. The model's parameters influence population dynamics through an interplay of bifurcations resulting in the stabilization of unstable states, the formation of loop dynamics, and the creation of half loop dynamics. The model's predictions can be applied to various ecological scenarios, including the interaction between invasive and native species, the coexistence of different animal or plant species within an ecosystem, and the competition for resources in microbial cultures. The model's flexibility allows the modification of its dynamics through the adjustment of demographic noise parameters, the substitution of regular lattice structures with small world networks, and the incorporation of preferred migration paths in the simulation of dispersal processes.
