Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods. The program's potential was evaluated in a theoretical study based on available historical data and existing research. A proposed model incorporating the principles of volunteer participation, research objectives, data collection processes, and evaluation criteria for sundial sites has been presented. The study suggests that the Suryakala-Nusantara program could effectively gather geographical and temporal data on Indonesian sundials, facilitate citizen science participation, and address research goals. To further develop this concept, necessary steps and operations for the program to function have been outlined, including the creation of a database, website development, volunteer recruitment strategies, and methods for evaluating the program's performance and citizen science participation. The study's findings can serve as a guideline for the program's implementation, enabling the collection of geographical and temporal data on Indonesian sundials through citizen science methods. The proposed program may face several challenges, such as the availability of volunteers and funding, but it has the potential to promote science education among the general public while exploring sundials in Indonesia. The study's theoretical approach can be put to the test in a real-world setting with actual citizen science participation. The evaluation of the program's performance and the collected data will contribute to the development of the Suryakala-Nusantara program, which can be used to study sundials in Indonesia more effectively. The program's success may also inspire the development of similar citizen science initiatives in other research fields. The study has the potential to contribute to the improvement of existing databases and research on Indonesian sundials through the collection of new geographical and temporal data. The evaluation of the program's performance will provide practical insights and address theoretical questions regarding the application of citizen science methods in this research area. The study's findings can serve as a starting point for further investigation and may be used to monitor the program's performance

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Moreover, our research reveals that the effectiveness of the 
design is largely independent of the electron source size and semi-angle, thereby 
validating the proposed design's broad applicability. Finally, our findings 
emphasize the importance of probe size versus current density in evaluating a phase 
plate's performance. By exploring different design materials, we also examine the 
potential for a phase plate to function as both an electrostatic phase plate and 
optical element in its own right, further enhancing its electron-probe-forming 
capabilities. Upgradable software tools developed during this study can be utilized 
to simulate custom phase-plate designs. By showcasing our results on various 
temperatures and electron sources, our research demonstrates the versatility of 
these tools. In conclusion, this study showcases the effectiveness of programmable 
electrostatic phase plates in correcting spherical aberration and highlights their 
potential for achieving high-resolution images on an uncorrected TEM. Or course, 
our findings are equally applicable to TEMs with corrected aberrations, where such 
a phase plate could maximize probe size while maintaining optimal current density. 
Our proposed design specifications, including corresponding atomic models and 
electrostatic potentials, have been uploaded to publicly accessible repositories for 
the community's review and to facilitate replication of the study findings. A 
replication of the research was carried out using the CASINO 3.4 code for review.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This suggests that encoder representations holding important contextual information may be difficult for these models to extract. To facilitate further research, we have made the proposed evaluation framework along with the code and models available for public access. This work is the first of its kind to analyze the underlying representations of encoder models in the context of dialogue and is hoped will direct researchers towards a deeper understanding of the workings of these models, urging them to evaluate both the generated text and the underlying representations responsible for it. This direction is crucial for the development of high-performing, human-like dialogue models. Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in autonomous vehicles and robotics by improving local re-localization and loop-closure detection rates in complex environments. However, extracting robust, orientation-insensitive 3D descriptors from LiDAR data remains a persistent challenge. To tackle this, this research introduces a novel, range-based, deep learning network called AttDLNet that leverages an attention mechanism to selectively emphasize contextual and inter-feature connections. The proposed network is tested and validated on the KITTI dataset, with experimental results showing its enhanced performance and loop-closure capabilities when incorporating attention layers. The study indicates that adding this attention mechanism yields more efficient loop closures and outperforms existing LiDAR-based place recognition approaches. Moreover, results suggest that encoder layers with middle depths exhibit the best mean performance and exhibit robustness to orientation variations, with code publicly available for review and replication.

Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different cloud machines, which is essential for predicting processing times and developing effective scheduling methods. Based on this analysis and the cost variability of cloud machines, the research provides a model that helps evaluate the suitability of each cloud machine for different transcoding tasks. This model can provide resource provisioning with the best balance of performance and cost, thus enhancing the efficient use of cloud services for video streaming. The proposed approach is applied to the transcoding of two significant video formats, MP4 to HLS and MP4 to DASH, and the findings are clinically tested on two popular cloud services. The research reveals that the proposed model can reduce costs by up to five times while maintaining comparable processing times, when compared to the traditional approach of using the most performant cloud machine. The proposed approach can also handle varying video content by introducing a new metric that measures the relative complexity of videos. The research concludes with future directions focused on integrating machine learning techniques to improve the model's accuracy and enhance the streaming experience through better prediction of processing times. This research has far-reaching implications for the cloud-based video streaming industry. By reducing the cost of video transcoding by up to five times without compromising quality, cloud providers can offer more affordable services, while streaming services can optimize their cloud utilization for video transcoding, thus minimizing costs and enhancing the viewing experience. Additionally, the proposed model's ability to handle diverse video content effectively can raise its adoption for other compute-intensive tasks. Ultimately, the approach's potential to handle a wide range of videos effectively can increase its adoption for other resource-intensive tasks. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. The velocity of charge carriers can be extracted from the thermal capacity measurements, and we discuss the possibilities of integrating this capability with current experimental capabilities. Additionally, we determine the temperature at which the thermal capacity reflects the thermal screening rather than the interaction with the lattice, and this temperature serves as an overall stability indicator for the system. Finally, we investigate the effects of including umklapp scattering and interactions with the lattice in our model, considering the scenario where the lattice interactions drive a transition to an insulating state. Umklapp scattering shifts the temperature of the thermal capacity anomaly, whereas lattice interactions shift it even more substantially, but also significantly alters the thermal capacity in the associated temperature range due to the development of a thermal gap. Umklapp scattering and lattice interactions exhibit distinct impacts on the thermal capacity anomaly, and the lattice may stabilize the Dirac liquid state down to very low temperatures, i.e., 1 K. Umklapp scattering may be minimized through careful material design, and we propose that charge carrier velocity can be extracted from the thermal capacity measurements, even when umklapp scattering is present. Finally, we propose that highly stable, robust Fermi-liquid behavior can be achieved in doped graphene even in the presence of lattice interactions when the carrier velocity is significantly greater than the velocity of sound in graphene, and this condition is met in the Kekule-doped case. The robust Fermi-liquid behavior in these situations enables reliable use of doped graphene in high-current, high-temperature applications. The method we developed for calculating the thermal capacity also makes it feasible to design doped graphene with desired thermal capacity characteristics, and the ability to manufacture patterns with precise control over the local carrier velocity, which can be as low as 10^4 m/s, making it possible to engineer the thermal capacity at the nanoscale. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study.

This is no longer the case when considering multi-symmetry scenarios, where the mass thresholds of the symmetries involved can significantly impact Q-ball properties. A new condition emerges in these scenarios, related to the sum of the Lagrangian densities of the underlying theories, providing lower and upper bounds for the Q-ball charge when the mass thresholds are above a certain value.

A key characteristic of the 'cored' state is that it cannot exist in a single-symmetry theory.

Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our analysis also provides a method for identifying all purely residually irreducible l-adic representations of the Galois group of Q, extending a previous result by David Savitt and Minhyon H Lee that focused on l different from 2 or 3. Additionally, we establish the equivalence of two conjectures presented by Brian Conrad, David Savitt, and Minhyon H Lee, relating the absolute integrity of a certain ring to the vanishing of a specific l-adic L-function. Our approach combines an analysis of the minimal operation of A4, S4 or A5 through group generators and relations, coupled with an examination of wild ramified non-abelian extensions of Q that incorporate faithfulness and freeness conditions, and further explores the geometric and arithmetic implications of our findings. Lastly, our study introduces an innovative application of the Magnus embedding and its interconnection with the Burnside problem. Consequently, our work offers an original framework that enriches our understanding of additive Galois modules, and its methods are versatile enough to be employed in related contexts.

This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. This issue is framed as a general mixed-intervention strategy within the context of an exchangeable random walk, and an innovative algorithm is proposed to generate high-quality code patterns based on non-negative factors, yielding impressive results when applied to both synthetic and real-world data, including actual video compression tests. This novel code pattern design methodology is expected to propel the development of compressed sensing technology, enabling more efficient video compression methods. Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as their primary means of communication. Due to their accessibility and private data storage, these emails are vulnerable to cyber threats and can serve as lucrative targets. Our proposed approach aims to examine research institutions' internal communication networks for potential security breaches. Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
Furthermore, our proposed theory aligns with existing experimental data, 
including thermal transport, heat capacity, and magnetic susceptibility 
in (La$_{1-x}$Sr$_x$)CuO$_4$. 
We also examine the implications of our concept for other electron systems 
exhibiting complex Fermi surfaces, and suggest necessary theoretical and 
experimental investigations to test our theory of exceptional van Hove 
singularities. 
In doing so, we introduce a general framework for classifying 
van Hove singularities in multi-band systems. 
This framework is utilized to analyze a range of materials, including 
BaCuO$_2$, Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$Fe$_2$As$_2$, and BaNiO$_2$, 
and their structural variations, and highlights the potential for 
electronic and magnetic changes resulting from exceptional van Hove singularities 
in these materials when they become filled. 
Ultimately, our study proposes a novel direction for understanding 
the physics of strongly interacting electron systems. 
It combines elements from the fields of topology, geometry, and materials 
science, to provide a more intricate and detailed description 
of the fermionic spectrum in these systems. 
In doing so, it sheds light on the underlying causes of 
the pseudogap phenomenon observed in certain materials, such as cuprates.

van Hove singularities in multi-band systems,

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. During a pilot study in 2018, it collected meaningful data for nearly the entire year. The apparatus has since run continuously from June 2019 to April 2021, gathering extensive data. The design of the apparatus and its data-taking system are discussed in depth. The implemented online analysis algorithms to ensure data quality and streamline collection are also described. The developed software is highly customizable, allowing for straightforward adaptation to new situations. The full-year data sets from 2019 and 2020 include around 480 million detected muon events per year, along with corresponding neutron pulses. The produced neutron spectra, calculated for specific cosmic-ray flare events, demonstrate the capability of the apparatus to detect the neutrons generated by these events. The apparatus has been upgraded to enhance its performance even further. The new version has been taking data as of April 2021. The upgrade's enhanced capabilities are being analyzed in the new data sets. The new results reveal a greater accuracy in determining neutron energies and a enhanced sensitivity to the neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons. The apparatus offers an ideal opportunity to investigate the neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons in depth. It has the ability to offer further improvements. The extension of the water equivalent depth to 814 meters through the integration of additional detectors is one such possibility. The apparatus is also suited to studying the neutrons produced by cosmic-ray flare events as well as the long-term recording of neutron data, which can be analyzed in depth afterwards. The apparatus has established a reliable data-taking system capable of collecting extensive data sets with minimal interruptions. The implementation of a distributed and flexible software design has a key role in this achievement. The software's customized nature makes it easily adaptable to new situations as well as various other neutron and muon experiments. The code is highly interoperable and in line with the principles of good software engineering. The success of the apparatus is a result of a collaborative effort involving researchers, students, and technical staff

Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The study presents early findings from the survey, including the discovery of two systems featuring multiple transiting candidates and several candidates participating in the exoplanet validation program. The full TKS dataset is incorporated into the exoplanet catalog maintained by the Open Exoplanet Catalogue. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. However, no firm conclusion can be drawn at this point due to the limited amount of observable data available for these asteroids. Ultimately, a longer duration of observation is necessary to fully comprehend the YORP effect's impact on their rotational behaviors. Nonetheless, the rotational characteristics of these asteroids, which have been extensively studied through various observations, make a significant contribution to the broader field of YORP research. The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. Interestingly, we found no correlation between online engagement and actual election results, with winners and losers displaying similar levels of online activity. Our findings provide valuable insights into online discussions and potential influencers within Instagram communities. We further explore community characteristics and their corresponding discussion dynamics through various analytical techniques, including degree distribution, clustering coefficient, and correlation analysis of comment durations. Our data also enabled us to compare online communities based on their activation schedules, identifying patterns that could indicate underlying clocks governing discussion activity over time. We open-discussed our methodology and findings with potential future research directions in our supplementary materials. We hope this study will contribute to the exploration of online communities through joint activity, while also shedding light on the dynamics of political discussions on Instagram. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This finding is accompanied by a broader result stating that certain actions featuring extreme transitivity properties cannot exhibit compactness properties within specific topological frameworks. Our initial proof employs the method of contradiction alongside an analysis of the dynamic properties of a homeomorphism's powers, followed by a computation of the topological compactness properties of this homeomorphism's action through the use of Vaught's theorem. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. It is shown that continuous functions, while similar to computable functions in some aspects, differ significantly in others. For instance, continuous functions can be uncomputable, and some computable functions must be uncontinuous. This distinction highlights the unique properties of each and provides a more detailed understanding of their differences. Lastly, various examples and applications are discussed that demonstrate the value of this work in fields such as music systems, data streaming, and rational function calculation.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems and can be trained on significantly smaller amounts of data compared to alternative methods. The latest version of this approach simplifies training by minimizing the need to adjust numerous parameters. In a recent experiment involving a highly complex system with distinct time scales and multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, a reservoir computer of the new design demonstrated several advantages over its traditional counterpart. Specifically, it used a much smaller amount of data for training, a much shorter time to adjust its performance, a smaller number of parameters to adjust, and a much higher level of accuracy in predicting patterns of behavior, even when those patterns change rapidly. In addition to this performance, it was able to predict areas of stability accurately, further confirming the benefits of this new algorithm. In order to analyze this performance, the characteristics of the system being predicted were compared to those of the reservoir computer itself, revealing how the system's characteristics transfer to the reservoir computer. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. Furthermore, we propose the integration of agency perception and the existing framework for the animacy network, expanding our knowledge of this intricate network. Ultimately, this research emphasizes the importance of considering multiple factors that contribute to the animacy spectrum in VTC.

This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. However, our study suggests that the benefit of implementing immediate and thorough testing within that community may significantly outweigh the costs, as it could prevent a large number of infections in the long run. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by designing an affine coupling layer that linearly scales the imaginary part of the covariance matrix, thereby eliminating the additional computational cost caused by the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight. Our study leverages this custom layer to utilize the exact instead of approximate numerical integration methods for Monte Carlo sampling, enabling the exploration of a wider range of filling levels without resorting to importance sampling. Our framework is further demonstrated by applying it to a study of the repulsively interacting one-dimensional Bose gas model. Our findings, obtained through the proposed exact Monte Carlo sampling, reveal a significant sign problem at filling levels $\lambda \geq 1$, which is confirmed by lattice Monte Carlo simulations. Our study presents a breakthrough architecture for linear scale problems, and our method for addressing the sign problem could be expanded to other models and more comprehensive simulations. Our proposed method is openly available on the PyTorch Neural Network repository. Our study also introduces a novel application of the Nadam optimization algorithm to counteract the effect of the negative Boltzmann weight in the Monte Carlo sampling. Our results demonstrate that this method not only mitigates the sign problem but also achieves more stable and faster convergence compared to the standard Adam optimizer, even in the presence of large filling levels $\lambda$. Our analysis and code are designed to facilitate the exploration of new architectures and the comparison of performance in addressing the sign problem and other computational challenges. Our study is a significant step towards overcoming the sign problem and making exact Monte Carlo sampling feasible for a broader range of models and filling levels. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. When the set S has a specific structure, namely being comprised of a single element, we demonstrate that the boolean complex's structure aligns with that of a combinatorial torus of maximal dimension. We also explore connections to shellable and balanced complexes, establishing sufficient conditions for these groups to apply. Finally, we present computational examples and intriguing conjectures related to the complex's homotopy type. 

Keywords: Coxeter groups, boolean complexes, discrete morse theory, homotopy type.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. According to our evaluations, the proposed models outperformed the existing classifier and achieved notable improvements, thereby demonstrating their effectiveness in analyzing the dynamics of online rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, our research lays the groundwork for more intricate studies of rumor propagation and offers a dataset of 10,000 COVID-19-related rumors in Chinese for further exploration. The source code and dataset are available online at https://github.com/ghoul-2020/COVID19-Rumor-Propagation. Our research was presented at The 43rd International Academic Conference of the Pacific Institute for the Second and Third World, held in Budapest, Hungary.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To further explore this concept, we conducted experiments involving comprehensive loss function libraries in both theoretical and practical scenarios, demonstrating the observable benefits of carefully selecting loss functions. Our research paves the way for loss functions to be viewed as trainable model components, thereby accelerating the exploration of novel loss functions that can lead to breakthroughs in deep learning. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method, called Multi-FEEDBACK Efficient Learning via Generalized Counterfactuals (MFEGL), utilizes a generalized counterfactual framework that allows it to exploit multiple types of feedback at once, resulting in highly efficient learning. By applying efficient algorithms for value function estimation, we can counterfactually reason about different scenarios and determine the optimal policy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of robotics tasks, showcasing superior performance when compared to current state-of-the-art IL algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/youngrae97/mfegl. Our proposal of a generalized counterfactual framework also opens up discussions on whether it can be applied to other online learning problems. We hope this sparks further research and improvement of efficient learning algorithms that can handle a variety of noisy feedback. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our work represents a significant advancement in the realm of everyday commonsense knowledge and its application in enhancing the overall performance of artificial intelligence models.  This is reflected in improved text generation and classification, as verified by multiple evaluation metrics, along with the introduction of a novel metric that measures the degree of semantic coherence within generated text.  We have made the ATOMIC dataset and all associated tools and experiments available for public access.  This includes over half a million text-based descriptions that serve as training content for the dataset itself, obtained from web-based discussions and forums.  We have also integrated the dataset into a publicly accessible API for the benefit of the artificial intelligence community.  This is in line with the open nature of the dataset's licensing terms. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. As such, NISQ-HHL is capable of streamlining the development of hybrid HHL versions suited to any problem type. The paper's findings with respect to Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware are expected to guide future NISQ-HQL research, addressing a critical shortcoming in the field. This work is presented at the 23rd Conference on Quantitative Finance.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This technique also proves effective on the Google Speech dataset, resulting in a 15.69% decrease in word error rate under the low-resource setting. The method demonstrates its effectiveness in low-resource and medium-resource scenarios, achieving the same error rates as strong pretraining methods but with much smaller amounts of speech data. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. This enables the application of established techniques for conditioned random walk, including methods from Gnedin and Pitman, Pitman and Pitman, and Pitman and Yor. The resulting asymptotic formulas for various moments or distributions of the first $k_n$ parking locations can be derived in this manner. Moreover, our results can be utilized to formulate sampling algorithms based on conditioned updates, leading to potential interest in our findings. Lastly, our research is represented in the broader context of parking function processes and their connections to other well-studied stochastic processes, including uniform random permutations and conditioned binary trees. The relationship between the first $k_n$ parking locations and Dirichlet processes is another interesting aspect explored within this work. The results presented here provide the foundation for exploring more intricate questions regarding the asymptotic behavior of parking functions in a broader context. The simplicity and conditional independence of the underlying random walk enable our derivation of the limiting distribution of the first $k_n$ parking locations. This further paves the way for examining the parking location distribution within larger contexts, such as when considering the interplay between multiple processes. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The existence of this phenomenon alludes to the potential for controlling superconducting fluctuations by adjusting voltage and gate settings, thereby considering the potential applications in random number generators and other technologies. Furthermore, this phenomenon may indicate the presence of unconventional pairs such as majorons or majoron-like bosons in these systems, particularly at higher temperatures or in response to changing temperature conditions. Three measurement techniques are presented to illustrate the presence of coherent quantum phase slips, namely, threshold voltage distribution, variance analysis, and current-time hysteresis measurements, demonstrating the ability to SLIDE (selectively lure, isolate, demonstrate, and examine) this phenomenon. The tools developed for this study could also be applied to investigating the presence of coherent quantum phase slips in other Josephson devices and systems. The duration of coherent quantum phase slips has been found to be in the range of 10-100 ns, depending on temperature, gate voltage, and the specific nanowire, and this result alludes to the potential for controlling the duration of superconducting fluctuations by adjusting gate voltage and setting, thereby considering the potential applications in time-domain random number generators and other technologies. The threshold voltage of these nanowires varies significantly, offering the possibility of programming superconducting fluctuations by adjusting Josephson energies and coupling energies, thereby considering the potential applications in research focused on parity-check operations and the stabilization of coherent quantum states in Josephson boxes and other multi-junction devices. The presence of this phenomenon provides an alternative explanation for capactively mediated spontaneous coherent quantum phase slip explosions observed in Josephson junctions consisting of superconducting nanowires. The study also presents a theoretical analysis of the SLIDE experiment, incorporating the effects of granular connectivity and capactive mediation, using a macroscopic quantum box model consisting of two junctions. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We hope our findings will serve as a foundation for future research aimed at exploring the theoretical aspects of training neural networks with limited Lipschitz constants. Our work is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/LipSmash and our findings are also detailed in the form of an extended manuscript that is openly accessible on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04876. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models.

Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. This methodology holds potential for addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, particularly those involving conflicting requirements for physical involvement and subjectively enjoyable experiences. Our research is publicly accessible as an open-source project on the GitHub platform. Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks. We demonstrate that this approximation efficiently captures the brittle fracture phenomenon, even in the absence of rigid elements, and provide a key step towards a full peridynamic theory. We also establish the convergence of our model as the viscosity parameter approaches zero, obtaining a precise approximation of the actual fracture energy. Additionally, we formulate an associated image processing problem, leading to a viable numerical solution, and present several examples highlighting the accuracy of our variational approximation. These examples encompass both numerical simulations within the actual structure and separate simulations of the corresponding brittle fracture problems at the element and rod levels. We also explore the impact of our approximation on the equilibrium states and corresponding rigid elements, achieving a suitable approximation of the actual fracture energy that efficiently captures the phenomenon of brittle fracture. Our work is further substantiated by an exhaustive analysis within a simplified setting, before concluding with a discussion on feasible research extensions.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Additionally, the code can be adapted to facilitate the search for monoleptonic decays of vector leptoquarks in events with missing energy and a single lepton. By utilizing this code to analyze various scenarios, we establish the sensitivity of the LHC to detect evidence of vector leptoquarks, either directly or indirectly, until the end of the LHC's current research program. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. The implementation of the proposed framework is now accessible as the DeepPET Uncertainty-Aware Neural Network (DPUANN). This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Ultimately, our work bridges the gap between theoretical discussions of the operator growth hypothesis and concrete, quantifiable examples.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. For nearly 60 years, researchers have been searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson Sphere as a primary target - an advanced megastructure capable of harnessing a star's energy for an advanced civilization. A study explores whether constructing such a structure around a black hole would be feasible and efficient in powering a civilization. Considering six potential energy sources, researchers found that an accretion disk, which can produce $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$ of energy, would be sufficient for an advanced civilization. Additionally, a Dyson Sphere could potentially collect energy from relativistic jets and increase its overall energy output fivefold. Calculations indicate that a Dyson Sphere constructed around a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way could be detectable with current telescopes using waste heat radiation in the ultraviolet to mid-infrared spectrum. Analyzing spectral energy distributions and radial velocity variations could aid in identifying possible artificial structures, such as Dyson Spheres. With many black hole candidates with suitable conditions waiting to be monitored, searching for artificial signatures around them becomes a viable strategy in the field of astrobiology and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. The approach is also relevant to studying the environments around black holes and neutron stars and could lead to improvements in solid-state instruments. The work is also applicable to other energy sources, such as stellar Dyson Spheres, and could result in significant advances in the field of the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying active measurement tools, which send test traffic and gauge performance. Nonetheless, these tools demand substantial resources and often fail to cover the whole network. Human administrators decide what parts to measure, which proves inefficient and unresponsive to rapidly changing network conditions. This article discusses the advantages of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the identification of SLA breaches. Initially, we explore the principles of steering active measurement tools via P2P. These principles involve autonomous decision-making across a network via a self-regulating system. Subsequently, we outline strategies for activating measurement sessions that are based on these principles, which do not need human input, can adapt to alterations in network conditions, and operate independently of underlying active measurement technologies. One such approach, based on our research, is outlined in detail, and its application in monitoring SLAs discussed. This approach, which we term the Multi-Modal Active Measurement Engine (MAME), is an advanced, autonomous decision-making system that is capable of activating measurement sessions in a manner that is independent of the underlying active measurement technologies, which is crucial for effectively identifying breaches of SLAs in dynamic networks. MAME has been implemented on a large-scale European network, which spans multiple countries. Our research indicates that MAME outperforms human-based activation policies by a margin of at least 15 percent in terms of Breach Detection Time, which is a key performance indicator, and also reduces the Breach Duration by a margin of at least 20 percent. Our research, which is the first of its kind, provides network operators with a method to activate measurement sessions that is scalable, autonomous, and effective, which is crucial for effectively identifying breaches of SLAs in dynamic networks. This, in turn, is key to effectively managing SLAs, which are critical to the revenue of these operators. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 5-25 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. In fact, installed energy recovery linacs like the S-Band SCART test stand and the X-Band SRFTestStand, both part of the research infrastructure at the University of Oxford, could benefit from such studies. Furthermore, upcoming multi-pass energy recovery linacs such as the HIGS and the ERLC will also require careful design to mitigate the effects of beam breakup instability. In conclusion, a thorough investigation of filling patterns in multi-pass energy recovery linacs is a vital step towards optimizing performance and reducing the beam breakup instability threshold current. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone neutron irradiation at the LANL beamline in both 2019 and 2020. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barn, in accordance with established external measurement standards. The most significant finding was the observation of neutral characteristics in 7-10% of detected events with energy above 100 MeV, indicating that a significant proportion of neutrons produced in neutrino experiments can be recovered through the application of sophisticated tracking algorithms and neutron detection properties of 3D scintillator detectors. In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth. In addition, we observed stickier dry samples by means of infrared analysis, which suggests that the absence of water allows for stronger chemical bonds formed between grains. In a broader context, our study suggests a more intricate scheme for how planetary material growth speeds up and slows down in response to varying temperatures, which could hold implications for the distribution of super-Earths. In addition, we propose a new expression that defines sticking forces based on surface energy and relevant grain properties. This theory, in turn, may be interpreted through a more comprehensive framework that looks at how planetary growth speed changes with location and intensity of the solar radiation it's under. In the case of our specific protoplanetary system, we anticipate a planetary growth cycle that goes from acceleration in the innermost sections, to slowdown in the middle, and then acceleration again in the innermost sections, which could be modeled with two key parameters - the temperature at which water evaporates from grain surfaces, and the temperature at which grain surfaces themselves evaporate, and eventually, the implications of this theory for our solar system as a whole. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The code for our research is available online. Despite its versatility, our method still faces performance bottlenecks, and possible improvements are identified through our analysis. Despite its various applications, our work on constrained imitation learning is still in its early stages, and several open problems remain unaddressed. EKMP represents a significant step towards the transfer of human skills to robots in real-world settings. It has the potential to enable the efficient imitation learning of complex robotic tasks, enabling the robot to execute these tasks autonomously in its operational environment. This has the potential to accelerate the development of robots that can work cooperatively with humans in various industries.
