To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. As an added geometric interpretation, the (spurious-free) part of the six-gluon amplitude under MRK limit can be represented as the sum of conformal cross ratios times the square of two single-emission CEVs for two different rapidity values. This representation allows a graphical display of the six-gluon amplitude in the (Nf=0, lambda=0) SYM theory. As an example, a graphical illustration of the dispersive part of an auxiliary process, relevant for studying Higgs-discrete state interference in prompt Higgs production, can be found in the attached file S6GAM.pdf. As a result, the two-gluon CEV for all helicity configurations can be derived, enhancing the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. This may facilitate the realization of robust topologically protected quantum computation states of matter.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. The starting point of this rotation state can be estimated to be around 30 T and 0.1 K, with the desired structural rotation completed at a higher temperature. The data also provide direct confirmation of the $d$-wave nature of the superconducting gap in this material. The discovered transition state may offer a more direct method for determining the superconducting gap symmetry in other materials. The observed transition, occurring far from the point of high singularity, reveals the complexity of the interlocked vortex lattice structure and the interaction between the vortex lattice and the superconducting gap, and shows the necessity for more advanced theories that take into account the rotation and the asymmetry of the lattice structure. The discovered transition state in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ can be distinguished from other proposed phase transitions involving interlocked vortices, such as spin-vortex pairs or magnetic field-induced domain wall transitions, due to its unique characteristics revealed by measurement and theoretical analysis. Theoretical calculations using the Ginzburg-Landau approach also support the discovered rotation state transition, with the predicted values for the rotation energy barrier in line with the measured stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice. The discovered transition state provides direct evidence for the complexity of the interlocked vortex lattice structure in this material, and the necessity for advanced theories that take into account the rotation and the asymmetry of the lattice structure. The rotation state transition offers a more direct method for determining the superconducting gap symmetry in materials that are $d$-wave superconductors. The discovered transition, occurring far from the point of high singularity, reveals the capability of magnetic field pressure to induce significant changes in the interlocked vortex lattice structure in these materials. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. In fact, we've already successfully utilized this approach in predicting brush properties on twisted surfaces, overcoming the limitations of previous models. This research lays the groundwork for a thorough investigation of the morphology of polymer brushes on complex surfaces with varied geometry. It also highlights the necessity of accounting for end exclusion zones in the theoretical analysis of elongated brush geometry. It further emphasizes the significance of employing highly elastic reference states that reflect the true brush geometry, as opposed to simplified models that ignore chain end constraints. It also stresses the importance of considering a range of stretching states, including both weak and strong stretching conditions, in order to accurately predict brush properties and assess the validity of various theoretical approaches. It also suggests that the strong-stretching theory, being a first-principle, brush-chemistry-based model, offers a powerful framework for a fundamental understanding of elongated brush properties in a wide range of scenarios. It also suggests that surface curvature can give rise to distinct regimes with end exclusion zones with positive, negative, or zero Gaussian curvatures, giving rise to unique brush geometry that is yet to be explored in the context of block copolymer morphology. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From a total of 2.5 million examined images, our technique yielded 
104 potential wide binary asteroid candidates, including 8 previously recorded 
binary asteroids. Among these candidates, 26 were deemed notable due to their 
large size or exceptional orbital separation factors. To enhance detection 
sensitivity, a statistical model was created to gauge the reliability of each 
candidate's classification. Ultimately, 104 candidates were presented, along 
with their corresponding data and images, available at https://doi.org/10.26194/
c5tp-ab02 for further analysis and validation. Many of these candidates 
await confirmation through high-resolution imaging or through astrometric 
analysis. Several existing wide binary asteroids were re-analyzed using our 
technique and resulting sensitivity enhancements, leading to newly derived 
orbital parameters and mass estimates for these asteroids. As astrometric

It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established. These formulas provide clarity on the composition rules for variables of differing orders. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the applicability of these formulas through concrete examples, highlighting the challenges and limitations of computing derivatives for certain functions. Our work is motivated by the potential of variable-order derivatives to enhance the performance of standard order methods in specific scenarios. The methods discussed in this study belong to the non-smooth category, thereby benefiting from the recent extension of the Newton-Kantorovich theory. Our findings also highlight the potential of variable-order methods to improve the precision of solutions in specific cases. Lastly, our research includes a discussion on the convergence properties of these methods. The results obtained indicate that the proposed variable-order methods converge faster than their standard-order counterparts in certain functions. However, the methods may exhibit slower convergence in other functions. Our study also provides a framework for analyzing the convergence properties of non-smooth methods within the context of fractional differential equations. This framework is applicable to a broad range of methods, both variable-order and standard-order. It is particularly useful in identifying the optimal method for a given problem by evaluating the methods' convergence properties. Our work is a preliminary step towards exploring the potential of variable-order methods to enhance the precision of standard order methods in specific scenarios. The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  This is evident in patterns of thickness and facies of the Pre-salt sequence, sedimentary fill of the S~ao Paulo High, magmatic rocks within it and along the conjugate Brazilian and West African margins, and the pattern of thinning of the lithosphere.  This study offers a new velocity and direction reference frame for analyzing the evolution of the South Atlantic and conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  It highlights the value of integrating magnetic, seismic, and well data, as well as the benefits of a multi-disciplinary approach to understanding this complex rift system.  This approach is now essential for predicting hydrocarbon reservoirs and trap configurations along the conjugate Brazilian and West African margins. A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task along with boundary-
preserving learning.  The experimental outcomes of applying our proposed
framework to two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate its
efficacy in improving segmentation accuracy with limited annotated images. 
Notably, our method achieves a notable 5.8% gain in DICE score on the ACDC
dataset when employing just 5% of the annotated data, and our code has been
made publicly available on the MMEditing hub.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Additionally, we uncover that this method not only boosts the players' learning outcomes but also elevates their overall skill levels within the game. Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes. The framework's components are: first, a method to evaluate the accuracy of pre-trained models on given words, followed by both methodological strategies for lexical semantic change analysis, and finally, a module for visualizing both model performance and lexical semantic change data. By showcasing our approach on previously conducted studies with added evaluation aspects, our work contributes significantly to the advancement of Lexical Semantic Change Detection and discovery. The proposed framework is currently available online at this link https://github.com/lepontus/LSDF.

Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. Our approach also identifies a significant link between knotted regions and the locations of intrinsic disorder in proteins. Notably, proteins with shallow knots tend to maintain their native state more effectively than those with deep knots. By leveraging these methods, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the folding processes of proteins with trefoil knots and potentially apply this knowledge to other types of proteins. To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. This methodology may be applied to various cosmological models to provide more accurate parameter estimations.

The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. A theoretical framework for renormalization group flow has also been proposed in an effort to further understand the complex dynamics underlying the anomalous NG theorem. A range of renormalization group flow patterns has been identified and categorized based on the presence or absence of the Riemann hypothesis's Dirichlet L-function zeros at specific values, which provides a foundation for exploring the anomalous NG theorem through the lens of the RG. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The code and data generated within this project are openly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/diversify-samples for replication purposes.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. A theoretical model incorporating surface energy and symmetry was applied to provide additional insight into this novel epitaxial process. These findings open up possibilities for the controlled synthesis of remote epitaxial relationships between various films and monolayer graphene substrates. This, in turn, may lead to the development of novel graphene-based materials and devices. However, further research is still needed to fully understand the benefits and limitations of this new epitaxial process. The suitable annealing conditions for clean graphene were found to be a crucial factor in this study, a consideration with implications for the broader applicability of remote epitaxy to clean graphene surfaces. Lastly, this work highlights the importance of differentiating true remote epitaxy from other processes that may appear similar but are caused by contaminates or alternative mechanisms. Contaminates between graphene and its substrate, for example, can sometimes be mistaken for remote epitaxy, as seen in the accompanying discussion of van der Waals and Contamination Epitaxy. The potential for misidentification serves as a motivation for a thorough theoretical analysis of the underlying physics and material properties involved in remote epitaxy, including a discussion of the associated energy barriers, symmetry rules, and preferred epitaxial orientations. This knowledge may be used to design and develop new materials with specific properties through the remote epitaxial growth on clean monolayer graphene. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets. The code and models are freely accessible on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/zwang84/Single2Multi-Label.  Every model that is trained on real image datasets is also embedded in the OpenImageKit library at https://github.com/autogluon/autogluon-image-classification/tree/main/tests/test_data/s2ml.  This novel single-to-multi-label sampling technique is awaiting extension to other generative models that use latent variables.  A preliminary study indicates that it is feasible with gan generators that use latent variables;  however, additional research is needed to make it work with other types of generators.  A key characteristic of this setting includes the development of a theoretical tight lower bound for the amount of available data that is required to achieve any particular multi-label accuracy when the condition is a single positive label alone.  This novel setting and the associated technique are awaiting expansion to the context of federated learning.  All relevant code, models, and results are freely accessible at https://github.com/zwang84/Single2Multi-Label. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. The code for our methods is available online and ready for use in practical applications.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The potential for these systems to be employed in low-resource settings is also highlighted.  A corresponding code for the proposed method and data preparation can be found at https://github.com/abhisheknandhawa/Cardiac-Auscultation. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. It is accessible on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. We experimented with these solutions using real data, presenting our findings. Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This project's code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashish72/hier-protos, with related data and experiments uploaded to Dropbox at https://www.dropbox.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the non-adabatic case, we obtained a more complex inelastic rotor model. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. The advantages of our novel storage design are demonstrated through the successful deployment of a large-scale genomics application. This application, with over 100 terabases of stored data, uses over 1 exabase of closed-reference compressed genomic data per day. This expanse of data is stored on approximately $160$ storage devices, with approximately $160$ gigabases of new data added daily, or about $4.8$ gigabases per second. This system represents a major breakthrough in the potential of DNA-based data storage, proving its feasibility for large-scale, high-throughput applications. The novel DNA storage system we've created also serves as a platform for exploring concepts in information theory within the context of genomics. This is made possible by the highly customizable nature of our index system, which allows us to conduct precise control over sequencing costs as well as object retrieval times. This is illustrated through an example involving the efficient retrieval of multiple compressed genomic sequences following DNA storage updates. This efficient retrieval is achieved through a procedure we've developed in conjunction with the index system, with both the sequencing costs and object retrieval times being accurately predicted through simple statistical analysis. This research is an important step towards realizing the full potential of DNA-based data storage, particularly for large-scale, high-throughput applications. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. This includes assessing the heat, electrical, and optical properties of these materials, as well as the preservation of topological properties under time-dependent external fields and the interplay between nodal lines and other electronic phenomena. This comprehensive overview is expected to propel the advancement of artificial topological materials centered around nodal lines. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Evaluations based on the dataset show that MAG-Net surpasses existing models and achieves high accuracy rates of 93.59%, 91.54%, and 92.19% for binary classification in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model's effectiveness is further confirmed by high dice coefficients of 0.775, 0.763, and 0.774 in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The source code for MAG-Net has been made available on GitHub, and it can be utilized for other medical segmentation applications due to the general nature of the attention guided network.  In addition, a visualization of the model's attention mechanism shows that it enhances segmentation results by highlighting the relevant features in the images.  The model's efficiency is demonstrated by evaluations based on the dataset containing pituitary tumors, and it is suggested that future studies incorporate a more diverse range of brain tumors for further improvement.  The outstanding performance of the model led to the development of a brain tumor detection mobile application, available on Google Play Store and Apple App Store, demonstrating the potential of MAG-Net for use in real-world tumor detection scenarios. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, enabling concurrent computation of render layers. By formulating visibility as an implicit function, we develop a method to compute its derivative, enabling backpropagation. Our approach, termed differentiable implicit diffuse spherical harmonics rendering, allows for shadow-free renderings and visible light source simulation. Building on this, we created a new approach, termed Light-Source-Aware Image Manipulation (LSA-IM), that utilizes this renderer as part of an image manipulation framework, allowing for simultaneous visibility and illumination optimization. LSA-IM is evaluated on various datasets, demonstrating its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods, and the code is openly available at https://github.com/yzcui/lsa-im. Our research showcases the capabilities of high-performance, accurate renderers in enabling efficient deep learning-based solutions for image-based problems. Additionally, LSA-IM provides a comprehensive framework for light-source-aware image manipulation, addressing prominent challenges in this domain. It offers implicit diffuse visibility and illumination, distinct light source directions, and primary visibility. LSA-IM has been successfully applied to several datasets, outperforming current alternatives in all cases. All code related to this research is now openly available at https://github.com/yzcui/lsa-im. A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. The code for this research has been made openly available on the GitHub platform.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. The models developed can be valuable tools for local authorities managing flood risks due to their low-cost, efficient, and precise flow velocity predictions, enabling early flood risk detection. In addition, this approach has potential applications in other fluid dynamics scenarios. The associated code is publicly accessible online. HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to
established methods. The implemented software is freely accessible and can be
acquired through the provided link: <https://github.com/abhishekp2000/HDRSmartphone>.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions. Several methods within the framework have already been successfully compared using this methodology. For further development of the framework and potential criticisms, the authors invite feedback through an open issue tracker.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. Additionally, it proves that the conventional Mumford Conjecture is a consequence of both the derivative of the birational Bogomolov's question and the extended version of the base of topological classification problem. It further establishes the relationship between these conclusions and the results from the research of Harer, Miller and Morita. It also presents a couple of other applications of the b-principle in the field of low-dimensional topological geometry. It concludes with an exploration of the related open questions and the potential for generalizing oriented colored broken submersions through the addition of additional colors. It notes that the validity of this extension is supported by the topological surface recognition theorem, but its geometric interpretation is yet to be established. It suggests that the extension could provide new insights into the topological analysis of low-dimensional manifolds and their geometric properties. It also posits that the valid cases of this potential extension could be used to apply the Madsen-Weiss theorem to derive new conclusions in the field of low-dimensional topology and geometry. It further proposes that the extension could also be used to analyze the topological structure of manifolds constructed through the repeated application of the rational blow-down procedure developed by Bogomolov, Fu, Tschogne-Leffler and Park. It also asks whether the application of this procedure to a rational surface always results in the removal of a specific set of singular curves with negative self-intersection numbers. It also poses several open questions related to the extension of oriented colored broken submersions and the related topological surface recognition theorem. It also mentions that the research on this topic is still ongoing and new conclusions may be derived from the successful validation of this potential extension. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. By demonstrating the effectiveness of an efficient BDDC solver for such intricate applications, the research aims to contribute to the development of realistic heart models. This contribution will, in turn, pave the way for further investigations of the heart, including studies of the electric system. This research was conducted in accordance with the techniques outlined in [5, 7]. The project, however, has evolved to use newer versions of the ALPS Message Passing Interface (MPI) and has incorporated additional features, including the integration of the Newton-Krylov solver, which was achieved with the help of the Trilinos Project. The research has resulted in enhanced versions of the solver and a comprehensive examination of the performance of the BDDC algorithm, with the outcomes presented in Chapter 5. The project has also led to the development of an innovative way to determine the optimum BDDC algorithm parameters, with the resulting parameter settings being used in an actual heart mechanics simulation, as described in Chapter 4. The research has produced the code, which is now part of the open-source, open-architecture, open-distribution Encodo Flow framework, a comprehensive software platform for building scientific applications. The code has the unique feature of being highly modular, with each solver method being implemented in its own separate module. The project has the potential to contribute to various other research projects and is being made available to the community to facilitate collaboration and further development. The code can be obtained from the author or downloaded from the Encodo Flow website at http://www.encodo.com/flow

The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, this limit can be understood through more extensive partitions, giving rise to intriguing combinatorial problems. As a result, several existing spectral distribution theories, such as those concerning standard Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be derived or further refined. Moreover, our findings establish the spectral distribution of generalized Wigner matrices under heavy-tailed assumptions, a previously unexplored area. To present these results, we introduce the concept of "upward shift" that extends the standard Brownian motion and "downward shift" which has an explicit form. Ultimately, our study demystifies the role of non-crossing pair-partitions within the context of matrix spectra. It also paves the way for potential applications in future research. It is essential to note that the underlying matrix can be of varying size, and our theory confirms the existence of a limiting spectral distribution prior to the onset of spectral instability. This achievement is made possible by the "rigidity" of the scaled matrix spectrum, allowing for a more detailed spectral structure analysis. It is further demonstrated that various matrix architectures, including Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be viewed as special cases with inherent spectral rigidity. It is the lack of this "rigidity" that gives rise to spectral instability in certain matrices, a concept that our theory effectively captures. It is also interesting to note that the complexity of combinatorial problems arising from matrix spectra can be understood through the lens of projective symmetry. It is only when this symmetry is broken that the problem's complexity increases, giving rise to intricate and challenging mathematical problems. It is also worth mentioning that the "upward shift" operation, which is an extension of the standard Brownian motion, is highly relevant in this context. Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. This taxonomy includes visual material extraction, storyline development, and post-production enhancements to optimize viewing experience. We will also discuss the most commonly employed evaluation metrics, associated datasets, and the advantages and limitations of existing approaches within this field, while exploring promising areas for future research and development. This survey is intended to serve as a reference point for both established and novice researchers in the field of AI-powered video creation, from which further innovations can emerge. Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations. Our work paves the way for further investigation into the measurement of gradient masking across different neural network architectures. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ghrua/Quantifying-Gradient-Masking. Our paper has been accepted for publication at the 13th International MindCogs Workshop on Cognitive Computation.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order. This breakthrough paves the way for developing acoustic memory cells and correcting axial shifts in ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This research also highlights the potential of acousto-optic and bio-acoustic applications benefiting from the integration of microacoustic Metagratings and their associated memory cells. This integrated approach could lead to the development of more precise ultrasound imaging techniques capable of monitoring axial shifts in cells or shiftless phenomena in cells such as the beating of heart cells. This could be achieved without the need for external devices by manipulating acoustic vibrations within the subject themselves. This could further enable the non-invasive monitoring of various cellular functions such as their chemical composition, shape, size, and internal structure, ultimately contributing to a more precise understanding of cellular dynamics. This new acoustic technology may also open up fresh possibilities for acousto-optical manipulation, enhancing the capability to manipulate light and thereby enabiling the development of new optical memories and a wider range of optical communication systems. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations in the motion of individuals. We introduce a unique multi-scatter approach to analyze spread kinetics in the presence of these factors. This method is applicable to a wide range of self-propelled particle spreads, from the discrete to the continuous, and includes the consideration of memory effects in the motion of individuals. We establish that diffusion spread can switch between two modes: the standard mean-square spread and a longer-term spread dominated by the second moment, in cases where the propagator's average is zero. The size and time scales that characterize the spread can be adjusted through a multi-scatter approach, and this has been demonstrated with noise, interactions, and spread models, including the Laplace propagator. This breakthrough could lead to a deeper understanding of spread dynamics and their connection to the fundamental properties of motion. Furthermore, this multi-scatter approach may be applied to spread spreading through different channels, like social connections, at various scales, like global versus local. This approach has the potential to reveal the underlying motion properties that govern the long-term spread of scattered particles. This has significant implications, given the increasing relevance of spread dynamics to study the spreading of opinions, viruses, and goods. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The relationship between the mode coupling and phase modulation terms is investigated in detail, with the results being applicable to waveguides with closely spaced resonators and proximity modes in a narrow waveguide, showing that the mode coupling term can be nonintuitive and may even lead to mode switching in a loop resonator even if the mode coupling is weak. The developed theory is also applied to a dielectric disk resonator, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms as a function of the grating radius, with the results showing that there are specific dimensions that lead to the mode coupling term being half the cross-phase modulation term, and this occurs over a broad frequency range but is highly sensitive to the grating material. The general approach is then utilized to analyze a range of nonlinear phenomena in microrings, including mode coupling, cross-phase, and self-phase modulation, with the specific case of a dielectric disk resonator showing that there are counterpropagating modes with the same nonlinear frequency and the same linear loss, enabling the demonstration of counterpropagating nonlinear mode interactions. The analysis is validated through comparisons with a finite-difference time-domain simulator and experiments in a ring resonator, with the results showing a good match between theory and practice. The developed theory is applied to a broader context, discussing the potential applications and challenges involved in the counterpropagating nonlinear mode interactions of dielectric optical resonators. This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions. Moreover, we establish that continuous control Lyapunov functions can be rendered discontinuous without losing their effectiveness in stabilizing the system. Moreover, we explore the relationship between control Lyapunov functions for open-loop controls and feedback stabilizers. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of our results through stabilization demonstrations with two polynomial systems in $3$-dimensional space. One of these systems involves an aircraft model with bounded control inputs. Our results extend prior research and provide novel insights into the relationship between control systems components in complex scenarios. They also serve as a foundation for investigating the properties and stabilizability of higher-dimensional polynomial control systems. The methods employed are centered around the theory of impulsive systems and set-valued dynamics, along with the use of Thau's stabilization theorem and the Grasse-Baillieul stabilization theorem. Two-dimensional graphical visualizations are included with the published version of this study.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on. The evaluation also revealed that the largest improvement in the reduction of the dissipation rate occurs at lower Reynolds numbers, with notable improvements seen in the kinetic energy spectrum at higher Reynolds numbers. Additionally, flow obstruction angles of 30 degrees and 90 degrees were tested. It was found that the model successfully recreates statistical measures such as the turbulent kinetic energy spectrum, skewness, and flatness from two different starting conditions. However, some discrepancies were found at higher Reynolds numbers primarily due to the influence of turbulent fluctuations. A notable aspect of this study is that low-resolution data with large scales similar to those found in the real world were used for training and evaluating the model. It was discovered that the model is sensitive to the specific architecture of the multiscale U-Net model, requiring numerous trials to achieve optimal results. It was also determined that the training of this model is computationally intensive, requiring over one month using a single GPU. It was found that the model successfully recreates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from low-resolution data across multiple Reynolds numbers, indicating its potential for use in simulations of real-world scenarios. However, further research is needed to further optimize the model's training process. The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series. Finally, it suggests that electron orbits may be stable due to this relationship between charge, current, and the non-radiative condition, rather than any inherent reason connected to the Rydberg formula. The paper also presents a mathematical proof that, given a stable atom, the speed of light must always be finite, and that the finiteness of the speed of light is a necessary condition for atomic stability. The derivation of quantised energy then follows, and it is demonstrated that this results in the Rydberg formula. The paper's key contribution is its demonstration that the relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations, combined with atomic stability and the finite speed of light, necessarily lead to the Rydberg formula. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, a qualitative analysis showcases the uncensored marginal data distribution learned by this model. This allows for unsupervised discovery of uncertainty boundaries, which can be used to improve the calibration of existing classifiers. Source code is available at: https://github.com/cytonus/ebsom.git

This paper introduces a novel approach to uncertainty modeling called Energy-based Open-World Softmax, in which an extra dimension is added to the traditional softmax formulation to capture uncertainty. A new objective function is also proposed, and the method is shown to effectively capture the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. The technique outperforms current best practices in confidence calibration and allows for the unsupervised discovery of uncertainty boundaries, which can improve the calibration of existing classifiers. The method learns the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension and shows improved performance in comparative experiments. The technique can be used to model uncertainty in a closed world and is applicable to a wide range of classification tasks. 

This work is the first to combine energy-based models with open-world softmax and is a key contribution to the field of confidence calibration. The method is easy to integrate into existing classifiers and can be used with a variety of activation functions in the extra dimension. The technique is designed to work with gradient backpropagation and can be used in a wide range of classification tasks, including multi-class classification

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in the real world. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In an effort to address this challenge, the field has seen growing interest in continual reinforcement learning, where the goal is to build systems capable of adapting to an infinite stream of task changes in a stable and efficient manner. However, existing approaches to continual reinforcement learning are limited by their focus on solving a sequence of separate tasks or requiring the knowledge of when a new task has been learned. This research tackles a more comprehensive version of the continual reinforcement learning problem, where the agent must balance exploring new tasks with learning to adapt to changes in tasks it already knows. A new algorithm developed as part of this research, the Random Shrink Maximum Entropy algorithm, achieves better results than state-of-the-art methods in this scenario by significantly reducing the computational cost while maintaining similar performance levels. A detailed analysis of the algorithm, along with new insights gained, has been incorporated into an extended theoretical framework that provides a clearer understanding of the fundamental components of continual reinforcement learning. This research was conducted in collaboration with the Lifelong Learning Center at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst. A supplementary document includes additional details, along with relevant experiments and algorithm implementations. This work has been made available as an open-access report. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. Despite the potential for processes to involve multiple cases (paths), our algorithm focuses on solo-case processes only. Future work aims to expand this capability. The current version of our approach can be used for processes involving only a single case by selecting the most frequent case as input. The selected case is then utilized to generate a declarative process model. The proposed algorithm is now capable of comparing its outcomes against real processes from various categories, such as those published by the ProM framework. The source code and associated data for our approach are available online at https://github.com/AdiYoga/DCR2DPM. The experiment results are detailed in the file 'experiment_results.zip'. The event data sets used in the experiments are hosted at https://data.mendeley.com/downloads/download-id/51719145 or directly downloadable as 'event_data.zip'. The generated declarative process models can be found in the file 'declaraive_models.zip'. The corresponding theories for the algorithm are documented in the file 'algorithm_theory.zip'. The algorithm itself is coded in Java and integrated with the Java Declarative Net (JDN) framework for declarative process models. The JDN library is an open-source framework available at https://github.com/AdiYoga/JDN, hosting the code for the Declarative Process Model Analyzer (DPA) tool. The DPA tool is not the focus of this research but is included in the developed algorithm as its implementation relies on the JDN library.
