In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a dimerized model that represents the self-consistent interaction between sites in the system. Our study demonstrates that even without considering inter-site interactions in a dimerized system, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states. This phenomenon can provide valuable insights into the dynamics of light in dimerized systems and systems with intrinsic disorder. Furthermore, it may facilitate the development of variable localization lengths by adjusting the strength of on-site potentials in dimerized systems. This could also contribute to a better comprehension of the transition from localization to non-localization in one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures. Our study combines theoretical analysis and experimental data from laser power-dependent measurements in a compact helium nanoscale waveguide filled with one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals. This hybrid approach enables a more in-depth understanding of light behavior in complex environments and can serve as a model for investigating other wave propagation phenomena in nanoscale structures. It further paves the way for applying this type of structure in the study of light localization in higher-dimensional systems and fractionally filled systems. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory. Furthermore, we have defined the data format that will be utilized across the observatory network. This format aligns with established standards and incorporates specific metadata to facilitate efficient data management and retrieval. The data processing system prototype will be positioned within the observatory's real-time data processing infrastructure and is designed to leverage the resources available within the Grid Resource Allocation and Management (GRAM) framework. This infrastructure will enable us to utilize the computing power and memory within the observatory and potentially outside resources, and allocate them on a first-in-first-out basis for data processing. This approach is anticipated to result in significant reductions to the overall data refinement time and make the most effective use of computing resources. The Liger Data Reduction System is slated for integration with the observatory's systems in time for the instrument's first light in 2023. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. We illustrate the effectiveness of this approach with a specific example involving SPADE of a horizontal separation of 10 km in a realistic scenario. Our work offers an innovative approach to overcoming the Rayleigh criterion in optical systems and paves the way for the development of more advanced SPADE techniques. Additionally, we propose the use of entangled Hermite-Gauss modes to enhance the capacity of free-space optical communication systems. Lastly, our research lays the groundwork for the utilization of SPADE as a tool for measuring minimal distances between complex light fields in various scenarios.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where species are connected through predation, with the top species preying on the bottom species which shares resources with an abundant intermediate species. The model is based on Rosenzweig-MacArthur dynamics and is adapted for continuous time. The adaptation includes incorporating a constant rate at which the top species controls its population growth in response to changes in environmental conditions. The model exhibits chaotic mixed-mode oscillations and alternating periods of explosive population growth and sudden declines in the bottom species population. To prevent this destabilization, the top species must reach a certain population threshold before its predatory effects become beneficial. The model demonstrates that early warning signs of the impending collapse include a slowdown in the time spent in the stable phase and an increase in the duration of the unstable phase. The findings are validated through numerical simulations using various parameter settings. The proposed model provides a framework for analyzing the interactive dynamics between species in multi-level ecosystems and identifying potential instability indicators. The methodology employed, involving the analysis of mixed-mode oscillations and shifting equilibria, offers a new approach to detecting early warning signals in complex systems exhibiting multiple coexisting states. The model is applicable to any system featuring coexisting stable and unstable periodic orbits and can be useful in identifying early indicators of transition between these states. The developed method is a valuable tool for enhancing our understanding of the dynamic interactions in multi-level ecosystems and the early detection of impending regime shifts in these complex systems. The proposed model is available online as an interactive module for the paper and can be accessed via the Center for Nonlinear Science at the University of Houston website. The model is written in the C++ programming language using the odeint library for numerical solving of differential equations and the eigen library for linear algebra operations. The source code for the model can be modified to accommodate a wide range of applications involving multi-level ecosystems. The code is highly customizable and is an excellent starting point for any research related to the interactions between species in complex ecological systems. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This analysis assumes the adopted definition of the bulge component is accurate and that the behavior observed is a result of bulge growth rather than alternative explanations. According to this view, the mass-star formation rate relation is a bimodal distribution describing the merging history of massive galaxies. Those that merge in major events have high specific star formation rates, while those that experience numerous minor interactions have low specific star formation rates. The mass-star formation rate relation then represents a split between the massive galaxy population's star-forming and quiescent components. The sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$ is therefore indicative of the transition from an universe dominated by major mergers to one dominated by minor interactions,

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The obtained outcomes demonstrate that, compared to the initial protocol, our method achieves significant reductions in fence count as well as average program slowdown. In the best-case scenario, programs experience no slowdown at all. The proposed technique for optimal fence insertion has been published in the paper "Verifying and Optimizing Programs for Coarse-Grained Caches" presented at the 21st ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles and Practice of Parallel Programming (PPoPP '16). The associated prototype and case studies are available for download at http://cs.nyu.edu/~santosh/ppopp16-cgc/. Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(B^{H}+f)$, particularly proving that if the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ exceeds $Hd$, then its density function is square-integrable, or if $A$'s Hausdorff dimension surpasses $Hd$, then its density function admits a continuous version, thus providing a result already mentioned. Additionally, we establish the equivalence between $(B^{H}+f)(A)$'s measure and the volume of the image $f(A)$ for sufficiently large dimensions, and explore applications and implications of our findings to existing literature. Lastly, we address the case where $f$ is adapted to a filter, a concept more extensively examined in an accompanying paper by Cazanclay and Xiao. This research is a preliminary step towards analyzing the reachability of Brownian paths and identifying connected components of set intersections in the context of Brownian motions equipped with independent drift components. It also paves the way for understanding the volumes of sets defined by path properties of Brownian paths. This work is part of the author's PhD thesis, supervised by Ravi Devrajan and Martin Hairer. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The code and model will be made available on the project page.

Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. The CAPP was tested on several scenarios, including a large IP routing table and a full-text string match, showcasing its performance and functionality. The design's unique features make it an innovative framework that can be applied to various data-intensive applications requiring out-of-order writes and value merging. The outcome of this research is a fully functional CAPP, along with its publicly accessible code and data, which can serve as a comprehensive tutorial for teaching computer organization and digital design to undergraduate computer science students using real hardware alongside the students' own software designs. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings, prompts the search for more flexible solutions. This research proposes a novel approach that leverages the strengths of both machine learning and human intelligence by establishing a mobile app called NewsGuardian. The app's primary objective is to gather a diverse range of users' opinions on whether specific news articles are true or false, especially on newly emerging events. By running the app, a robust and dynamic truth-value database is created that can provide labels for the app's users and enable the detection of false information on emerging events. In order to maintain the diversity of users' opinions in the database, a personalized user selection algorithm is proposed. This algorithm prioritizes user recruitment based on their geographic location, news consumption patterns and previous opinion-providing activities, ensuring a range of diverse viewpoints. Furthermore, the proposed system is examined theoretically and empirically through a mobile app-based experiment, revealing its capacity to build a robust database that can identify false information on emerging events with high accuracy. The evaluation of the system also demonstrates its capacity to maintain diverse labels through user recruitment, outperforming the existing approach by achieving a 0.96 accuracy level compared to the baseline's 0.78. The design of the mobile app ensures the users' data security and privacy are maintained, in accordance with the proposed system's guidelines that comply with the major mobile app stores' guidelines. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Our study represents a significant advancement in the scientific understanding of graph neural networks and their potential for generalizing to novel instances of the same system types. It also paves the way for related research in modeling complex systems, analyzing the underlying structure of time series data, and developing novel methods for extracting system properties. Alongside the code and data used in our analysis, this research is now available as an open-source project on the Graid-31 repository. Future generalization strategies could be improved through the incorporation of theoretical system properties and learning the network's parameters in an efficient and data-efficient manner. Several promising research directions have also emerged from this investigation, including the application of this approach to modeling biological neural networks and analyzing the underlying structure of financial time series data. By doing so, we may be able to better comprehend the underlying architecture of these networks and their resulting dynamic behaviors. Ultimately, this study represents a crucial step towards enabling graph neural networks to generalize to novel instances of the same system types and has the potential to significantly contribute to our understanding of complex systems and their component networks. It is possible that future generalization strategies could be enhanced through the inclusion of additional theoretical system properties and the adoption of more efficient and data-efficient methods for learning the network's parameters. Additionally, this approach may be applied to a broader range of networks and could be used to analyze the underlying structure of various biological, physical, and social systems, leading to a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture

Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol was proposed, using less entanglement than previously known protocols. This research therefore not only answers research questions but also improves efficiency and reduces entanglement requirements in the local manipulation of multipartite states. It also highlights the need for a comprehensive understanding of strong quantum nonlocality in UPBs of large sizes.

The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. Ultimately, this method demonstrates the astrobots' ability to converge to stable states in various scenarios, laying the groundwork for further research into their dynamic behavior and potential applications. The developed algorithm is integrated into the DRILL component of the SDSS-V and is currently being implemented for real-world operations. The algorithm's efficiency is sought through collaborations with astrobot manufacturers and potential alternatives are welcome. The source code for the algorithm is available online.

In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. These improvements have a significant impact on the compiler's overall effectiveness and demonstrate the feasibility of the GP 2 approach for program analysis and verification. Consequently, the upgraded Bak's compiler serves as a prime example and key validation for the GP 2 language in its own right. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. The source code for this study has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. The resulting project is currently hosted on GitHub.

Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. This category also includes the Johnson graphs $J_n$ for $n$ in ${9, 10}$. Our work contributes a general classification to describe the structure of locally arc-transitive graphs, especially those featuring quasiprimitive action on a large vertex orbit, and this classification under star normal quotient twisted wreath structures significantly delines the space of locally arc-transitive graphs with quasiprimitive groups. Moreover, our classification enables the derivation of bounded degree upper limits for a substantial array of these graphs. Lastly, our findings pave the way for the investigation of various twisted wreath structures that potentially support local arc-transitivity. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Notably, when applied to categorical data from elections research, our method successfully identified key factors influencing voting behavior. Additionally, we find that among the methods evaluated, the adaptive Group Lasso consistently results in the most interpretable models. This algorithm's code is openly available on an established repository for computational research.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. We also investigate how different components of our approach, such as the type of triple construction and the use of labeled edges, affect performance and provide detailed analysis to facilitate further innovation in this domain. The code and data utilized in this research are available for public access at this link: https://github.com/ghruus/wikidatat5. Our approach also merits consideration for addressing real-world challenges involving large-scale knowledge graphs and a variety of related text data. Lastly, substantial improvements to this research can be achieved with easy algorithmic adjustments, thereby making it suitable for further research and potential real-world applications.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. Furthermore, applicable variations of the proposed techniques are discussed from a methodological perspective. The implemented algorithms have been made publicly available to promote the development of panoramic image stitching. The source code and additional details can be found at https://github.com/aliamirp/panostack. The results achieved indicate that the accuracy of modern stitching algorithms is largely determined by the accuracy of camera movement and optical parameters, rather than the specific method used. The research includes an investigation of the impact of misaligning cameras to the vertical axis on stitching precision, finding a significant increase in errors under such conditions. The study concludes by suggesting the potential applications of the proposed methods to related problems, such as multi-view image fusion and scene reconstruction. The developed code has been integrated into the recently introduced Panostack framework, providing a suite of methods and examples for stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras. The framework is available at https://github.com/amirzadeh/panostack and has been employed in the creation of the Sun360 dataset, featuring 1,440 high-resolution images from 12 cameras with the same optical centers, along with accurately tracked directions of the cameras. The dataset and the related research, including the methods discussed above, have been incorporated into the Panostack framework as part of its initialization, enabling the reproduction of the results presented in this study. The Panostack framework is designed to facilitate the development and evaluation of algorithms for stitching and reconstructing panoramic scenes from rotating cameras, offering a set of methods, tools, and the sun360 dataset as part of its functionality. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. In this research, the proposed model demonstrated potential as an instrument for evaluating disease mechanisms and could spark new discussions on employing multi-scale brain circuit models for computational neuroscience. The code for this research is available online as an open-source project. The project includes a Python module for the brain circuit model, a differential evolution method for parameter optimization, and a data viewer for concurrent electrophysiological recordings. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of the galactic centers. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend supported by 8 out of 9 observed galaxies. The outflow of gas as oxygen III displays a linear relationship with the bolometric luminosity of IR, while the outflow rates vary between 10-100 times the galactic consumption rates as predicted by standard galaxy evolution models. The outflow of gas as oxygen III tends to be more intense as merge stages progress, with rates doubling on average when comparing late stages to early stages. The outflow of gas as hydrogen alpha/gamma, on the other hand, tend to maintain steady rates regardless of the merge stages. The outflow of gas as double-ionized nitrogen, observed in 5 out of 9 targets, tends to originate internal to the outflows of gas as oxygen III. The outflow of gas as sulfur II, observed in 3 out of 9 targets, tends to display the highest velocities relative to the other emission lines, as well as the largest projected distances from the galactic centers. These outcomes suggest the possibility of various physical processes driving the outflows of gas, as well as the possibility of the interactions between different components of the galaxy influencing the outflows. Finally, our analysis shows that far-infrared colors tend to correlate with the strength of the outflows, while no correlation exists between AGN classification and the outflows. The results we have obtained will be made publicly available through a data base suitable for scientific analysis and visualization through our upcoming data release. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
The unparalleled size of the dataset, comprising over 15000 high-resolution images with accompanying bounding box data, contributes to its utility as a standard benchmark for this research area. 
Our innovative method for classification, relying on two Branch Multi-Scale Feature Fusion CNN models trained on the RFS dataset without additional training data, achieves remarkable accuracy levels of 93.59% and 92.41% on test data according to Softmax and Macro F1 scoring methods respectively. 
The outstanding performance of this model when subjected to rigorous testing conditions and the quality of the RFS dataset make it suitable for use in a wide range of adverse weather scenarios. 
The code and the RFS dataset are available online at https://github.com/rahulrajkumar2000/RFS-Dataset and have been incorporated into the ADVENT library https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11567 offering an open-source autonomous driving dataset platform alongside other innovative methods. 
The exceptional accuracy achieved through this model, utilizing the RFS dataset, has been successfully applied in a real-world scenario with New York City taxi data. 
The detailed analysis and visual representations of classified vehicles based on weather conditions have been detailed in the accompanying paper included at https://arxiv.org/abs/2307/08219. 
The code for the real-world application has been shared at https://github.com/rahulrajkumar2000/NYC-Taxi-WD. 
The outstanding results attained utilizing the proposed algorithm have yet to be outdone according to available research metrics. 
The innovative approach to multiweather classification through the use of the proposed algorithm and the RFS dataset offers numerous opportunities for further innovation and has the potential to significantly contribute to the advancement of autonomous driving technology.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints into open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The code
and data developed as part of this project are now available at https://github.com/ghrua/open-domain-dialogue-role-constraint.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida. The results of our method show a more reliable ranking of treatment efficiency than the conventional approach and provide actionable recommendations for farmers. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution in solving the problem and set the stage for exploring additional applications of this technique. Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. Our proposed method also offers a direct solution strategy for the Muller-Herberich-Rossenbach equation, enabling the calculation of time-evolved thermal correlations and expectation values. Ultimately, we showcase the advantages of this new approach through specific examples.

By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. We would be delighted to incorporate suggestions from other experts in this area.

Additionally, we analyze the model's behavior when starting with a random distribution of frogs, obtaining both upper and lower bounds for the cluster size, with the latter relying on a novel technique involving the tree's minimal covering time. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. Our paper has been accepted for publication at CVPR 2022.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more. The method also broadens the applicability of using algebraic methods to analyze physical systems based on Lie superalgebras, by making it possible to study their spectral patterns, and allows us to identify all possible unitary irreducible modules, which can be used as building blocks for constructing more complex modules, and ultimately, all possible lattice structures of submodules in this family of Lie superalgebras. 

As an example, the characteristics of all possible unitary irreducible modules of type $M(\gl_2)$ are determined, and used to construct the lattice structure of all submodules for this specific case. The study is finalized by applying the method to analyze a well-known self-duality problem in the $\osp(3,2)$ system, and a central charge problem in the $\osp(5,2)$ system, both based on Lie superalgebras. 

Furthermore, the method is expanded to handle modules that contain toroidal factors, for a particular class of Lie superalgebras, and specifically for the $\osp(3,2)$ system, it is demonstrated that the constructed lattice structure still matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when the module $M(\gl_n)$ is considered, but this time for $n$ being either one or more. 

The method is open to further expansion, for a broader range of Lie superalgebras, or for modules based on other algebraic structures.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the use of bi-directional depth-first search, iterative deepening depth-first search, and breadth-first search. Notably, a time-efficient algorithm is developed for identifying strong geodetic subsets in trees and chordal graphs. A chordal graph that is not a tree can contain a strong geodetic subset, providing evidence against the chordal graph class having a linear-time strong geodetic vertex subset identification algorithm. A chordal graph that is a tree can have a strong geodetic subset that is not a vertex subset, demonstrating the complexity of this problem in tree graphs. The study also explores the interrelation between strong geodetic subsets and other graph subset theories. It is demonstrated that the clique graph of a strong geodetic subset is a distance graph, and a strong geodetic subset can be derived from a distance graph, establishing a bi-complexity relation between strong geodetic subsets and distance graphs. Additionally, the study presents a strong geodetic subset contained within a distance graph, which is not a strong geodetic subset itself, indicating that the derivation is a strictly bi-complex relation. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Furthermore, the study explores specific types of QFS-spaces, including their distinct substructures and properties. We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. This analysis is an independent confirmation of a previous result by Berenstein and Brucks. We classify V's time complexity as equivalent to that of solving a highly symmetric 3x3 grid puzzle. This new understanding of V's time complexity is an outcome of a deeper study of the dynamics of V's action on the free group's space, leading to a non-context-free recognition criterion for the free group's space itself. This research may have further implications for the overall time complexity of V, though that question remains unanswered. Lastly, we outline a broader theory surrounding V's time complexity, and propose a few related questions for further investigation.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. As a result of this analysis, we are able to utilize a range of observational limits including those from CDMS, XENON, and Planck in order to constrain the model parameters and thereby determine the relative abundance of the different DM components. It is found that in the case of the axion production from the alignment mismatch and in the case of the sterile-neutrino creation via the resonant mechanism, the model results in the coexistence of axion and sterile-neutrino components with relative abundances varying in response to changes in the axion decay constant within the range of U(1) symmetry breaking scale. It is also found that in the case of the model involving CPT symmetry, the axion and sterile-neutrino components undergo symmetry breaking in a mutually exclusive manner. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Moreover, the egated architecture demonstrates superior data efficiency, showcasing lower learning curves and fewer required training samples. To facilitate replication, the code and model weights are freely available for download. Overall, the EG-CNN module serves as a versatile edge extraction component that can be easily integrated into a wide range of CNN applications. It has been successfully applied to two complex medical imaging scenarios, demonstrating its practical usefulness. Nonetheless, the theoretical potential of the EG-CNN module extends beyond medical imaging scenarios, making it suitable for any image recognition task dominated by edge cues, such as scene understanding, road detection, or handwriting analysis. In these contexts, the EG-CNN module can operate as a standalone edge extraction tool, capable of processing input images regardless of the underlying CNN architectures used in those applications. In our analysis, we explore the egated module's edge extraction capabilities in the context of the well-known Cityscapes dataset. As a result, we are confident that the EG-CNN module will prove valuable to the deep learning community, offering a versatile edge extraction solution that can be easily integrated into a wide range of CNN applications. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Furthermore, we analyzed the properties of these protocols, identifying potential bottlenecks and areas for improvement in scenarios like concurrent write operations and transactional updates with foreign keys. Our findings and protocol pseudocode can serve as a foundation for further research and development of MongoDB's transaction protocols. We also introduced a method for automatically generating pseudocode for transaction protocols based on their formal specifications. Our work includes the formal definition of a variant of snapshot isolation suitable for MongoDB's replica set deployments, providing consistency guarantees for single-node and multi-node scenarios. The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Furthermore, our findings highlight the critical difference between intrinsic and extrinsic biases in medical image analysis.  Our framework's code and models are freely available for use at https://github.com/cuming9017/BiasDetection, and the associated datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/cuming9017/BiasDatasets.  While our research focuses on medical images, our proposed framework is versatile and can be applied to detect biases in other image datasets as well.  In conclusion, our study presents a comprehensive analysis of biases in medical image datasets, presenting a framework that is both theoretically and experimentally viable.  This research paves the way for a deeper exploration of the concept of bias in medical image analysis.  It is essential that the community addresses the issue of bias detection and mitigation to ensure the development of reliable and generalizable models.  Ultimately, our framework is an initiative towards a comprehensive study of biases in medical image analysis, and it is our hope that it sparks a collective interest in this critical area of research. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. One important discovery is that we could model the electron temperature and the thickness of the plasma layer based on the solar wind speed, with the temperature increasing around 0.45 times the square of the speed and the layer thickness increasing around 0.7 times the speed. However, we couldn't find a clear link between energy flux and the size of the solar wind'switch' region, but we were able to model the thickness of this region based on the solar wind speed, with it increasing around 0.8 times the speed, and we found that it only takes up a very small percentage of the solar corona, likely due to the definition we used for the thickness of the switch region being too limited, and that it may not exist at all in some areas, like near the poles of the sun. Another important discovery is that the solar wind energy flux and the thickness of the plasma layer based on the solar wind speed are closely linked and follow a similar pattern, with the flux being about 0.16 times the square of the layer thickness, indicating that the layer plays a key role in determining the solar wind behavior. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. The proposed system's ability to adapt in real-time is further highlighted by its success in predicting emotions in videos, where a 12% increase in accuracy was observed. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  Additionally, FS at 6.4GPa utilizing $^{57}$Fe, discloses a magnetic transition from a spin-glass like state to long-range magnetic order in BFTO.  Our combined studies reveal the intricate structural and magnetic adaptations of BFTO under high pressure and highlight the necessity of multi-disciplinary in-depth examinations of materials behavior.  Furthermore, our research shows that high pressure can offer an innovative approach in tackling magnetic disorder in materials.  In conclusion, Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under high pressure presents a fascinating opportunity for study, offering valuable insights into the intricate relationships between structure and magnetic order in this material, and potentially holding the key to innovative technological applications.  Therefore, it is crucial to continue exploring the behavior of BFTO under varying conditions in order to fully comprehend its capabilities.  Finally, our study demonstrates the significance of collaborative scientific research, involving the combined use of synthetic and analytical techniques, to gain a deeper understanding of the complex phenomena observed in materials science. A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property. We also establish the relationship between potential polynomial index and spectrum discrete multiplicity, as well as examining the interplay between oscillatory potential behavior and spectral type. We conclude by discussing implications for operators in higher dimensional spaces and the potential for extension to logarithmic potentials. These findings open pathways for further exploration into the spectral properties of these operators, especially in the context of emerging random matrix theories that prioritize monodromy-free properties.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the proposed method can be utilized within a pricing framework for Asian options that incorporate hedging costs as an option is being developed. The proposed method is compared to widely adopted methods such as the LongDevilleBA method and the HawkesBA method, and it is revealed that it outperforms them in terms of speed and accuracy. Finally, the research is extended to cover options on multiple underlyings and it is shown that the proposed method adapts well to this more complex scenario. By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators. Ultimately, our study provides insight into understanding the impact of material structure on energy storage at both macroscopic and microscopic scales. Additionally, we establish a relationship between our limit functional and a related homogenized functional, yielding a meaningful interpretation of our results within the broader framework of homogenization. We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations indicated an exponential decline in the number of galaxies as tidal features became more pronounced. Additionally, within our defined stellar mass scope, we observed tidal features increase in frequency by two-fold when shifting from $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ to $10^{12}M_{\odot}$. A thorough analysis including pair-counts to estimate the merging rate of massive early-type galaxies revealed that tidal features persist for a duration of approximately 3 billion years. This outcome was found to align with findings from prior studies. A substantial proportion, accounting for 73 percent, of tidal features went undetected in our data set, attributable to tidal features undergoing transformation into diffuse stellar tails, as observed in our pair-specific analysis. Our research also uncovered a notable correlation between tidal features and the formation of blue cores in early-type galaxies. A minimum of twenty-five percent of our detected sample exhibited blue cores, and it was discovered that tidal features were present in a minimum of sixty-five percent of this subset, as compared to field galaxies where this percentage was forty-five. It is our hypothesis that tidal features contribute to the growth of blue cores through the incorporation of star formation following mergers, with time-scales that are prosaic. We anticipate that future studies will provide further insight into the dynamics of tidal features and their role in the evolution of massive early-type galaxies. Certain objects identified in our research are recommended for further analysis using high-resolution data, including a candidate resembling a stellar tail observed in the galaxy UGC 8839. The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control. The generated models can be found in an open-access repository along with detailed documentation, and we evaluate the performance of our software against established LCLS-II requirements and in-depth numerical analysis. Furthermore, we explore innovative ideas for further improving our software and invite collaborative feedback and suggestions. All code and modeling data are available online at https://github.com/linacnet/AMPs and explicitly stated in the paper's licenses and attributes. For more information, please contact [jason.barkley@linacnet.org](mailto:jason.barkley@linacnet.org) or [alejandro.lascione@linacnet.org](mailto:alejandro.lascione@linacnet.org).

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Throughout the study, the promoter base is estimated by analyzing user engagement metrics on videos and social media posts. Lastly, the study discusses the implications of Forsage's existence for users of blockchain and cryptocurrency, users of smart contracts, and the digital economy as a whole. The research is based on open-source data and is available at the mentioned repository. The research is also discussed on the thread mentioned in the reference section.
