The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. Our ultimate outcome included classifying nine proposed clusters as validated globular clusters located within the galaxy's bulge, seven others needed additional study, and three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We suggested RR Lyrae star populations could be linked to three of the open clusters and one of the proposed globular clusters required further research. Our study utilized the VVV survey's extensive database, incorporating 2 million observed stars to determine likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and established a catalog of proposed cluster movements, metallic content, and ages. Our study marked the initial comprehensive research on each of the nine confirmed globular clusters. We provided comparisons with the galaxy's bulge's general movement patterns and typical movements of RR Lyrae stars, metal content, and ages, discovering a metal rich group among the confirmed globular clusters located far from the galaxy's center

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs alongside the primary contributions of heavy-quarks in hard-scattering processes. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions as mass dependent entities. Our study provides detailed NNLL$'$-resummation order analysis (combining NNLL evolution with NNLO boundary conditions) to fully comprehend the primary and secondary quark-mass influences for $q_T$ and $\mathcal T$ across all pertinent scale relationships. Notably, in case of the $q_T$ distribution, distinct rapidity divergences arise, leading to an intricate understanding of rapidity evolution features, paving the way for precise quark-mass measurements at LHC in a ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra at low $q_T$, critical for determining the precision mass of the $W$ boson. A demonstration of our framework's applicability is shown through a comparison with existing literature and a discussion of expected outcomes at LHC at various scale hierarchies. Furthermore, expected outcomes at future hadron colliders are also highlighted for exclusive differential distributions in the Drell-Yan process. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We demonstrate the significance of these findings through numerical calculations of absorption spectra, polarizability, and screening, validating our TB models against the predictions of first-principle simulations. The methods discussed in this study are highly versatile, applicable to a wide range of materials and light interaction scenarios. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range. This new class of tensor networks may provide valuable insights into our understanding of holographic codes and their relationships with quantum systems that behave phenomenologically. Additionally, this research introduces the concept of 'code duality' - a property enabling the conversion of existing codes into equivalent ones with superior resistance to error damage. This error conversion technique is illustrated by transforming the HaPPY pentagon code into a variant of the haPPY hexagon code. Lastly, this research suggests a possible connection between holographic tensor networks and the exact calculation of system properties when these systems exhibit power-law behaviors, offering a potential direction for future investigation. A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored. Notably, this sensitivity could potentially enable the remote detection of changes in complex biological systems via light exposure. Additionally, considerations for linking optical threshold signals to internal concentrations are discussed, offering a framework that could be applied to a broader class of biological molecules affected by light. This study demonstrates the existence of an optical 'taste of light', a notion first proposed in 1970. This concept could pave the way for innovative, optically-based methods for monitoring internal concentrations in complex biological systems, leading to new possibilities for remote monitoring and feedback mechanisms. This report delves into an existing theoretical model for retinal chromophore photoisomerization and utilizes it to explore the sensitivity of quantum yields to system parameters, further highlighting the potential for optically-based concentration sensing. This concept could enable the remote detection of internal concentrations in complex biological systems via analysis of optical threshold signals, a framework that could be applied to a broader class of light-sensitive molecules, offering new possibilities for innovative, optically-based monitoring and feedback methods. This could effectively create a system of optically-based concentration codes, enabling the remote identification of biological organisms based on the behavior of their light-sensitive molecules. This innovative approach could also be used to investigate the dynamics of light-sensitive molecules in living organisms and their environments. This approach could be particularly useful in studying organisms that possess proteins sensitive to light, such as rhodopsin found in retinas, cryptochromes involved in circadian cycles, and phytochromes that regulate plant development, among others. This study could further consider factors like movement, cell membrane properties, and the effects of other light-sensitive molecules, to better understand the fundamental principles and enhance its broader applicability. This concept could be explored experimentally through techniques like pump-dump spectroscopy, optical threshold signal analysis, and stimulation duration modulation

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. The comprehensive data set and the code used for this
research are openly accessible for further research purposes.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Our approach utilized LDA for topic modeling and BERT for sentiment analysis. Results show users shared supportive messages and engaged with relief efforts, expressing their desire to have their concerns heard by authorities. The implemented methodology demonstrated success, and future directions for related studies are also outlined. Additionally, the implemented system is made available online to handle recent earthquakes in Turkey. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, where the dynamics occurs simultaneously for all elements in the network. Equilibrium is evaluated by modifying and applying a method for systems that update in parallel. Similarly, dynamic behavior can be assessed using an advanced version of the method for systems that update at different times. Nonetheless, applying this technique to networks that interact with themselves is challenging because it causes the network to rely heavily on past events, making it difficult to model the network's behavior over extended periods of time. However, it has been proven possible to transform the network into an equivalent bipartite network with double the variables, allowing for analysis of systems that interact with themselves using traditional methods. This breakthrough enables a deeper examination of how systems behave during transitional and extended periods of time. Lastly, we investigate networks that interact with multiple components and are utilized in gene regulation systems by transforming these systems into equivalent bipartite networks that interact through pairs of elements. It is shown that these types of systems, where the flow of information is bidirectional, have the capacity to develop multiple equilibrium states, a key requirement for systems that manage life across various cell types. Consequently, we propose bidirectionality in the flow of information as a crucial element for systems that interact with multiple components and maintain equilibrium states during transitional periods. Furthermore, we propose a method for prioritizing elements in systems that interact with multiple components by ranking them based on their influence over equilibrium states. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for analyzing systems that interact with multiple components and suggests that a limited number of elements are sufficient for creating complex equilibrium states in systems that interact with themselves. This, in turn, has implications for the examination of systems that interact with multiple components over extended periods of time. We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems. Additionally, we incorporate their utilization within the framework of the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov approach to calculate response functions and strengths of low-lying states within the context of relativistic mean field theory. This integrated approach facilitates more accurate and faster calculations of essential properties of large nuclei, such as neutron drops and nuclei comprising multiple protons and neutrons. A specific example is presented where we calculate half-life values for states undergoing beta decay within the range of $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-8}$ seconds, which cannot be directly obtained through experimental observation with current technology. Our study presents results for the calculation of neutron drops and various nuclei comprising multiple protons and neutrons, comparing theoretical values to available experimental data. This research is an enhancement to our previous studies presented in Studies on Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov Configurations and Calculation of Low-Lying States and Structures of Complex Nuclei and Their Decays. The applied methods are also suitable for the direct calculation of matrix elements essential in processes involving the interaction of complex nuclei with other particles or photons. This includes the determination of form factors, electromagnetic multi-nucleon probabilities, monopole currents, current distributions, and magnetic moments, among others. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. A clear picture of the complex energy spectrum surrounding $^{16}$O's ground state has been created for the electric dipole multipoles up to lattice rank $L=4$, providing a solid foundation for further exploration of this concept. Moreover, a comparison between calculated and observed resonance properties has demonstrated excellent agreement, thereby validating the application of the Jost function method to this problem. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. In all cases, our approach yields accurate community detections compared to empirical standards and the Stanford large network. Additionally, we explore the method's scalability through progressive reductions of the 39-bus network while maintaining its cluster structure, revealing that its dynamical properties are captured in a submatrix, along with a notable finding that in rainforest data, community structure appears only during specific time periods. This method's limitations and potential for further research are also discussed. The code for this work is available online at https://github.com/andersonbraz/KoopmanCluster. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The ability of SparseGAN to generate compact sentence representations also enables admissible variations of existing models, such as a generator network, by simply adjusting the dictionary matrices. This technique allows us to explore various generator architectures while maintaining efficient adversarial training. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. If future experimental findings align with the predictions made by the model, it could provide evidence supporting the theory of interstellar panspermia. However, the model also forecasts that even with the discovery of thousands of extraterrestrial life forms, a clear signature of interstellar panspermia may remain elusive. Consequently, a more indirect approach to detecting interstellar panspermia is proposed which involves analyzing the statistical distribution of life-bearing planetary systems across the sky. Conditions that need to be met in order to increase the likelihood of observing this distribution include the ability to observe a large segment of the sky, the use of a sensitive detection system, and the study of systems consisting of multiple planets, as well as studying planetary systems located a certain distance away from the Earth. A potential indicator of interstellar panspermia may be identified through the implementation of a statistical test which evaluates the unusualness of the observed distribution of life-bearing planetary systems. The proposed method can be applied to existing and future astrobiological databases an it is intended to stimulate the development of new strategies for investigating interstellar panspermia. The ultimate goal remains the thorough examination of the theory of interstellar panspermia through the combination of observational and theoretical astrophysics. The proposed method is the first step towards achieving this goal and it is hoped will contribute to a better understanding of how life is dispersed across the universe. Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that we vary during the analysis consist of 3 cosmological and 7 non-cosmological parameters. The 4 most relevant parameters are the cold dark matter density, the Hubble constant, the primordial power spectrum amplitude and the linear HI bias. When assuming that foregrounds can be effectively removed, our best case scenario finds that the estimated parameters are accurate with less than a 3% error. When including the impact of foregrounds however, all parameters are estimated inaccurately by more than 5 sigma, indicating that foregrounds removal has to be more accurately handled to avoid biases. Scale cuts, specifically a minimum k-value of about 0.03 h/Mpc, need to be imposed in order to get an accurate estimation of the two most relevant cosmological parameters. The price for this accuracy, however, is a loss of precision, while two of the other parameters still end up biased in their estimates. The implications of these findings are relevant to the ongoing analysis of actual data and will be relevant in forthcoming data analysis. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest. The scalar particles associated with the intermediate energy levels will likely be heavy, making them challenging to detect through particle physics experiments, but potentially viable candidates for the gravi-dilaton scenario, which could be tested through searches for extra scalar particles in low-energy experiments like COSIC at IBS. The proposed concept is also applicable to the universe during its inflationary period, allowing for the creation of primordial black holes or non-Gaussian fluctuations in the cosmic density field through the collapse of unstable domains resulting from the symmetry violation. The violation of the cosmological scale symmetry could lead to the generation of the baryon asymmetry through the mechanism of leptogenesis. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models are likely to yield biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which suggests that using spatial capture-recapture models integrated with RSF could provide more accurate population density estimates.  Our findings are validated using simulated data and real-world examples involving the mountain lion, the bobcat, and the jaguar.  This research offers a capture-recapture-based framework that can enhance studies on the spatial ecology of wildlife.  We hope this leads to a more widespread use of integrated space usage and resource selection studies in the field.  The code used for these analyses is publicly available as part of the Rcsamp package on GitHub.  We also include a tutorial that demonstrates the step-by-step application of these methods to a real-world example.  We recommend visiting the GitHub repository for the most recent version of the code and for further guidance on utilizing the capture-recapture and resource selection functions incorporated into Rcsamp.  We believe that making this research available in an open-source format will contribute to the advancement of a comprehensive understanding of the spatial ecology of free-roaming animals.  We anticipate that the capabilities showcased in Rcsamp will serve as a foundation for the development of future methodologies that combine capture-recapture and resource selection data, eventually leading to better estimation of population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters. In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings. Additionally, we examine the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem under the scenario of unit costs and provide a $2\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm. Our techniques involve a progressive expansion approach combined with the structure of k-edge disjoint st-paths within the source-s-t triangle structure. This innovative approach allows us to develop an efficient and effective algorithm for minimizing network power while meeting specific criteria. Further, we apply our methods to multiple related problems, providing novel algorithmic solutions and further contributing to the understanding of approximate algorithm design in this domain. Our work is distinguished by an unconventional approach to ratio-based approximation algorithms where the ratio is expressed in terms of problem instance parameters rather than being expressed in terms of $\frac{1}{\delta}$ for error tolerance $\delta$. We hope this style of presentation will spark discussion and further research in this area. This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking. The research focuses on evaluating the performance of this planning approach through simulation, considering factors like detection data from individual UAVs and their respective computation burdens. A* pathfinding is implemented on a central controller to determine optimal swarm trajectories, with target detection used to initiate route adjustments. The simulation examines the effect of increasing target distances on tracking and the algorithm's efficiency in determining new paths. The research finds that more precise initial estimations yield better tracking results and that greater differences between successive estimations can lead to larger A* pathfinding computation times. The study also compares the performance of A* with respect to target distance and tracking, revealing that A* can handle shorter target distances more quickly. The investigation into the impact of detection data quality on A* indicates that fewer false positives and false negatives can speed up the computation time. The research further finds that greater computational capabilities of individual UAVs can reduce the time for A* calculations, thus allowing for more frequent route adjustments. The study demonstrates that the proposed planning approach can effectively handle moving targets and that A* can determine optimal trajectories within reasonable computation times, given suitable algorithm implementations and computational resources. However, the approach may struggle with very large target distances, significant target movements, and extensive search spaces. The research provides a foundation for further exploration into the application of probabilistic methods in swarm planning. The developed code is made available for the purpose of demonstrating the described concepts. The research is part of a book chapter that will be published in Springer's Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing series. The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding dynamic processes on complex networks, particularly near critical transitions. This study tackles this issue by measuring nodal activity to quantify localization in networks undergoing dynamic changes. The proposed method is widely applicable and can be employed with theoretical models, simulated data, and real-world observations. The researchers analyze spreading processes on various networks, demonstrating that nodal activity can display intricate patterns depending on the network's architecture. The findings indicate that localized and widespread patterns are not mutually exclusive features in a spreading process. Additionally, the prevalence of an epidemic near a critical transition is influenced by the delocalized component of the network. Furthermore, different critical exponents can coexist with similar localization patterns. The study also reveals a more intricate behavior in quenched networks, influenced by the type of activation and degree exponent. The work sets the stage for future investigations of localized activity in network processes. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. By publishing our method, we aim to stimulate further research into the analysis of broadcast location data in team sports. Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the analysis of the detected text features. Our research indicates that our relationship-determination technique performs better than rule-based methods and confirms that visual features play a key role in achieving high accuracy in these situations. Our model's performance also shows that enhancing text recognition improves the accuracy of identifying relationships. Our research has the potential to open up new areas of historical research by making it possible to analyze large quantities of deteriorated historical documents. Our technique and database are available online for further exploration and development. This could also contribute to other fields like optical formula analysis and medical document understanding. In the future, we plan to focus on recognizing handwritten text in graphical user interfaces and optical character recognition assisted by user input. This could reduce the necessary amount of input and increase the effectiveness of optical character recognition in general. Our approach has already shown potential when tested with modern documents containing handwritten text, which could indicate that our relationship-determination technique is applicable to a broader range of situations. However, our research in this area is in its initial stages and requires further exploration. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. The code for this project is available on https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/hip_rssm.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles. Outlier eigenvalues can be characterized as roots of a specific polynomial that incorporates the location of the perturbation. We define and examine this polynomial over its full expression. We observe that its roots reflect the dynamics of the unitarily invariant matrix's spectral distribution. We note a critical feature: the asymptotic conditional freeness of type $A$ results in an overlap of spectral support in situations where the spectral support would otherwise exhibit an outlier. This overlap of spectral support can be interpreted as evidence of the existence of outlier eigenvalues. Conversely, the existence of an outlier in the spectral distribution of a unitarily invariant matrix implies that its spectral distribution cannot be freely asymptotically equivalent to that of a GUE matrix. This line of reasoning allows us to visually examine the unitarily invariant matrices' spectral distribution in various scenarios, including both simple and complex spectral structures. This enables a clear distinction between conditional freeness and freeness in asymptotic analysis. We also identify specific scenarios where the spectral distribution exhibits an outlier, in contrast with cases where it does not. This distinction results from a more refined analysis of the spectral distribution's structure, made possible by our derivation of the BBP phase transition through conditional freeness, and by the resulting definition of a specific polynomial that characterizes the location of outlier eigenvalues. We take a degree-2 cover of a genus-1 curve D over a non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curve C, in a field of characteristic not 2. We construct a genus-2 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of D and X's Jacobian, the Jacobian of C being an isogeny. This construction makes previous results more flexible and also proves a special case of Haessig and van der Hendrik's conjecture. Additionally, we establish a cover of X by another curve E, such that E's Jacobian is a quotient of E's Jacobian, and this relationship can be extended to a higher-degree cover. We achieve this by applying the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer's method, and our main step also solves a special case of a question regarding Zeta functions of curves over finite fields. This solution also enables us to prove a certain 'opposite' construction, and we conclude by discussing the potential applications of our methods to other problems. Lastly, we outline a strategy to extend our genus-1 curve cover to a higher-degree cover, and we hope this approach can be useful in solving more general cases of Haessig and van der Hendrik's conjecture. This involves forming and analyzing a certain graph that represents the relationship between multiple curves, and we believe that our current results only scratch the surface in this area of research. This work is part of the candidate's thesis, and it aims to explore new approaches to understanding and working with curves and their Jacobians, particularly in relation to isogeny and cover relationships. By applying various techniques such as the Riemann-Hurwitz formula and the construction of certain curves, we are able to demonstrate the feasibility of specific cases, and we also propose additional conjectures and questions for further investigation. Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. As such, we are able to identify key factors influencing the emergence of synchronized activity in multilayer networks. Additionally, our results can inform the design of optimal intervention strategies in applications such as brain stimulation. Our method is made publicly available through an user-friendly Python code hosted by MIC-COSMOS. This code can be found on the MIC-COSMOS code repository under the reference 'Multilayer Kuramoto'. A corresponding demonstration notebook has also been provided on the NBViewer. In the future, we intend to expand our research to a broader class of continuous-time systems and explore novel applications. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. If he was, Einstein would have been able to pose and solve a related geometric problem involving the $Ric$ operator in the negative space. This work also establishes that (i) determining whether a differential operator is of the Bianchi type is equivalent to solving a discrete algebraic Riccati equation, and (ii) this solution can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if the associated differential module has a constant differential rank, namely zero. Consequently, we can define a cohomology operator $\Delta$ that induces the following differential systems: the Einstein equations, the Einstein--Ricci flow equations, and the conformal Einstein--Ricci flow equations. A discussion on future research directions, including the adaptation of $\Delta$ to treat multi-component equations and its potential application to the study of geodesic flows, is also presented. Lastly, our work is illustrated through various movies showing the solutions to these differential systems. These movies demonstrate the efficacy of this operator and the related algebraic Riccati equation in defining discrete-time trajectories that correspond to solutions of these complex differential equations. These results provide a novel framework that may be applied to a broader range of multi-component partial differential equations. Moreover, this framework has the potential to be adapted for use in studying the geodesic flows on the infinite-dimensional version of the Bianchi operator. This could lead to a greater understanding of how the underlying geometry of these manifolds influences the behavior of these flows. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The change areas are highlighted in a coding editor linked to the testing environment, so the developer can make changes directly within the editor and test the fixes immediately. The ability to visually explore the underlying causes of errors during testing is based on an innovative application of a method called proof by contradiction, in which an imaginary perfect program is used as a benchmark to measure the program being tested against. Any significant differences between the two indicate areas where the program may be faulty. These areas can be further analyzed to determine the actual causes of the errors found during testing. The entire process, from writing the code to identifying and fixing errors, is based on mathematical concepts known as predicates and functions, in which the properties of a set of data are defined and the relationships between different sets of data are defined as functions. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5. The robust performance of HyperPrompt is also evident in low-resource and few-shot learning settings. Additionally, thorough analysis is conducted from both theoretical and practical perspectives to illuminate the capabilities of HyperPrompt. The code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zwang84/HyperPrompt.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena. Furthermore, it paves the way for applying symmetry protection theories to describe and engineer the spontaneous emission of quanta from closed systems. This involves considering the interplay between unitary dynamics, symmetry, and dissipation within these systems. This approach may also be extended to other areas, such as the study of parity-preserving multi-quanta emissions in drones of electrons and superconducting nanocircuits. This research finds its relevance in the context of current experiments in cavity QED, resonaance-fluorescence in drones of electrons, and superconducting nanocircuits, and it forecast future progress in the field. This research is further enriched by its connection to theory on symmetry-protected topological phases of matter. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments conducted on various types and sizes of networks. In addition, we contribute a novel method for generating networks with specified characteristics that can be used as benchmarks. The algorithm and related code are available online at https://github.com/rafael33/sparsify. The project is based on the BA model described in Barabasi and Albert (1999). The algorithm's decentralization makes it applicable to massive networks. In particular, it can be used to estimate the size of Twitter users simply by running the algorithm between users for a few minutes. The algorithm can also be adapted for detection of malicious nodes by modifying the estimation algorithm to calculate the degree distribution within a limited number of rounds. The modified algorithm can detect up to sqrt(n) malicious nodes. The project's code is based on the Python implementation of the Barabasi-Albert model and the iGraph library for network analysis. Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
The method is implemented in a traffic management system and demonstrated with
data from a real-world traffic management center. The system was tested on seven
intersections equipped with signal controllers and showed consistent performance. 
The method's accuracy and low computational requirements make it suitable for use
with low-cost traffic management systems that rely on inductive loop data. The
code is openly available online. 
The method's accuracy depends on accurate detection of when the approach lane
becomes occupied and empty, which is addressed in a companion paper using data
from inductive loop sensors. The proposed method is particularly useful for roads
equipped with actuated traffic signals that do not require extensive coordination. 
The method also enables the estimation of queue lengths for multiple lanes at
an intersection, providing a range for each lane instead of a single estimate. 
The method is flexible and adaptable to various signal control types, making it
a valuable tool for traffic management operations. The method is also suitable
for use with low-cost traffic management systems that rely on inductive loop data.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The performance of this algorithm is also compared to a widely used alternative, showcasing its superior time-criticality across a broader set of randomly generated scenarios. The code developed as part of this research will be incorporated into the SpEC project's thorn for numerical relativity initial data. The new approach also provides a fresh perspective on understanding the dynamics of gravitational waves in complex gravitational systems. The findings resulting from this research may have far-reaching implications for the study of gravitational waves and the behavior of matter in spacetime. The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra. Upper limits are concurrently set on the branching ratio of this decay process ranging from $6.02 \times 10^{-9}$ at $7.2$ GeV $\gamma$-function scale to $2.18 \times 10^{-9}$ with a minimum at $10.4$ GeV. These results supersede previous findings and highlight the need for further investigation to either confirm the $\Sigma^+ \Sigma^-$ resonance or determine the cause of the observed anomaly. Additionally, upper limits are established for the flavor-conserving $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay process with a dimuon invariant mass threshold of $0.5$ GeV, excluding the $\Sigma^+$ resonance region unless noted, at a branching ratio of $4.2 \times 10^{-9}$ (3.1 $\times 10^{-9}$) considering all dimuon mass spectra or only the $0.5$–$1.8$ GeV range respectively. These results are based upon an optimized strategy that minimizes background and enhances signal visibility through the use of two-dimensional dimuon invariant mass distributions in place of the previous one-dimensional approach. This study's results, incorporating an in-depth background suppression technique utilizing two-dimensional dimuon spectra, reveal an anomaly in the dimuon invariant mass spectrum in the $\Sigma^+ \Sigma^-$ resonance region; specifically, an excess of events observed in the decay of $\Sigma^+$ particles at a significance level of four standard deviations without noticeable features in dimuon invariant mass spectra, resulting in a branching ratio of $1.54 \times 10^{-8}$ (1.00–$1.93 \times 10^{-8}$) and concurrently upper limits on the branching ratio of this decay process ranging from $6.02 \times 10^{-9}$ at $7.2$ GeV $\gamma$-function scale to $2.18 \times 10^{-9}$ with a minimum at $10.4$ GeV. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate the ability to design and fabricate devices capable of detecting both the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects, enabling the discovery of materials with novel transport properties. Notably, our research indicates that antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials may serve as the foundation for the development of advanced spin-valve thermal isolation devices and other intricate magnetic materials-based technologies. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. This lecture will provide an elementary overview of both transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics, in addition to key beam loss phenomena in circular accelerators, catering to attendees with minimal to no prior understanding of this topic. We aim to facilitate future collaboration between our beam physics and machine learning communities by presenting the basic concepts and terminology used in the field of particle accelerator physics. We will cover the fundamentals of accelerator design, as well as the principles of beam stabilization and control, in addition to discussing potential applications of machine learning in this area. This discussion is set within the broader context of the current global efforts to develop future circular colliders, such as the Future Circular Collider (FCC). These ambitious projects require significant advances in accelerator technology to achieve the desired levels of particle energy and luminosity. We will also highlight the importance of international cooperation in the scientific community, as exemplified by the ongoing involvement of CERN in the development of accelerator research worldwide. This cooperation is reflected in projects such as the Asian Collider Network and the recent joint study between CERN and the Doyle Research Group at Princeton University on future colliders. Finally, we will outline the key challenges that need to be addressed in the development of the FCC and other circular colliders, such as the need for compact, high-gradient particle accelerators and effective beam loss inhibition strategies. We will also touch on the potential role of machine learning in tackling these technical hurdles. Throughout the lecture, we will supplement theoretical concepts with visual aids and supporting diagrams to enhance understanding. This presentation is part of the "Machine Learning for Particle Physics" workshop at ICRC 2021.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. By integrating these models with experiments, users can achieve real-time feedback, accelerate measurements, reduce data necessary for interpretation, and ultimately accelerate scientific progress. Several of these models will be demonstrated across beamlines, covering applications in solid-state chemistry, organic chemistry, biology, and materials science. Additionally, this work highlights future directions and potential for integrating machine learning more seamlessly into experiments at user facilities. By doing so, it aims to motivate further development and integration of this technology into the research loop at synchrotron light sources. Facilities like NSLS-II can accelerate scientific progress in understanding and identifying functional materials by integrating machine learning tightly with experimental and theoretical research through a closed loop. By doing so, they can unlock the full potential of machine learning to effectively tackle grand challenges in this field.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio. Additionally, the effects of mode radius, ion cyclotron frequency, and plasma density on the ion response are investigated, demonstrating the interplay between ion dynamics and the generation of the mode. A comparative study is performed with incompressible fluid theory, revealing similarities but also notable discrepancies caused by the ion finite radius. The findings also identify potential observational markers related to ion phenomena. Numerical simulations are validated through comparison with existing linear GAM studies. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Moreover, our study offers the potential to develop more resilient quantum annealing protocols, as well as a deeper understanding of complex quantum systems affected by environmental influences and coherent processes. This knowledge also extends beyond combinatorial optimization problems, holding relevance for a broad spectrum of quantum state-transformation applications. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Alongside associated personal accounts and internal correspondence, this narrative provides a comprehensive account of the lab's evolution during that period. The path that lay ahead for the lab, now renamed the Kapteyn Institute, would significantly diverge as it became an integral part of the Kapteyn Astronomical Institute within the Astron Network 2000. The associated correspondence and discussions surrounding this transition hold valuable lessons for the future of Dutch astronomy institutions. The author of this essay is an Emeritus Astronomer at the University of Arizona and a former director of the Kapteyn Institute. The central themes of this study were initially presented as part of the author's Honors Thesis at Harvard University in 1964 under the supervision of Dr. Donald H. Menzel. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
This integrated approach has the potential to facilitate a breakthrough in utilizing composite materials safely in high-risk applications. 
By utilizing this multidisciplinary technique, researchers can overcome the limitation of using composite materials, which are prone to failure, in applications where safety is paramount. 
This breakthrough also opens up new avenues for utilizing composite materials prone to failure in safety-critical applications. 
This groundbreaking technique is also expected to facilitate the development of novel sensors and monitoring systems utilizing composite materials with built-in sensing capabilities. 
Finally, this integrated approach provides a viable platform for investigating the material's piezoresistive properties in depth, which is essential for optimizing these materials and enhancing their self-sensing features. 
In this study, CNF-GFRP was used as the primary material of interest. 
This integrated approach is not limited to CNF-GFRP and can be applied to any self-sensing composite material that can be modeled using a finite element method.

We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and the system's general properties. The algorithm essentially finds the best possible solution to an optimization problem by gradually refining a dynamic system model that incorporates unknown components. This model is based on streaming data from ongoing experiments. The algorithm uses a method to predict all the possible system outcomes and establish a theoretical limit on its performance when the actual dynamics are known. This helps demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in real-world applications. The algorithm works well in practice, as proven by successful trials with a variety of complex systems, including a sensitive flight system and a challenging robotics scenario. The algorithm also compares favorably to other state-of-the-art methods for controlling unknown dynamical systems in a rigorous evaluation. The algorithm's code is openly available online.
