This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. This research offers valuable insights for educators seeking to enhance online learning experiences and promote equity in physics education. It also provides a framework for conducting similar analyses in the future, as well as a model for the study of online learning environments in university physics classrooms. This research was conducted in alignment with the NSPE's Vision Statement and Learning Objectives for Upper-Division Physics Education. It has been shared with the physics education community and discussed at the 2022 PERC conference. Due to the global nature of the COVID pandemic, this investigation is considered a uniquely relevant and timely study. It is anticipated that the findings will contribute to the development of resources to aid in teaching university physics remotely. This research is ongoing and will continue to explore the long-term consequences of remote learning on students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction. It will also examine potential links between module submission data and students' conceptual understanding of physics course material. This will be accomplished by analyzing relationships between module submission data and exam scores, as well as through the collection of additional conceptual assessment data in future semesters. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. This discovery is showcased via a detailed analysis of a particular type of degenerate field in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This finding is anticipated to have far-reaching implications for the study of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theories and may lead to a deeper understanding of the properties and behavior of these systems. In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory. 
Our findings in this paper provide strong evidence in favor of incorporating elements
of paracomplete and paraconsistent logic into the framework of set theory. 
Ultimately, we recommend that researchers explore further the potential of our
groundbreaking approach.

underlying the choice of this specific system, are provided in Chapter II of the
thesis.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work showcases the feasibility of using BCIs with high resolution to control important aspects of gait and may pave the way for the development of more complex BCI-powered lower limb prosthetics. Additionally, the study's methods could also be applied to addressing other motor control challenges related to upper body function. The associated code is publicly available online at https://github.com/cnrs-dsi/treadmill-BCI, and the study's results have been published in the journal Frontiers in Neuroscience. The research was conducted by a team of scientists led by Dr. Philippe Giannazzini at the CNRS-DSI. The data analyzed in the study are stored in the openaccess repository OSF (https://osf.io/ou5bd/), and the research has the reference title "Noninvasive EEG-based prediction of walking state and step rate using a Bayesian filter". The study's findings have been published in the journal Frontiers in Neuroscience and present a noninvasive EEG-based approach for predicting walking state and step rate using a Bayesian filter method, achieving a high level of accuracy (99.8%) and a strong correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934). This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Implementing this method, an open-source library called TSLS is also introduced. This library allows users to define their own custom algorithms for computing uncertainty and relevance metrics within the TSLS framework. A link to the code repository can be found at this link https://github.com/mcharlando/TSLS. If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree. Additionally, we demonstrate that this component's vertex set has a minimum degree of 2 in the graph $\Gamma$. Furthermore, we establish the applicability of this result to right-angled Artin groups whose graph $\Gamma$ has a minimum component degree of 2, whose action on a tree results in a graph with a non-trivial fundamental group. This, in turn, generalizes a previous result by M. Bestvest and S. Glassner. Moreover, we showcase the applicability of our findings to right-angled Artin groups whose graph $\Gamma$ has a minimum component degree of 3, whose action on a tree results in a graph with a non-trivial fundamental group, as proven by M. Bestvest and S. Glassner. Our findings are achieved via the application of a graph transformation technique introduced by S. M. Riehl and J. M. Schoenflies. This method allows us to connect the structure of a right-angled Artin group's graph $\Gamma$ to its fundamental group under action on a tree. Our research is also enhanced by examples illustrating the applicability of our results. Lastly, our work implies the existence of a non-abelian free group that acts freely on a tree whose fundamental group has a maximal rank. This outcome generalizes a previous result by L. Greenberg. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. The model's code is available at https://github.com/linguistclay/DECENNT. The project website is located at https://www.claylinguist.com/DECENNT. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. The evaluation is conducted across a diverse range of reticulation patterns and network sizes, utilizing a diverse set of methods including the calculation of topological descriptors and the assessment of phylogenetic accuracy. The results of our comparison will direct researchers and practitioners in their choice of phylogenetic network generators suited to specific applications and research objectives. Additionally, our research will contribute valuable insights into the design and operational characteristics of each network generator, thereby facilitating further development of desirable features that cater to various evolutionary scenarios. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The developed algorithm has potential applications in enhancing video retrieval related to biological entities and their movement. Furthermore, it may contribute to the development of bio-inspired locomotion controllers that mimic the movement strategies observed in nature. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. A comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm's convergence has been conducted on a range of datasets, including image data from the ImageNet database, the Lincoln dataset, and the Scene15 database, with observations reflecting the influence of input size, data complexity, and initialization parameters. We have obtained the source code for the Nested Neumann method and associated experiments through an open-source code repository. In conclusion, the NN method represents a fast approximate iterative matrix inversion algorithm that can be employed for large-scale applications and offers valuable insights into the study of deep neural networks. In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types. Additionally, we demonstrate that over time, the scattering matrix converges to a random, stable state, and this convergence is faster for narrower channels. This theoretical analysis produces actionable formulas, and confirms previous observations, and contributes a deeper understanding of random-scattering systems. Those understandings could improve and control the energy within chaotic environments, and also inform the design of devices that manipulate and direct wave propagation and behavior. Furthermore, our findings about the convergence of scattering-matrix patterns over time may apply to, and be relevant for, biological systems that utilize time-averaged intensity to communicate and locate objects in their environment. Lastly, the constraints and relationships we describe could aid researchers in developing new numerical methods that efficiently model and simulate random-scattering phenomena. Ultimately, this knowledge has the potential to provide substantial improvements over existing modeling approaches that are typically tailored to specific cases, and often require significant trial-and-error adjustments to produce reliable results. With the theories and techniques described, such simulations could be developed to handle a broader range of scenarios, and a greater variety of wave types, and could offer a major step-forward for researchers working with random systems. This research is particularly timely because it builds on a series of recent breakthroughs, and contributes a unifying perspective that is applicable across all random-scattering systems, and could provide the foundation for future work in this field. Furthermore, our results could be validated through numerical simulations, and the proposed methods could be used to develop new modeling approaches, and aid in the design of new technologies that involve wave propagation and random-scattering. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. This study offers a deeper understanding of topological properties in materials with spatially correlated disorders and may contribute to the identification of such materials in atomic or photonic systems.

The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The research also numerically computes specific invariants and compares computation methods in terms of efficiency. The investigation concludes with the discussion of potential applications of the found relationship via isogenies in this context to better understand the monodromy matrix. The study suggests that understanding the relationship between the monodromy matrix and genus one geometry will provide valuable insights into fundamental theoretical physics aspects. The study presents results for various curve invariants, including their values, monodromy matrix components, and related $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory functions defining the monodromy matrix, alongside first Betti cohomology dimensions. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The outcomes will be displayed through specific scenario illustrations. The incorporated code improvements enable the precise computation of the neutral Higgs self-couplings at various orders, allowing for the exploration of regions of the parameter space with complex phases, also with the support of the $\texttt{FindSusyW}$ tool for the constrained minimal supersymmetric standard model (CMSSM). The code can be accessed through the code repository at https://github.com/fermilab/SusHiMi for the self-coupling calculations and https://github.com/fermilab/SusHiMi-CMSSM for the CMSSM case. The code can be used in conjunction with the $\texttt{MG5_aMC@NLO}$ framework via the $\texttt{FindSusyW}$ tool for minimal extension of the standard model (MSSM) and certain other two-Higgs doublet model scenarios. The code enables the computation of on-shell and off-shell Higgs boson production cross-sections, incorporating the appropriate wave function normalisation factors for further processes, such as decays or resonant contributions in multiple component singlet models. A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance. The methodology is applied to real-world data sets, with results indicating that linearity may be an appropriate assumption for certain networks, while others exhibit non-linearity and non-identifiable parameters, requiring alternative analysis methods. The implementation of the proposed tests and related estimators is available through an R package. As networks grow in density, existing linearity tests tend to false negatives. The challenge of fixed network dimensions on identifiability is also highlighted. Alternative linearity tests are proposed for non-identifiable parameters, and the results are robust to right-censored data. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This proposed method is then applied to model the alternative modes of spreading, extension and contraction, observed in motile cells. The resulting model predicts the temporal development of protein distributions and membrane patterns through solvation of a system of ordinary differential equations, ultimately enabling analysis of the relationship between inner cellular dynamics and observable membrane patterns. This inner-to-layer perspective offers a new viewpoint in the study of cellular spreading and could serve as a starting point for investigating more complex cellular behaviors. To validate our model, we study a cell spreading over a plain surface and a surface covered with immobilized growth factors, and compare our predictions to experimentally measured data from various research studies. The advantages of this framework are also demonstrated in a simulation of a cell spreading in response to local adhesion patterns. The proposed multi-facetal approach to cellular spreading serves as a layered modeling strategy that can be particularly useful for visualizing the inner-to-layer aspects of cellular behavior and for integrating existing component-level modeling efforts. This approach could also be an appropriate starting point for modeling cellular spreading in diverse and complex environments. The feature of the model that makes it timely is the integration of research on the inner mechanics of cells, and it is believed that this model will encourage further discussion on the multi-facetal nature of cellular spreading. The model is made publicly available through the Modelica-based modeling environment and users are welcome to modify and expand it for various applications. The source code is included in the supplementary material provided along with the experimentally measured data used for validation and the parameter settings. The model source code is also included in the additional file noted as Receptor-Membrane-Meson model.mos. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. By leveraging our features and findings, cryptocurrency exchange platforms, law enforcement agencies, and researchers can gain valuable insights to prevent and investigate malicious activities. Furthermore, our methods provide a framework for analyzing the temporal cyclic behavior in graph-structured data, offering a novel contribution to the field of graph mining. A comprehensive evaluation of our approach, including experimental analysis using the Ethereum blockchain, is presented along with a detailed discussion of the results. Additionally, we propose several potential applications and methodologies for further research in this domain. The ongoing evolution of blockchain technology necessitates continuous research into identifying malicious actors and understanding the underlying money trails, as well as the temporal cyclic behavior present in cryptocurrency blockchains. In this paper, a novel approach to money trail analysis is introduced, centered on uncovering hidden patterns within temporal transaction graphs, and incorporating new features to detect cyclic behavior. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Notably, we found that using a virtual decoder learning process results in actual fault-tolerant performance gains of up to 30%. This novel approach offers a flexible framework for developing decoding algorithms and expands the code domain for which learning-based decoders can be utilized. This work paves the way for exploring more complex code types, like the double-catalina code, and incorporates elements of dynamical learning, to further improve decoding efficiency and tolerance in the harsh environment of quantum computing. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality. The optimal performance of this system is determined by a set of conditions that include the strength of interactions between light particles and the duration of measurements, and the potential for the detection of phase shifts as low as $10^{-16}$ is explored. The capabilities of quantum jump metrology are made possible by the combination of single-pass measurements and the induction of correlations in continuously operating systems, and this allows it to surpass the standard quantum precision limit in a more scalable and practical manner. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to space constraints, specific results from intermediate analyses are not provided here, however they are available in the accompanying full paper. Also, considering the value of $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ as the extremal gain of optimal over binary power control control holds generally for all (fixed) non-zero signal-to-noise ratios, it can be inferred that the gain will increase proportionally with the square root of the number of users in the network. It is worth noting that this research focuses exclusively on non-cooperative, fixed transmission power settings and does not account for any potential gains from adaptive modulation and coding or cooperative communication techniques. The findings from this analysis could provide a starting point for exploring these topics in future studies. The work presented also incorporates a novel approach to analyzing GDoF values, providing a more flexible alternative to computing the extremal gain of network techniques. The methods used here could be used to analyze other networks by adapting the introduced approach. The results from the analysis conducted here are confirmed through numerical studies and the approach is applicable to any non-cooperative, fixed transmission power network, making it versatile and universally applicable. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Therefore, our multiple-time-step integration algorithm is an efficient and accurate solution for simulating complex sediment transport. Additionally, this algorithm is highly versatile and can be applied to various particle-based modeling techniques. Furthermore, our research offers a preliminary framework for investigating the impact of collision schemes on simulation outcomes. In the future, we plan to further develop this algorithm for a wider range of applications.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. One proof technique utilizes a argument by contradiction along with Galois theory, while the other approach leverages the first cases analysis and the QZK (Zassenhaus' Quaternion Zolotov) theorem to demonstrate the proposed strategy's efficacy. Additionally, this paper explores the potential extension of this concept to other types of algebraic expressions and discusses related topics. Furthermore, this work implies that for any prime number $p$, there will always exist at least two integers, $a$ and $b$, which are congruent to each other modulo $p$ yet not congruent to $p$ itself, with the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ being divisible by $p$. This paper also discusses several instances, including prime numbers $7$, $13$, and $19$. Lastly, this work identifies potential directions for further inquiry. This paper is intended to honor and pay tribute to Dr. Zolotov's contributions to mathematics. Dr. Zolotov was a distinguished and accomplished mathematician known for his groundbreaking work in various areas of algebra and number theory. He was a highly respected figure in the mathematical community, celebrated for his brilliant ideas and his ability to pose intriguing, challenging problems that inspired others to delve deeper and become involved in the field. Among his numerous achievements, Dr. Zolotov is particularly famous for formulating $24$ distinct cases of the Impossibility Theorem, a landmark achievement that represented a major breakthrough in the field of number theory. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot reached a height of 14.2cm, a distance short of its intended target due to unforeseen forces acting on the robot's body during flight. To validate the feasibility of the proposed method, a physical experiment was conducted using a reduced-scale robot. The outcomes of the simulation were used to inform the design and optimization of the feedback controller, which was subsequently employed in the physical experiment. The successful implementation of the feedback controller on the actual robot demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed method. Additionally, the results from the simulation and physical experiment revealed that the robot's performance could be optimized through detailed design optimization, taking into consideration the behavior of individual grains during hopping. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. These values demonstrate the form factor's sensitivity to quark mass and momentum, consistent with expectations derived from the Salpeter equation. Additionally, a detailed analysis of the $a_0$ and $\eta'$ mesons reveals that their extended structures significantly contribute to the magnitude of their charge radii, with results indicating a notable discrepancy between the elastic form factor and the charge radius in the $\eta'$ meson. A comparative study with existing literature is also presented. Lastly, the inclusion of a scalar meson subset with ambient properties has been incorporated into the study. Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass. The current study focuses on the droplet's impact on its surrounding air, with initial observations suggesting the influence of electrical forces on the transport of particulate matter, potentially leading to the development of new theories that could bridge the gap between continuum-based models and more fundamental approaches like direct numerical simulations. The researchers also propose a new concept, electrocapillarity, as a means to describe the droplet-air interaction and suggest applicable simulation methods, including the use of computational fluid dynamics, for better understanding and modeling the behavior of this two-phase system. The proposed approach and simulation tools could also find practical applications in various scenarios, including the design of droplet-based reactors and the avoidance of droplet contamination in gas streams. The potential for heat and mass transfer enhancement through electrical means has yet to be explored scientifically. The researchers demonstrate the capabilities of their proposed framework by simulating a pendulous water droplet exposed to a resonating electric field, revealing the presence of nonlinear oscillations that affect the air circulation and, in turn, are influenced by the surrounding air. The resulting behavior is characterized by shifts in droplet frequency, airflow patterns, and aerosol particle circulation. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our research strives to initiate a broader movement to create NLP models capable of accurately processing negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. The CONDAQA dataset is available at this link: https://github.com/google-research-datasets/CONDAQA. The code for our challenging tasks can be found at this link: https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/condaqa_challenges. We look forward to collaborating with researchers looking to tackle this complex NLP problem.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. When assessed against human-made hierarchies, our method's topic suggestions correlate strongly with the existing categorization systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the topics generated by HDTM have a high degree of diversity, allowing for more precise categorization and thus making them exceptionally suitable for use in applications like search engines and web-based navigation tools. Our research is accompanied by a publicly accessible implementation on the MCMCChaLearn repository. For more information and live demonstrations, please visit our project website at the indicated URL.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Despite the model's simplicity, its physics retains key aspects of quantum annealing's fundamental nature. Furthermore, the statistical analysis employed here introduces a robust way to extract rich physical insight from complex dynamics within quantum systems subject to quench or annealing. In this case, the insight gained facilitates the development of efficient quantum annealing algorithms. The described statistical approach may also be applicable to other dynamic systems that exhibit complex behavior. This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes. Prior landau damping theory is an extension of this research. This work is an early stage of an ongoing project, and further investigation is required to explore the full implications of the derived phase mixing estimates. The ultimate goal of this project is to analyze the long-term existence of solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation. We use radiance data from space to study wave slopes in oceans during the day, specifically using about 300 channels between 3.6 and 4.0 $\mu$m, which takes into account solar radiation reflected off the water. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to 15 m/s. Our method reevaluates Cox and Munk's methodology for determining wave-slope probability distribution from photographs of sun glints, offering an alternative, more robust approach for retrieving parameters of a probability distribution function. Our results for wave slope statistics are comparable to previous findings, yet our data exhibits reduced uncertainties that pinpoint potential discrepancies between observed wave behaviors and previous models at moderate wind speeds. Our study also highlights how wave slope statistics change as wind speed increases, specifically noting the impact on skewness, kurtosis coefficients, and the behavior of updown wind asymmetry. Our results also show that wind speed has a noticeable effect on the probability distribution of wave periods, with variations becoming more pronounced at higher wind speeds, and the occurrence of shorter periods decreasing as wind speed increases. Additionally, our analysis reveals the relationship between wave periods and slopes, including how specific probability distribution parameters change as wind speed increases, and offers a theoretical explanation for the observed wave dynamics based on Moffat's model. Moreover, our study shows that in order to accurately model wave dynamics, it's necessary to account for wind-induced changes in wave slope and period distributions, including aspects like asymmetry and the occurrence of extreme events. Our approach also paves the way for analyzing wave behaviors at night, using night-time radiance data, which could provide valuable insights into how waves evolve during the day and at night. Our results are consistent with physical intuition and other research on ocean waves, also offering a framework for further research and potential applications in oceanography, renewable energy, and naval operations. This approach can offer a free, satellite-based alternative to measuring wave slopes, which could be particularly useful in areas with limited in situ measurements or missing buoy data. When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. Concrete results and
performance gains resulting from this method are also included. A publicly
accessible implementation of our technique is available online.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored. Our research employs 10 distinct classifiers and achieves accuracy rates of up to 87.76%. Furthermore, context learning was applied to distinguish actual news from fake news, achieving accuracy levels of up to 85.59%. Our study utilized a dataset containing 10,000 tweets and demonstrated the efficacy of combining sentiment analysis with context learning to enhance understanding of large social media datasets. Our research contributes to the development of cutting-edge techniques for managing big data and advancing the cause of women's empowerment through social media awareness. Additionally, our study offers practical applications in crisis management, public awareness, and the dissemination of beneficial opinions. In the future, we plan to expand our research by incorporating more sophisticated deep learning algorithms. Our study is accessible online at https://github.com/AnuGupta1091/Twitter-Context-Learning. Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of planar stripes and charge domains enabled alternative Josephson coupling theories. Our study finds the average intralayer interaction to be greater than interlayer coupling and comparable to condensation energy, ultimately yielding long-range phase order-driven superconductivity. As an outcome, the relationship between the square of interlayer and intralayer penetration depths to the respective resistivity ratios exhibits proportionality near the superconducting transition, corroborated by multiple measurements. The ratio of the two penetration depths is found to be proportional to the ratio of the two condensation energies, further substantiating the long-range phase order-driven nature of superconductivity in these materials. The discovered relationships hold true across various cuprate materials. The inherent nature of planar stripe and charge domain architectures prevents the onset of superconductivity by themselves, instead requiring long-range phase order for superconductivity to emerge. Ultimately, our analysis offers an alternative explanation for the observed ratio of interlayer and intralayer magnetic penetration depths in cuprate superconductors. The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  Interestingly, such quark star profiles could be distinct from soft quark star candidates, potentially leading to a new pathway for confronting theoretical models with observational data.  Furthermore, our findings suggest the adiabatic index could be a crucial indicator for different quark star phases, providing a prerequisite for a more in-depth analysis of our proposed scenario through models that incorporate magnetic fields and crusts.  Last but not the least, our theoretical framework can be applied to scenarios like the PSR J0030+0452, allowing for a range of parameters that accommodate its data while highlighting the significance of obtaining accurate and independent measurements of the pulsar's radius and mass.  With such information in hand, our research highlights the value of high-precision pulsar radius and mass measurements, a key aspect of the next generation of pulsar detectors that will be crucial in confronting theoretical gravity theories with observational data. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present the results of experiments utilizing this lower bound to improve the efficiency of the cutting plane method for determining maximum-weight Tai mapping between two trees. The anti Tai mapping concept is also applicable to multiple trees, leading to new upper and lower bounds for the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem. The most significant improvement, obtained with the new lower bound, was an optimal solution for a tree with 108 nodes in 15.8 minutes, compared to the previous best time of 12 hours. The new methods are expected to contribute to future research on tree isomorphism and related problems. The associated source code is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/anti-tai-mapping/anti-tai-mapping. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. A vertical extent of 1-10 d units, depending on the disk, characterizes the VSI's vertical stability interval. As particles continue to develop, their depth increases, eventually reducing dust growth-driven VSI in areas around 1-10 AU. Nevertheless, smaller particles can stimulate VSI in these areas, creating an odd-sized particle pattern. As particles settle towards the disk's center, their depth increases, reducing VSI-driven turbulence, eventually causing it to disappear entirely. This analysis provides a foundation for a more comprehensive study of particle effects on VSI and could be integrated into models predicting the evolution of protoplanetary disks. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Our proof draws from the work of Ni and Souplet, incorporating an analysis of the harmonic function's norm and applying Liouville's theorem to obtain estimates. Finally, this research is an expansion of a paper presented at the 2009 CMS-CRM workshop on nonlinear partial differential equations.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we established that the associated measurement error in parallax can exceed 100 $\mu$as under certain viewing conditions, which may be relevant for future missions like Euclid and Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope. Additionally, we identified areas of the sky that Gaia will find particularly challenging to accurately measure parallaxes for, primarily due to its orientation and the solar system's position. These areas include the solar compass and regions within $10^{\circ}$ of the Sun, where the satellite's viewing angle contributes significantly to large parallax errors. We also outlined strategies to mitigate these challenges, including shifting the satellite's orientation in flight. By implementing these changes, we believe that future missions can significantly reduce the uncertainty associated with variable PPN $\gamma$. Consequently, future missions like Euclid and WFIRST may be able to achieve overall parallax measurement errors of less than 10 $\mu$as. This represents a notable improvement over Gaia's expected error of around 24 $\mu$as and could substantially benefit various scientific applications. Which of these potential improvements most significantly enhances the effectiveness of Euclid or WFIRST? How does this improvement relate to the challenge of variable PPN $\gamma$?

Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical-lattice potential and utilizes interaction forces with opposite signs to create an equilibrium where both solitons accelerate equally. Meanwhile, the total momentum remains conserved. Another model, derived from Gross-Pitaevskii equations for resonantly-coupled atomic components using a microwave field, facilitates an exact transformation to a moving frame of reference, thus providing predictions for one- and two-dimensional stable self-accelerating solitons, including vortex rings. Notably, this research extends the scope of models featuring stable self-accelerating modes beyond the parameter space of linear Airy waves. It is also demonstrated in this analysis that self-accelerating modes can be achieved through modal interaction in the presence of an optical-lattice potential. This novel approach may offer a practical pathway for creating self-accelerating solitons in laboratory settings. A photograph illustrating a self-accelerating ring soliton in an optical-lattice environment is included. This innovative work is expected to pave the way for exploring self-accelerating modes in binary Bose-Einstein condensate systems. It is anticipated that the unique characteristics of these models will shape the future of applications and directed self-assembly in multicomponent Bose-Einstein condensates. This research is also expected to spark the investigation of nonlinear effects in other systems exhibiting Galilean invariance. It is hoped that the analysis presented in this report will spark the investigation of nonlinear phenomena in directed self-asssembly in binary Bose-Einstein condensates. It is further expected that the unique characteristics of these models will shape the future of applications in this field. It is also hoped that the work will spark the investigation of nonlinear effects in other systems

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. SIMC 2.0's enhanced design may serve as a starting point for optimizing other ML models that incorporate linear and non-linear layers. Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. In addition, three previously undetected HI clouds have been discovered near the southern edge of the M101 disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields (including finite fields, global fields, and local fields). In this work, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global or local field into the sum of the minimal integers of its absolute value and a new component. This new component can be expressed as a sum of the unit powers of its corresponding field, significantly simplifying the application of Regula Falsi Method in such fields. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. Several of these devices have already been designed and manufactured at the University of Sydney's research facility, and we are collaborating with multiple international astronomy projects to further develop and utilize these innovative devices. This innovative approach to spectroscopy has numerous applications and may soon become the new standard for traditional spectroscopy methods. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms.
