Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. Moreover, the study showed that the rotation rate can be divided into three distinct regimes, each characterized by a unique bi-stable relationship between geostrophic vortices and wave turbulence. Two of these regimes were previously identified, while the third, most rapid regime is discovered in the current study. In this highest rotation rate regime, the stable geostrophic vortices state breaks down, and the flow transitions directly to a turbulent state, supporting the triad interaction of three independent waves, which is theoretically predicted but yet to be analytically confirmed. The discovered regime also expands the previously proposed 'triplexity transition' theory. The need for higher resolution simulations is highlighted to accurately capture the transition to the new regime, and the study paves the way for the development of new numerical models that can tackle the highest rotation rate regime. The findings are also expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of the Earth's turbulent core. The study reveals the possibility of multiple frequency combinations existing within the Earth's core and may aid in the identification of the'split' window period phenomenon. Moreover, it is proposed that the newly discovered triad frequency combination $S(2,0,0)T_{2,0,0}$, present in the Earth's outer core, could provide valuable information on the dynamo's strength and direction. The study's results are validated through comparisons with previous experiments and theoretical analyses, and the findings are further illustrated by analyzing the velocity field and spectral energy diagrams. The discovered regime is also shown to follow the $E(k)\sim k^{-3}$ wave turbulence spectrum, and the study concludes by discussing the potential applications and outstanding questions for the two regimes that exist between the stable geostrophic vortices and wave turbulence. The study also sets the stage for future research to be conducted with the Earth's core in mind

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, the research also uncovered an unfortunate finding that mental health treatment is not provided to all eligible offenders as court decisions appear to be influenced by the type of crime they committed with more serious cases being given treatment more frequently.  Therefore, the research suggests that mental health treatment should be provided to all eligible offenders as part of their rehabilitation regardless of the crime they committed and that the benefits to both the offender and society outweigh the expenses.  Furthermore, mental health treatment could be used as a way to monitor and measure the effectiveness of the justice system's rehabilitation efforts.  The research also offers suggestions on how to gather more data and conduct additional analyses to further understand the relationship between mental health treatment and recidivism rates.  The methodology used to collect and analyze the data is outlined in the additional appendix materials included with this report.  The research is relevant to the broader debate on the effectiveness of rehabilitation within the justice system and could be used to guide policy decisions related to funding and providing mental health treatment to offenders as part of their rehabilitation.  Ultimately, the research suggests that a bigger emphasis should be placed on providing mental health treatment to all eligible offenders as it is likely to reduce recidivism rates which will in turn lower future crime rates and ultimately cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Therefore, it is in the best interest of both the offender and society to provide mental health treatment as part of their rehabilitation efforts.  Future analysis is proposed to conduct a more in depth examination of the relationship between specific types of mental health treatment and recidivism rates as well as to conduct a financial analysis of the costs and benefits of providing mental health treatment to all eligible offenders.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub. The results show that the proposed technique achieves higher overall scores and reduces the gap between supervised and labelled data performances. In particular, the technique yields improved average Dice scores of 0.792 (baseline 0.767) and 0.824 (baseline 0.793) on the ACDC and MMWHS datasets, respectively. Moreover, contrast agent equilibrium MRI images can be generated using a technique called contrast patching, which is an efficient adaptive data augmentation method that is simple to implement and is now publicly available as an open-source Python tool called SmartAug on GitHub. This methodology is adaptable to various medical image segmentation applications. Additionally, further research is recommended to explore the technique's potential applications in other semi-supervised image segmentation contexts. Lastly, in accordance with the guidelines laid out in the paper, the code should be made open-source and the methodology's potential limitations explored through theoretical analysis. This technique has the added benefit of reducing the requirement for extensive annotation by generating realistic unlabelled data, which in turn speeds up training and enhances segmentation accuracy when using limited annotated images. To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This deployment will result in the ATLAS trigger being capable of processing up to 12.8 gigabits per second of raw data with a maximum latency of 25 microseconds, representing a significant improvement over the current generation of such systems. This improvement is made possible by the design's high performance, low latency, and excellent scalability, which positions the jFEX design as a relevant solution for any future particle collider projects that may arise. This design also serves as a model for other possible FEX extensions, such as those involving electrically identifying calorimeter clusters or muon trigger systems. This project has contributed valuable expertise and knowledge on high-speed FPGA processing, board design, and digital design overall, with many lessons learned during its development slated for inclusion in relevant future projects. This expertise has been used to optimize the design for maximum performance within the given latency constraint, with the resulting design boasting a impressively tight 25 microseconds latency. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. The method is particularly applicable to the estimation of a component of a mixing distribution, a problem commonly faced in cluster analysis. The relevant R package is available on the CRAN website. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Our results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in a range regime not previously analyzed. Furthermore, experimental outcomes validate the algorithm's performance on synthetic data and real-world settings, observing rates of convergence comparable to those of conventional federated learning algorithms once sufficient data is available. The source code is available at: https://github.com/CompGamer/FedBuffAsync.git. The modified FedBuff algorithm addresses scalability limitations and provides a foundation for further asynchronous federated learning research.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). These findings have the potential to contribute to the development of more advanced multilingual ASR systems. Additionally, we have made our data and code available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/luosong84/cz-asr. Employing a perturbative QCD approach, we calculate the di-kaon distribution amplitudes from LHCb data, specifically from quasi-two-body $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$ decays containing the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  The calculated distributions can be used to explain BaBar's measurements of the $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ decay at an invariant mass $M(K^+K^-)\sim 1.5$ GeV, showing the contribution from $\rho^0(1450)$. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions within a general quartic potential that is compatible with the global and gauge symmetries. By analyzing minimum-energy configurations and performing Monte Carlo simulations, we've studied the phase diagrams, Higgs phases, and corresponding symmetry-breaking patterns. The influence of the quartic potential has also been considered. Additionally, we explored whether lattice model transitions relate to the behavior of continuum field theory at its stable charged fixed points, particularly for 2 color gauge group SU(Nc=2) where we found some evidence that charged critical behaviors occur when there are more flavors (Nf > Nf*) of scalar field, and that this value of Nf lies within the range 20 to 40. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and a real-world underwater navigation experiment using a Remotely Operated Vehicle. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. We also discovered that k is equal to n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3. Interestingly, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 when d = 4, indicating that it grows sublinearly in n. Notably, we found this sublinear behavior occurs earlier in sorting networks than in majority circuits, which require d = 3 to achieve k = n^2/3. Additionally, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 (rounded up) for any depth (d) of n/2, providing further insight into the relationship between k and d. Our research builds upon and enhances existing knowledge by establishing lower bounds on k in terms of n and providing a comprehensive framework for studying sorting networks composed of comparators with arbitrary arity. We hope this framework enables future exploration and contributes to a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties and behavior of such networks. Notably, our method's performance in particular excelled at differentiating between the most challenging COVID-19 grades, thereby highlighting its clinical utility. Moreover, our technique successfully mitigated over-reliance on individual data components, ensuring a robust classification outcome. Through comprehensive experimentation, we validated the efficacy of our innovative lesion-aware classification approach. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code and model are available online for further research.

A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we established a lower bound showing that for any mechanism with more than two agents, or that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, there exists an instance and corresponding equilibrium in which the induced allocation is not fair up to one good. Our investigation provides a detailed analysis of the equilibria resulting from various allocation methods and a lower bound on the complexity of achieving fair allocations in such scenarios. Our findings open up new research directions at the intersection of algorithmic game theory, mechanism design, and the fair allocation of resources.

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle the variability within a domain. Our proposed CoSA method is an example of strong adaptation, where we distinguish it from alternative approaches like CoSA, a method of weak adaptation. Through our experiments on renowned UDA benchmarks, we demonstrate significant improvements over strong adaptation baselines, even surpassing several leading weak adaptation approaches. Our code and dataset generated based on our method are now available for public access at https://github.com/Alivio/CoSA-UDA. Moreover, we have incorporated our adaptations into open-source implementation repositories, including PyDAAlib and MMD Toolbox. Lastly, our project page is located at https://alivio.github.io/CoSA-UDA/.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Moreover, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with a larger dataset, thereby highlighting the method's immense potential as the dataset continues to expand in size and diversity. By making the code and model weights available to the public, we aim to accelerate the development of person re-identification methods that can be trained directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video. Our code and model weights can be accessed via the links provided in the references.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. Like previous research, our findings indicate that people's opposition to reducing the wealth gap is limited. However, unlike them, our results suggest this opposition is not solely driven by an inability to distinguish luck from skill. Rather, people seem capable of distinguishing between the two, but their willingness to act on this distinction is shaped by the specific circumstances presented to them. Moreover, our data show that people's opinions on income inequality are more sensitive to luck's influence when it affects job success rather than overall income, a distinction often blurred in laboratory research. Finally, our study includes a larger and more diverse group of participants than some existing research, which can make its findings more reliable in the long run. Nonetheless, our data were collected over ten years ago, which raises the question of whether people's opinions on this matter have changed over time. Consequently, there is a clear need for updated research in this area. The additional analysis we conducted in response to concerns about demand effects also suggests that the relationships we observed between people's opinions on income redistribution and the circumstances presented to them are real and not the result of exerting pressure on participants to respond in a certain way by researchers. Finally, our study's results can be applied to various real-world scenarios, such as understanding why people may be more willing to provide financial assistance to those who have lost their jobs due to external factors rather than company layoffs. In summary, this research advances our knowledge of how people's opinions on income inequality are shaped by their perceptions of chance influencing worker outcomes and provides methods for modeling these opinions. It also highlights the importance of incorporating a broader perspective and diverse groups in laboratory research aimed at understanding complex, society-wide issues. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. The underlying theoretical computations are the focus of a related theoretical framework, which provides a comprehensive discussion of the computational issues and presents a new approach to approximating the Shapley value through a simple and efficient Monte Carlo-based method. The source code for DataScope is openly available online.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. The validity of our methods is demonstrated through numerical simulations and experimental data analysis of a single-section DBR lasers operated at threshold and above threshold. The proposed techniques provide quantitative assessment of directional emission and could be useful in optimizing microcavity laser design. Additionally, they hold potential for analyzing other resonant emitters undergoing spontaneous emission.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The empirical studies reveal that our method not only outperforms current benchmarks but also showcases the influence of different components on performance. Additionally, an in-depth analysis of the learned models provides valuable insights into offline multi-agent policy learning. The code is available at: \url{https://github.com/awhaoli/SIT}. All datasets used in the experiments can be found at: \url{https://github.com/awhaoli/SIT_Datasets}.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Additional tests using 20 abdominal images and 10 liver images confirmed the method's effectiveness. Our results indicate a CNN can learn optimal weights to register images with limited capture ranges, yielding superior performance compared to intensity-based methods. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Moreover, our study proposes the utilization of single-particle entanglement in epimeric atomic states in a network comprising three stations, enabling the non-local manipulation of these atoms based on the results of measurements taken during the transmission process. This technique could potentially facilitate the development of non-local quantum communication protocols employing single particles instead of entangled states shared between two parties. Consequently, single-particle entanglement's minimal information density may no longer be a limitation for protocols involving genuine non-locality. Ultimately, our analysis highlights single-particle entanglement's inherent non-locality and its potential to empower a wide range of non-local quantum tasks and applications. The described setup may also serve as a foundation for exploring single-particle entanglement in various scenarios. The proposed network setup may also be employed in research focused on single-particle entanglement's generative capabilities and the relationship between single-particle and multi-particle entanglement. The described method of single-particle entanglement generation based on spreading and interference may also be applied to a broader range of atomic systems, offering a novel approach to creating single-particle entanglement. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Further study extends this concept to multi-user scenarios, with encouraging results.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our research offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters and predicts numerous future detections of such events. This framework can be refined with the help of data from future gravitational waves missions like the Enhanced DeciHan All-Sky Gravitational Wave Antenna network and the third-generation gravitational waves detectors. This research can also be expanded to incorporate the influence of Population III binary remnants that fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with stellar streams. This addition will provide a more detailed understanding of the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters and the merging of these remnants, thereby offering greater insight into the early universe's structure and evolution. This research will be made publicly accessible through an interactive visualisation tool that enables users to explore and analyse the movement and development of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters. This tool will be accompanied by a comprehensive user manual and will be available at a public webpage.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold. Furthermore, a extensive examination of the slowing period uncovered several insights, revealing for instance that the effectiveness of new knowledge more than doubles in fields like high energy physics and mathematical physics. In addition, the distribution of new knowledge efficacy was found to adhere to a fat-tailed pattern, characterized by heavy tails in fields like plastic surgery, orthopedics, and economics, indicating a considerable gap between the most innovative and the least innovative contributions. Moreover, an examination of the time it takes to produce the same level of new knowledge revealed a substantial acceleration in fields like computer science, that is in proportionate to the literature growth. Finally, by employing survival statistics, researchers identified the probability of producing new knowledge within a certain time frame for specific fields, that can be as low as 20% in fields like planetary sciences or as high as 60% in fields like clinical neurology. Ultimately, the developed framework provides a universal tool for measuring the effectiveness of new knowledge production, offering a flexible approach that enables the analysis of new knowledge efficacy through various methods, that can be used to monitor the evolution of scientific disciplines and guide strategies for improving the productivity of scientific research. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical foundation for the development of secure dual hop OFDM communication systems. Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of the system. In our research, we combine these photonic setups with quantum sources, using a Harper-Hofstadter model to illustrate scenarios where quantum emitters display nearly quantized emission rates. These increased emission rates can result from interactions with multiple edge modes within different energy gaps. Notably, we find that spontaneous emission from these sources can separate spatially, creating time-bin entangled states upon applying a single control pulse. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of emitters selectively interacting with distinct channels via light-matter coupling. These capabilities provide the foundation for implementing quantum operations among protected photons and generating complex, entangled states of light within these topological channels. These developments hold promise for realizing efficient and stable quantum light-matter interactions in photonic topological circuits. These findings also pave the way for employing quantum emitters in sensitive measurements, such as detecting subtle changes in topological edge currents and identifying rare events associated with topological phase transitions. These advancements integrate quantum emitters with protected photons, enabling a broader exploration of quantum phenomena in this field.

In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability. Additionally, we investigate the predictive capabilities of our model by assessing its consistency across multiple traffic light cycles. The design of the predictive model-extractor filter has also been evaluated in terms of its consistency and ability to adapt to short-time scales. Our results, obtained through simulation and the analysis of real-world data, demonstrate that this approach enhances the safety of connected automated vehicles when interacting with human-driven vehicles at traffic signals. Our research offers a novel solution to an critical problem and can serve as a starting point for further exploration of predictive control systems in similar scenarios. The developed code is available online.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our analysis reveals that this immense improvement in speed comes from a subtle balance between two factors: dramatically reducing memory usage (from 100MB to 10MB) and switching from sequential to concurrent evaluation methods. 
Consequentially, high-speed testing identifies significant flaws in two popular evaluation metrics, including unexpected issues with performance reliability. 
Notably, trusted secondary evaluation metrics, despite being subjective and more nuanced, reveal striking correlations with results obtained from extremely fast tests. 
Thus, we confidently recommend TextWorldExpress as a reference platform for testing text-based game agents, given its unparalleled speed, affordable memory usage, and remarkably consistent outcomes. 
Additionally, we proactively address potential limitations and several actionable suggestions for further optimizing text-based game challenges and evaluation methods. 
The source code and benchmark data are available for public review and utilization at https://github.com/ThangLuu/TextWorldExpress. 
Its official website is located at https://textworldexpress.github.io/. 
We cordially invite the public to join the discussion and contribute to TextWorldExpress.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. As a result, this research provides a comprehensive solution that can be applied to a broader range of sequence analysis applications beyond video recognition. Meanwhile, the customized hardware platforms may serve as reference designs for developing efficient accelerators for LSTMs. As for the customized hardware, the designs and simulations are publicly available to facilitate further research and experimentation. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the U(1) case, can be validated by testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. Our exploratory examination reveals that the Charge Convexity Conjecture is upheld in each instance examined, yet we have not discerned the underlying reason for this behavior from the perspective of conformal field theory. On the other hand, in the context of gravity within anti-de Sitter space, the mass-to-charge ratio of scalar particles can be interpreted as constituting a convex function of charge under a U(1) symmetry and, not surprisingly, displays conformity with the Weak Gravity Conjecture. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity is further substantiated by its association with another formulated conjecture, namely the Bound Conjecture, which posits that the product of the mass and decay width of a particle should be non-negative and, under certain circumstances, can be interpreted as the imaginary component of its scalar gravity field. To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results. Through chemical potential simulations, we investigate the electronic properties of the Hubbard model, discovering that model-space constraints have minimal impact on the phase diagram results. However, this effect should be considered when interpreting excited-state calculations. We conclude that unitary approximation within MSQITE is generally acceptable; nonetheless, its validity relies on the specific problem at hand. Lastly, we suggest that quantum simulation studies make use of a smaller model space before its unitary approximation is validated through comparison with full-space quantum imaginary time evolution or other reliable methods. This research is relevant to current quantum chemical state simulations on quantum computers and can contribute to the development of chemical theories using the quantum computer. Additionally, it may be applied to the study of dynamical systems via the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. We have made our model-space QITE algorithm publicly available on GitHub to facilitate its use in research.

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model and its methodology are available for further research and policy analysis at no cost on the MESA modeling platform. The full source code can be accessed via https://github.com/pardee-courses/ElecAncillaryServices2023S2/tree/main/code. The model's results and data are hosted on the MESA data platform at https://data.pardeeTank.org/pardee-courses/ElecAncillaryServices2023S2. The model's source code and data are subject to change based on user feedback and research advancements. The model's current version is compatible with Python 3.8 and earlier versions may also function with these earlier Python versions but have been tested with the latest available Python 3.8 standard. The model's file structure and naming conventions adhere to the MESA naming standards available at https://mesa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/agentbased_model_best_practices.html. The model's development was conducted using the MESA Python toolset for Power System Analysis and the PyPSA-AlRes PyPSA module. The model's results and data have been reviewed and validated by Pardee Center for International Development's research and editorial staff.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. The foundation for our analysis is laid by a combinatorial argument highlighting the prevalence of distinct elements in the Galois group, followed by an application of the fundamental theorem of counting. The resulting expression for the Galois group's order enables us to establish several conjectures as theorems. The developed techniques also enable us to derive additional consequences, including the generalization of Fano's conjecture to all finite fields. The connection between the Galois group's order and Fano's conjecture was initially explored by Jones and Prendiville in the context of large finite fields. The current research generalizes this finding to the context of function fields over finite fields. The general framework established here is further utilized in our accompanying paper, where we explore the properties of the Galois group of an iterated polynomial with coefficients from a global field. The common thread uniting these various results is the concept of Fano's conjecture, which is examined in its own right throughout the discussion. The combination of methods employed, including the application of the fundamental theorem of counting and the properties of the symmetric group, provides a framework for further investigations into the Galois group of an iterated polynomial. The results presented here also give rise to new conjectures related to the distribution of distinct elements within the Galois group, where this conjectures are linked to broader theories, including the Bateman-Horn conjecture, before concluding with the general case of Fano's conjecture.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency. This study underscores the challenges associated with measuring Higgs boson pair interactions through non-resonant decays at the LHC. Further advancements in methodological research will be crucial for in-depth analysis of Higgs boson pair production data in future LHC runs.  Additionally, we provide standalone software for generating top quark pair events with explicit $\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ final states, which can be used in conjunction with ME treatments of $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$. The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of systems with strong correlations.  Our data suggest that changes in hybridization, effective carrier density, lattice volume, and spin degrees of freedom, possibly in the order of Coulomb interaction, are the underlying factors for such a transfer of spectral weight, thus facilitating a deeper understanding of the physics governing V$_2$O$_3$.  Lastly, our research offers a multidisciplinary perspective on investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films, taking into consideration the effects of surface termination, in an effort to develop a more holistic framework.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Furthermore, this technique may be extended to different types of light-matter interactions and systems with multiple components. As a result, we're able to study the hyperfine interaction's influence on the scattering dynamics of the M\"ossbauer nuclei by analyzing the phase and amplitude information in our data. This study could lead to a better understanding of the system's dynamics and enable the development of new applications based on the characteristics of the target itself. As an example, we propose a method for creating a entanglement source with a high probability of success. This proposal stems from investigating the dynamics of elastic scattering, demonstrated with an example involving a pair of protons. By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware. As such, we suggest considering error correcting codes as a valuable tool for understanding the fundamental limitations of quantum circuit performance in noisy scenarios. This perspective is demonstrated using the quantum repetition code, where we discuss the effects of failing stabilizer readout circuits on code performance and investigate the impact of periodically malfunctioning circuits on this code's ability to correct errors. Our findings, which were determined through Monte Carlo simulations of a corresponding classical spin model, reveal that the ability of the quantum repetition code to withstand errors follows a classic threshold behavior, where above a certain noise threshold the code fails to provide significant benefit over unencoded quantum computation. We also compare our results to the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder and find that this decoding strategy can provide improved results, particularly at higher noise levels. However, our findings also indicate that the code can perform well with certain decoding strategies, even in scenarios where the noise level exceeds the threshold for correctable errors. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. The main aspects of our approach are further analyzed through a priori error estimates, with additional research needed to investigate the methodology's applicability to higher-order elements. The method's usability and efficacy are also showcased through the inclusion of two realistic case studies. One such case involves fractural porosity evolving over time, addressed through an implicit numerical time-stepping approach. The other case examines the effects of varying fluid viscosity on flow patterns within blocking-fractured media. Our proposed method offers a novel numerical framework for modeling blocking fractures, while also providing conductive fracture resolution. This could potentially lead to the development of more precise models for modeling flow within fractured media. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. This innovative approach to studying discourse indicators is demonstrated by analyzing the top-ranked indicators in each of the four primary categories (contrast, condition, cause-effect, and linkage), as defined by the Katz back-off n-gram model. A manual examination of the relationships expressed by the top indicators in each category reveals some interesting findings. For example, in the contrast category, "by contrast" remains the most frequently occurring indicator across all registered instances, accounting for over 370 out of 400 instances. On the other hand, in the condition category, "happily" is not as universally accepted as previously thought and can be replaced by more situational indicators such as "since" and "as". Taking a large-p limit, they found the model reduces to a relativistic sigma model in three-dimensional space, described by the SU(3)/U(1)^2 manifold. Consequently, this study suggests the spin model may effectively represent a combination of descriptions for high-temperature superconductors, accounting for both VBS and Néel phases. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Lastly, we outline potential future research directions.

The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Finally, our research highlights the importance of considering the effects of gravity and weather on evaporation and virus survival in models of infection spread.

The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. This research is relevant to multiple applications, including debt collection, company benchmarking, and tax revenue optimization. The applicable solvers and our methodology for scalable optimal netting solutions are made publicly available as part of the ROMAN NETTING PROJECT. This project comprises an open-source suite consisting of C++ implementations and integrates the BLIS graph library, delivering superior performance on large-scale graphs. The computational performance of our algorithms is evaluated utilizing Roman Netting data, along with general graph benchmarks. The project's findings and outcomes are derived using up to 1.5 terabytes of RAM and powered by IBM's Cloud. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The developed framework is further incorporated into the training of multiple leading dialogue state tracking models, demonstrating its universal applicability. The code and models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/leezhousail/ASSIST.
