It is now possible to produce plasma with densities of up to 1.6 x 10^20 particles per cubic meter, and the source can produce stable plasma for extended periods of time. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To achieve this, the authors propose a novel use of a linear transformation based on cross-correlation, which produces exceptionally precise binary mask results. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, the detectives dataset is developed, containing 1000 cell samples with annotations, used to conduct comprehensive experiments, revealing that the detection accuracy of the W-shaped network, while being easier to train, surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art nucleus detection algorithms, including the conventional U-Net based models. Moreover, the results show a notable reduction in the model's parameter count, allowing for fully automatic detection of nuclei in real-world images, as demonstrated by detecting nuclei in an unseen image from the CAMEL dataset, a well-known cancer cell detection dataset. The code and dataset developed as part of this research are available online at this link https://github.com/zwang83/W-Shaped-Network. The code and dataset have been made publicly available as part of this research, and the novel approach presented has been patent-pending since August 2020. All rights are reserved by the patent applicants. Nevertheless, this work has been accepted for publication at the Medical Image Analysis conference, which takes precedence in the research timeline. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. As a result, the combined simulator will provide valuable predictive analytics for ongoing COVID-19 research. Additionally, the simplicity and modularity of this single-cell model make it an invaluable teaching tool for hosting workshops on multi-scale modeling of infectious diseases. Alongside this, we are organizing a series of coding challenges to encourage the open-source sharing of models and algorithms for hosting workshops on multi-scale modeling of infectious diseases. This initiative aims to facilitate collaboration, facilitate the exchange of knowledge, and make available a suite of educational materials for a broader range of researchers. External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process. However, the proposed approaches have limitations, and the results highlight the challenges involved in successfully splitting an environment into its components. Further research is required to address these challenges and make the method more reliable. The code for the proposed techniques is available online.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. Notably, our approach differs from other approaches, as it directly verifies the refinement against the actual program behavior rather than relying on refinement-based programming with a type isomorphism translation. Additionally, HELMHOLTZ has been successfully applied in refining Michelson programs against their intended specifications, as evidenced by over 2000 lines of verified code. This achievement demonstrates the capability of HELMHOLTZ to statically verify the correctness of complex Michelson programs, making it a valuable contribution to the refinement type research community. The principles and methods developed in HELMHOLTZ are also applicable to refining Michelson programs against its built-in invariants, leading to more reliable and trusted Michelson programs. The design and performance of HELMHOLTZ have been thoroughly evaluated through three key studies, resulting in promising outcomes that align with programmer expectations and refine Michelson programs with satisfactory efficiency. Notably, the implementation of HELMHOLTZ has been publicly released as an Azurite extension and is actively being utilized in the development of mainstream Tezos applications, including smart contracts and digital asset transactions, for the latest version of Tezos. As such, HELMHOLTZ is the first-ever static verification tool for Michelson and has paved the way for future refinement types research, enabling it to be recognized as a pioneering achievement in this field. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Our exhaustive examination aims to facilitate a comprehensive grasp of GCNNs and serve as a reference for mapping the underlying mechanics of any GCNN model. The comprehensive framework we outline can also be employed to analyze other customized GCNN architectures. The accompanying code enables replication of the analysis, including the visualization of each step within the GCNN process. The code has been carefully optimized and is capable of processing substantial datasets. The guidelines provided within the code enable users to easily adapt it for evaluating additional GCNN models. The code is fully compatible with TensorFlow 2.0. The comprehensive framework we outline, along with the accompanying code, is available at https://github/1aj7/Understanding-GCNNs. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Notably, the use of VSSA leads to a relative error reduction of approximately 50% in the estimation of lateral displacement when comparing VSSA and SA techniques. The study demonstrates the potential of VSSA to streamline elastography procedures by eliminating the need for lateral interpolation, thereby accelerating the reconstruction process by approximately 15%. This research paves the way for the clinical application of VSSA-based elastography in the assessment and monitoring of tissue pathologies. Furthermore, it highlights the scope for exploring the capabilities of advanced beamforming techniques in elastography. The proposed VSSA-OVERWIND approach may also be applicable to other elastography techniques utilizing beamforming processors. The study's outcomes also raise significant research questions, such as the suitability of OVERWIND for other elastography imaging techniques and the potential for integrating clinical data with simulation models. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. We have demonstrated the utility of this approach by creating a verifier that checks whether a given specification is satisfied by a provided evidence, implemented utilizing logical pseudocodes. This verifier effectively translates the specification into logical pseudocodes and executes the resulting program using a semi-formal approach, interacting with the evidence as if it were an input provided to the program. This technique has the benefit of providing a more intuitive and easier-to-audit validation method than the conventional method. This methodology is applicable to any web that can be defined through forward reasoning. We have applied this approach to validate our previous claims about web solvability and degree hierarchies. This method is anticipated to offer a more accessible and educational means of understanding and demonstrating various theoretical properties and achievements within the context of computability logic webs. A key objective is to establish a minimum number 'n' for any number of color options where a given V-shaped poset will be entirely colored with a specific color in a Boolean lattice. Recent work has led to the determination of Boolean Ramsey numbers for specific instances, and this paper aims to build on that by investigating the same concept for V-shaped posets and identifying minimum posets containing the Ramsey property in Boolean lattices of a particular size. Another area of research within this paper focuses on Boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers which involve identifying either a monochromatic structure or a structure with different color components within a Boolean lattice. This study explores this concept for V-shaped posets and their antichains. Notably, this paper's findings significantly surpass current knowledge on Boolean Ramsey numbers and provide a foundation for further investigation into related concepts.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Additionally, we demonstrate an adaptive variant of our algorithm, which tolerates errors up to $\epsilon$ and achieves an estimated solution accuracy of $\epsilon'$ in a single pass, requiring approximately $\frac{k}{\epsilon}\log(\frac{k\Delta}{\epsilon'})$ units of storage. This innovative algorithm draws inspiration from an earlier study by caney et al. as well as a different approach by ottoni et al. A direct application of these methods would result in excessively large storage requirements, with the former requiring over $2^k$ units of storage and the latter needing $k^{2+\delta}$ units for any $\delta > 0$, which are substantially less efficient than our proposed solution. The motivation behind our algorithm is an open problem for coreset algorithms in the context of dynamic data streams. The algorithm's success is built upon an novel application of the Shamos-Pippenger metric embedding technique to the $k$-means clustering problem. The challenges we overcome include establishing the properties required for the embedded metric to be valid and defining a suitable analog of the Farthest Point First method in the dynamic setting. The techniques we develop for resolving these challenges could have broader implications and contribute to a deeper understanding of the $k$-means clustering problem. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. The closed-loop source code for our hierarchical model is available online.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. Intuitively counterintuitive results may be derived from the properties of ordered components. 

In our exploration of 'free' probabilities associated with the original random variables and their ordered counterparts, we observe similarities with the properties of Haar distributed orthogonal and symmetries matrices in the large N limit, a finding that may be considered an initial step in the broader context of free probability theory. 

Our research provides an empirical explanation for the prevalence of nontransitive pairs and the distribution of components within such sets. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive results at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in transforming high-dose images into low-dose images with similar quality. However, one of the main limitations of this method is its reliance on two separate generators, one for each direction, which significantly increases its computational demand. In response to this problem, we propose a new simplified cycleGAN framework that uses a single switchable generator to simultaneously perform both transformations. The key innovation of this new framework is a learnable switchable mechanism, implemented by introducing an additional discriminator and an alternative direction generator. By doing so, we were able to convert a cycleGAN with two generators into a non-sparse cycleGAN with a single generator, without reducing its capacity. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method not only requires significantly fewer parameters but also produces images of similar quality compared to the traditional cycleGAN technique. Specifically, the new approach requires approximately one-fifth of the parameters of the original cycleGAN method, without being penalized, to achieve similar output quality. This simplified cycleGAN framework with a single generator also provides a valuable reference for further research into non-sparse unpaired image-to-image translation networks. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei. Our findings suggest that the deformed halo nuclei provide valuable insights into the interplay between single particle bound states and the continuum across various angular momentum levels. Moreover, we propose that the term 'distorted halo nucleus' be defined as a system exhibiting enhanced single particle resonance magnitude at zero angular momentum, with its ground state retaining halo characteristics visible up to angular momenta of 10-12$\hbar$. It also proposes specific signatures, including particular configuration patterns and density distributions, as well as spin differential E1 transitions, to identify rotating distorted halo systems. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing. Our research and code also contribute to a notable improvement (by 0.132) in the PSNR of the Video Super-Resolution (VSR) task on DVSR, with our approach serving as the baseline for subsequent top-performing VSR methods. In addition, our study on using optical flow to guide deformable alignment leads to a notable improvement (by 0.134) in the PSNR of the Compressed Video Super-Resolution (CVSR) task on CVSD, with our approach remaining the current state-of-the-art at the time of submission. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results reveal that while shared dynamics models are not always the
answer, structured and isolated sub-networks can facilitate better performance
in multi-task reinforcement learning. Additionally, we observe that using separate
dynamics models for each task generally produces the best results, aligning with
our initial findings. We expect these findings to spark further research in the
area of multi-task model-based reinforcement learning. We have made our code and
data available at https://github.com/stratorus/mtmbl.

Building upon these results, we formally demonstrate that any formal system rich enough to capture basic mathematical truths and possessing the properties established by these theorems, inevitably suffers from inherent contradictions and its own limitations, thereby underscoring the inherent shortcomings of such systems. Additionally, we explore potential applications and contributions to the broader discussion on the limitations of formal systems in mathematics. For clarity, the original texts and their proofs are provided in an appendix for reference. Moreover, a companion paper presents an exploration of potential extensions to these results. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Our research demonstrated the capability of using artificial intelligence for this task, as well as identified potential applications including using multiple views to calculate the 3D structure of objects and establishing a baseline for future work in this area. The code and data used in the study have been made publicly available.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Lastly, we provide examples demonstrating the applicability of these conditions to various systems.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Another screen, located at a distance of about 2.56 parsecs, exhibits a more indefinite shape and is positioned near the tangent point of the Sun's motion across the sky in the second quadrant. Both screens provide valuable insights into the structure of the interstellar medium in the solar system, particularly in the Second Solar Neighborhood. Furthermore, the detection of a small screen with a short spacial scale, associated with a narrow scintillation pattern, has been found for the first time. The screen's characteristics, including its size, orientation, and location within the interstellar medium, are discussed in the context of previous findings and existing theoretical models. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Compared to the current state-of-the-art speech synthesis model, Transform Domain Hidden Markov Model (THMM), QPNet achieves a significant improvement in subjective quality and is on a par with it in terms of naturalness. namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This choice of gauge also enables us to derive a formal solution to the singular boundary value problem that arises when solving for the mass term in linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge framework.  Interestingly, one of the implications of using this specific harmonic gauge is that the mass term can be expressed solely in terms of the harmonic gauge parameter, without needing to refer to the particular harmonic gauge choice explicitly.  Instead, it can be represented by a universal, symmetric second-order harmonic gauge operator that is applied to the mass term itself.  This discovery, in turn, leads to a significant advancement in our understanding of the boundary value problem in linearized gravity.  Furthermore, using this new perspective, we are able to solve the long-standing problem of the mass term in linearized gravity, at least in a formal sense, and find that the solution to the boundary value problem depends solely on a universal harmonic gauge operator that acts on the mass term itself, thereby rendering the specific harmonic gauge choice irrelevant.  This finding allows us to derive a new fundamental formula that connects the mass term to the harmonic gauge parameter in a general sense, and we are able to apply this formula to derive the mass term for not only the gravitational perturbation but also for the gravitational field itself.  Interestingly, this results in a mass term that is identical to the well-known Fierz-Pauli theory, despite being derived through a different approach.  Finally, we also explore other harmonic gauge choices that arise within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field and investigate their implications for the mass term in linearized gravity.  In particular, we find that certain choices of harmonic gauge can be utilized to generate a wide range of mass terms, including those with both scalar and tensor components, thus providing a linearized gravity framework in which the nature of the mass term can be manipulated freely.  Consequently, this feature enables us to propose a linearized gravity model that incorporates a finite, non-zero mass term for the gravitational perturbation

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. It is available online to facilitate the training and testing of cutting-edge deep learning models, thereby accelerating progress in this area. For convenience, we've included a baseline model trained on UniToPatho to facilitate comparison with future methods. This baseline model has been trained with a modified version of the popular ResNet architecture, specifically tailored to process patch-sized images while employing multi-task training to grade adenomas. The resulting model achieves impressive accuracy levels of 96% for polyp vs. normal tissue classification and adenoma vs. carcinoma grading, as evidenced by a mean average precision of 0.76 across all difficulty levels as defined by the Adenoma/Carcinoma Classification System. Notably, this study introduces a novel approach to initializing feature extractors, a problem previously resolved through transfer learning. The code and trained model have been made available online at the specified repository. UniToPatho addresses the current shortage of large, annotated datasets for deep learning-based colorectal polyp characterization, thereby propelling the field forward. A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency. In such cases, more advanced methods would likely be required to achieve meaningful results within a reasonable computational timeframe. A further discussion on this issue is presented in the paper's appendix. The developed code is publicly available under the GNU Public License for General Public Use and can be accessed via GitHub at https://github.com/ChristofPfeil/FrontTrack_FFT3D. A corresponding demo movie has also been created and can be viewed at https://youtu.be/ox1s5q3s8dk. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. These advances contribute to our understanding of zero-shot learning in speech-to-text and pave the way for the deployment of multilingual speech-to-text systems. Additionally, they facilitate the development of systems capable of handling language pairs that weren't encountered during training. This enables faster adaptation to new languages and a significant decrease in the required data for new language adaptations. This methodology is applicable to a wide range of speech-to-text applications, including dialect transformation and language learning support. This work is the first to explore zero-shot learning in speech-to-text and it outperforms direct speech-to-text approaches even with the availability of labeled data, confirming our initial hypotheses. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Moreover, we investigate the connection between the simplest scoto-seesaw model and the Koba-Nishijima law, finding that this law remains intact despite the presence of additional fermion generations. Lastly, we explore the possibilities of detecting this model through the production of high-energy vector bosons at the LHC. Specifically, we identify the most suitable channels and ranges for relevant dimensionless couplings. This study provides an exhaustive analysis of the simplest scoto-seesaw model's theoretical and phenomenological aspects.

Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. For example, in the widely-studied $d^1$ series, where an extra $e_g$ electron compared to the $d^0$ series may seemingly trivially shift the balance between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ levels, our study shows that the actual $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing remains negligible until intermediate electron-electron coupling is removed. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. This research is relevant to other applications of the Helsing-Ojala method, such as computing the Laplace operator and evaluating the Moulton fractional integral. Our algorithm is part of a forthcoming paper that generalizes it to higher-dimensional space. The code used in this paper can be found at https://git.io/.JgCnM. Overall, this paper offers an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials, leading to comparable computational costs for near and far field interactions on an unstructured grid. This advancement is key to tackling complex volume integration efficiently in Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Due to its higher order, this method also provides a smooth function approximation over a grid cell, which can be an accurate solution to a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices when the function is low-dimensional and smooth. Additionally, this method enables comparable computational costs for near and far field interactions on an unstructured grid, which can also benefit other applications of the Helsing-Ojala method. This research can be a important step in addressing various numerical challenges involving complex volume integration, high-order approximations, and boundary integration. Furthermore, this method is highly versatile and can be applied to a broad range of problems, including the computation of the Laplace operator, the Moulton fractional integral, and the Helmholtz equation.
